docs.text: Name What it does Example PageNAND flash organisation · Concept · Current · Beginner Smallest unit NAND can read or program, typically 16 KB plus spare bytes; it is programmed once between erases. When Zoe saves a 4 KB note, her SSD buffers it with other data to fill a 16 KB page before programming. BlockNAND flash organisation · Concept · Current · Beginner Group of hundreds or thousands of pages erased together; the erase unit and the unit in which wear accumulates. Changing one page means writing the new data to a fresh page and later erasing its whole old block during garbage collection. PlaneNAND flash organisation · Component · Current · Intermediate Independent section of a die with its own page buffer, allowing parallel reads and programs across planes on one die. A four-plane die programs four pages at once, roughly quadrupling that die's write bandwidth. Die (LUN)NAND flash organisation · Component · Current · Intermediate One piece of NAND silicon, the basic unit a controller addresses; leading 2026 dies hold about 1-2 terabits. A 2 Tb QLC die stores 256 GB, so a 4 TB QLC SSD needs only sixteen dies. Die stacking in a packageKioxia, Samsung, SK hynix, Micron, Sandisk · Component · Current · Intermediate Several dies stacked and wired inside one BGA package; enterprise packages stack 16 or 32 dies to maximise capacity. Kioxia's 245.76 TB LC9 stacks 32 two-terabit QLC dies to put 8 TB in each package. Word line and bit lineNAND array wiring · Concept · Current · Advanced Word lines connect the gates of cells in a row, forming pages; bit lines connect strings of cells to sense amplifiers. In 3D NAND each stacked layer is a word line, so a 321-layer chip has about 321 active word lines per string. NAND stringNAND array wiring · Concept · Current · Advanced Series chain of cells sharing one channel; to read one cell, all others in the string are switched fully on. To read one cell, the chip puts a pass voltage on every other cell in its string so only the selected cell decides current flow. Spare (out-of-band) areaNAND page layout · Concept · Current · Intermediate Extra bytes per page outside user data, holding ECC parity and controller metadata such as logical addresses and sequence numbers. After a crash, SSD firmware scans spare areas to rebuild which logical block each physical page holds. Bad block managementSSD and flash controller firmware · Concept · Current · Intermediate Firmware tracking factory-marked and worn-out blocks, retiring them and redirecting data to spare blocks. A USB stick keeps reporting full capacity for years while its controller quietly retires blocks that fail to erase. ONFIOpen NAND Flash Interface workgroup (Micron, SK hynix and others) · Standard · Current · Advanced Industry standard for the NAND die interface: commands, timing, parameter pages and high-speed NV-DDR bus modes. A controller reads a die's ONFI parameter page at start-up to learn its page size, block count and supported bus speed. Toggle-mode DDRSamsung and Kioxia; aligned with ONFI in JEDEC JESD230 · Interface · Current · Advanced High-speed NAND bus used by Samsung and Kioxia dies; JEDEC's JESD230 helps controllers support both Toggle and ONFI parts. Controller vendors support both bus types so one controller design can be paired with Kioxia, Micron or SK hynix NAND. Channels and interleavingSSD controller architecture · Concept · Current · Intermediate Controller buses each shared by several dies; the controller overlaps operations on different dies to multiply throughput. An eight-channel client controller with four dies per channel keeps 32 dies busy at once during a big file copy. Raw NAND with MTD and UBILinux MTD subsystem, UBI and UBIFS · Software · Current · Advanced Linux layers that manage bare NAND chips without a controller, doing wear levelling, ECC and bad-block handling in software. A home router's firmware keeps its root file system on raw SPI NAND using UBI volumes and the UBIFS file system.

docs.title: 3.3 SLC, MLC, TLC, QLC and PLC: Bits per Cell
docs.text:
Each flash cell can hold one to five bits by splitting its threshold voltage into 2, 4, 8, 16 or 32 levels. More bits per cell means cheaper, denser storage, but the levels get squeezed closer together, so the cell writes more slowly, wears out sooner and is more sensitive to leakage.

Voltage states each cell must hold. Every extra bit doubles the number of voltage levels squeezed into the same window.

Think of it like…

Like marking a glass of water: with one line (more or less than half full) anyone can read it at a glance; with sixteen lines you need a steady hand to fill it and a careful eye to read it, and a little evaporation causes a misreading.

Real-world example

Fictional Northwind Media buys 61.44 TB QLC SSDs for its video library, which is read constantly but rarely rewritten, and TLC SSDs for its busy database. QLC stores 4 bits per cell versus TLC's 3 — a third more data from the same silicon — but its endurance and sustained write speed are lower, which suits read-heavy data.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. SLC — 1 bit, 2 states: fastest and toughest; now mainly a write cache and an industrial option.
  2. MLC — 2 bits, 4 states: mainstream until the mid-2010s, now a niche.
  3. TLC — 3 bits, 8 states: the 2026 mainstream for client and performance data-centre SSDs.
  4. QLC — 4 bits, 16 states: cheaper and denser; for read-heavy and very high-capacity drives.
  5. PLC — 5 bits, 32 states: demonstrated in prototypes, not a mainstream product in 2026.
  6. Each extra bit doubles the states but adds less density: TLC to QLC is +33%, QLC to PLC only +25%.

Who uses it

SSD product managers, storage architects choosing drives, buyers comparing datasheets, and firmware engineers tuning read voltages.

Key takeaway

Remember states = 2^bits and the shrinking reward: SLC to MLC doubles density, but QLC to PLC adds only 25% while halving the voltage margin again.

Going deeper

  • Reading TLC can need up to seven reference voltages and QLC fifteen; Gray coding arranges states so neighbouring levels differ by one bit, so a slight drift corrupts only one bit.
  • Approximate rated P/E cycles vary by vendor: SLC tens of thousands, MLC several thousand, TLC roughly 1,000-3,000, and QLC from several hundred to around 1,500, stretched by strong LDPC error correction.
  • QLC program times are several times longer than TLC; drives hide this behind an SLC cache, so a consumer QLC drive's sustained write speed can fall to a few hundred MB/s once the cache fills.
  • pSLC (pseudo-SLC) mode runs TLC or QLC NAND storing only one bit per cell, trading two-thirds or more of the capacity for much higher endurance — common in industrial and automotive parts.
  • Solidigm showed a PLC SSD prototype in 2022 and Kioxia has published PLC research, but 2026's highest-capacity drives still rely on QLC rather than PLC.
  • A TLC word line holds lower, middle and upper pages; each page type needs a different set of reference voltages, so read latency differs depending on which page is read.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming QLC is simply 'bad': for read-heavy data it offers excellent cost per terabyte; the weakness is sustained heavy writing.
  • Judging a drive by its burst speed alone: many consumer QLC drives slow sharply once their SLC cache is full.
  • Taking 'MLC' on a datasheet to always mean two bits: some vendors used 'MLC' for any multi-level cell, such as '3-bit MLC'; check bits per cell.

docs.title: Try it: States and read reference voltages per cell type
docs.text:
for bits, name in [(1,'SLC'),(2,'MLC'),(3,'TLC'),(4,'QLC'),(5,'PLC')]:
    states = 2 ** bits
    print(f"{name}: {bits} bit(s), {states} states, {states-1} read reference voltages")

docs.text: Name What it does Example SLC NANDAll NAND makers · Technology · Current · Beginner One bit per cell with two voltage states: fastest writes, highest endurance and best retention, at the highest cost per bit. A fictional factory logs sensor data to SLC industrial microSD cards rated for tens of thousands of P/E cycles. MLC NANDAll NAND makers · Technology · Legacy · Beginner Two bits per cell with four states; the consumer mainstream until TLC took over in the second half of the 2010s. Samsung's 850 PRO (2014) and 970 PRO used 2-bit MLC; its 980 PRO (2020) moved the PRO line to TLC. TLC NANDAll NAND makers · Technology · Current · Beginner Three bits per cell with eight states; the 2026 default for laptops, desktops and performance data-centre SSDs. Samsung's 990 PRO and most 2026 laptop SSDs use TLC, balancing speed, endurance and cost. QLC NANDAll NAND makers · Technology · Current · Beginner Four bits per cell with sixteen states; the cheapest, densest NAND, best for read-heavy and huge-capacity drives. Crucial's P3 and Intel's 670p were popular QLC consumer drives; data-centre QLC now reaches 122.88 TB and 245.76 TB per drive. PLC NANDSolidigm and Kioxia research · Technology · Emerging · Intermediate Five bits per cell with thirty-two states; denser still, but with tiny voltage margins, slow writes and low endurance. Solidigm demonstrated a PLC SSD prototype in 2022; makers see it first suiting read-mostly, archive-like data. pSLC modeIndustrial and automotive flash vendors · Technology · Current · Intermediate Running TLC or QLC NAND at one bit per cell, sacrificing capacity for far higher endurance and reliability. An automotive supplier sets a TLC eMMC to pSLC mode for a dashcam, cutting capacity to a third but greatly raising endurance. Gray codeBit-to-state mapping in multi-level cells · Concept · Current · Advanced Assigns bit patterns to voltage states so that neighbouring states differ by only one bit, limiting damage from small drift. In TLC, adjacent states such as 011 and 001 differ in one bit, so a slight drift creates a single bit error that ECC easily fixes. Read reference voltages and read-retrySSD controller firmware · Concept · Current · Advanced Voltages a die compares against to decide each cell's state; read-retry shifts them to compensate for drift and wear. When an aged page fails ECC, the controller retries with shifted reference voltages, adding latency but recovering the data. Page read time (tR)NAND datasheet parameter · Metric · Current · Intermediate Time for a die to sense a page into its buffer: tens of microseconds for TLC, noticeably longer for QLC. A 4 KB random read on an NVMe SSD takes very roughly 50-100 microseconds end to end, mostly NAND read time. Page program time (tPROG)NAND datasheet parameter · Metric · Current · Intermediate Time to program a page: a few hundred microseconds for TLC, and longer again for QLC because of finer voltage steps. QLC's long program time is why drives write incoming data to an SLC cache first and fold it into QLC later. Bit density (Gb/mm²)Analyst measure (e.g., TechInsights) · Metric · Current · Advanced Bits stored per square millimetre of die; the real cost metric for comparing NAND generations, better than layer count. TechInsights measured YMTC's 294-layer TLC at about 19.8 Gb/mm², comparable with SK hynix parts of the same era. Lower, middle and upper pagesMulti-level cell page mapping · Concept · Current · Advanced In TLC, each word line stores three logical pages; reading some page types needs more reference voltages and takes longer. Latency tests on a TLC drive show a spread of read times partly because some reads hit slower page types.

docs.title: 3.4 3D NAND and the 2026 Layer Race
docs.text:
Around 2013 flash makers stopped shrinking cells sideways and began stacking them vertically. Modern 3D NAND stacks more than 300 active layers of cells, threaded by vertical 'channel holes', with the control circuits built underneath the array or on a separate wafer bonded on top.

The 3D NAND layer race. Layer counts rose from 24 to over 400 in about thirteen years.

Think of it like…

Planar NAND was a town of bungalows that ran out of land; 3D NAND builds skyscrapers, with lift shafts (channel holes) running through every floor.

Real-world example

Ana compares two 1 TB SSDs. A 2016 model with 48-layer NAND needed 32 dies of 256 Gb each. A 2026 QLC model built from 2 Tb dies needs just four. Same capacity, one-eighth the dies — which is why flash keeps getting cheaper per terabyte over time, even though small drives lose some parallelism.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Deposit alternating thin films hundreds of times to build a tall stack.
  2. Etch deep, narrow channel holes through the whole stack — the hardest and costliest step.
  3. Line each hole with blocking oxide, charge-trap nitride, tunnel oxide and a polysilicon channel, forming a vertical string of cells.
  4. Cut a 'staircase' at the edges so each layer (word line) can be wired out.
  5. Stack two or three decks when a single etch cannot go deep enough.
  6. Place logic under the array (CuA/PUC) or build it on a separate wafer and bond the two (Xtacking, CBA).

Who uses it

Semiconductor process engineers, equipment makers such as Lam Research, Tokyo Electron and Applied Materials, industry analysts and anyone tracking SSD cost trends.

Key takeaway

Know the vocabulary — layers (word lines), decks (string stacking), CMOS-under-array and wafer bonding — and remember that layer count alone does not equal density.

Going deeper

  • Layer counts are reported differently: YMTC's 294-layer part has about 232 active word-line layers, so compare active layers and bit density rather than headline numbers.
  • String stacking joins two or three separately etched decks; Micron's 232- and 276-layer NAND use this because a single channel-hole etch through every layer would be too deep and tapered.
  • CMOS under Array (Micron), or peri-under-cell (SK hynix's '4D NAND'), puts page buffers and logic beneath the cell stack, shrinking die area compared with logic beside the array.
  • Wafer bonding — YMTC's Xtacking since 2018, Kioxia and Sandisk's CBA from BiCS8, and Samsung's V10 — builds logic and memory on separate optimised wafers and bonds them face to face.
  • Reports in mid-2026 said Samsung's 286-layer V9 made up most of its NAND output while 400-plus-layer V10 was under 5%, with a 400-500-layer V11 in trial production.
  • Kioxia's 332-layer BiCS10 is reported to be about 59% denser than its 218-layer BiCS8, with volume output planned within its fiscal 2026 (April 2026 to March 2027).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing layer counts across vendors as if equal: dummy layers, deck counts and hole spacing differ, so bit density is the fairer measure.
  • Assuming more layers automatically means a faster SSD: interface speed, planes and the controller matter more for performance.
  • Thinking 3D NAND uses ever-tinier cells: 3D cells are physically larger than late planar cells, which helped endurance.

docs.title: Try it: How many NAND dies make a 4 TB SSD? (approximate)
docs.text:
# 4 TB = 32,000 gigabits (decimal); die sizes in gigabits
for die_gbit in (256, 512, 1024, 2048):
    print(f"{die_gbit:>5} Gbit dies -> ~{round(32000 / die_gbit)} dies")

Equipment makers such as Lam Research market cryogenic etch tools for channel holes in 300-plus-layer NAND. String stacking (decks)Micron, SK hynix, Samsung and others · Concept · Current · Advanced Building a 3D NAND stack as two or three separately etched decks joined together, so holes need not span every layer at once. CMOS under Array (CuA / PUC)Micron, SK hynix ('4D NAND') · Technology · Current · Advanced Placing the die's control logic and page buffers beneath the memory array instead of beside it, shrinking die area. Wafer bonding (CBA / hybrid bonding)Kioxia and Sandisk, YMTC, Samsung V10 · Technology · Current · Advanced Making logic and memory on separate wafers and bonding them with dense copper connections, optimising each process. Kioxia and Sandisk's BiCS8 uses CMOS directly Bonded to Array (CBA) to speed up the NAND interface. Staircase contacts3D NAND manufacturing · Concept · Current · Advanced Stepped edge structure exposing each word-line layer for its own vertical contact; it grows as layers are added. Designers fight to shrink staircase area because every extra layer needs its own step and contact. Lateral scaling3D NAND design · Concept · Current · Advanced Raising density by tightening the spacing of channel holes and removing dummy structures, instead of only adding layers. Because each new layer adds deposition and etch time, vendors combine more layers with tighter hole spacing. 1,000-layer roadmapsIndustry roadmaps (e.g., Samsung) · Concept · Emerging · Intermediate Long-range plans to approach around 1,000 layers by about 2030 using more decks, bonding and new materials. Industry reports in 2024 described Samsung targeting roughly 1,000-layer NAND by 2030.

docs.title: 3.5 NOR Flash: Boot Code, Firmware and Execute-in-Place
docs.text:
NOR flash is NAND's sibling. Its cells are wired in parallel, so any byte can be read quickly and directly, which suits code a processor runs at power-on: PC firmware, microcontroller programs and car electronics. It is far less dense and costs much more per bit than NAND, so it is sold in megabits to a few gigabits.

NOR vs NAND flash

NOR flash NAND flash Cell wiring Parallel to bit lines Series strings Random read Fast, byte-level Page-level, tens of µs Write and erase Slow Fast Cost per bit High Very low Typical size 1 Mbit - 2 Gbit Up to ~2 Tbit per die Main use Boot code, XIP firmware SSDs, phones, cards

NOR trades density for fast random reads; NAND trades random access for low cost per bit.

Think of it like…

NAND is a warehouse where you fetch whole pallets; NOR is a reference shelf where you can grab any single book instantly — perfect for quick lookups, too expensive to store everything.

Real-world example

When Diego's desktop powers on, the processor starts executing UEFI firmware fetched from a 32 MB SPI NOR chip on the motherboard. Because NOR allows random reads, early boot code runs straight from the chip before the system's DRAM is even initialised.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. NOR cells connect in parallel to bit lines, so each can be read individually with low latency.
  2. Reads are random-access; serial NOR streams code quickly over Quad or Octal SPI.
  3. Writes program individual bytes or pages, but erasing still works in sectors, typically 4 KB to 256 KB.
  4. Most NOR today uses serial buses: SPI, Quad SPI and Octal SPI (JEDEC xSPI).
  5. Execute-in-place (XIP) lets a CPU fetch instructions straight from NOR without copying them to RAM.

Who uses it

Embedded firmware engineers, motherboard and BIOS developers, automotive and IoT hardware designers, and security researchers studying firmware.

Key takeaway

One-line answer: NOR = fast random reads and execute-in-place for code; NAND = dense, cheap, page-based storage for data.

Going deeper

  • Serial NOR in 2026 ranges from about 1 Mbit to 2 Gbit; JEDEC's xSPI (JESD251) Octal interface running double-data-rate reaches several hundred megabytes per second for fast boot.
  • Typical NOR datasheets promise around 100,000 erase cycles per sector and about 20 years of retention, far above TLC NAND, which suits rarely updated firmware.
  • Automotive NOR is qualified to AEC-Q100 and often supports ISO 26262 functional-safety designs, because instrument clusters and driver-assistance controllers boot from it.
  • Major NOR suppliers include Winbond, Macronix, GigaDevice and Infineon (which acquired Cypress and its Spansion NOR line); Micron also sells serial NOR.
  • Microcontrollers embed NOR-type flash on chip, but it becomes hard to scale below roughly 28 nm, pushing chipmakers toward embedded MRAM, RRAM or PCM for newer nodes.
  • SPI NAND competes with NOR in routers and IoT above about 1 Gbit, offering cheaper bits but needing ECC and bad-block handling that NOR does not.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using NOR as bulk storage: per bit it costs many times more than NAND; keep it for code and small configuration data.
  • Assuming execute-in-place code runs as fast as code in RAM: NOR latency is higher, so microcontrollers add caches in front of XIP flash.
  • Forgetting that programming can only change 1s to 0s: restoring 1s always needs a sector erase.

docs.title: 3.6 Anatomy of an SSD: Controller, NAND, DRAM/HMB and Firmware
docs.text:
An SSD is a small computer. A controller chip with its own processor cores runs firmware that manages many NAND flash chips, usually helped by DRAM (or some borrowed host memory) that holds the drive's address map. It talks to the PC over NVMe or SATA and hides all of flash's awkward rules behind a simple 'read block, write block' interface.

Inside an SSD. The controller sits at the centre, juggling host commands, NAND channels, memory and background tasks.

Think of it like…

The SSD is a library: NAND chips are the shelves, the controller is the librarian, the DRAM is the librarian's card index, and the firmware is the rulebook the librarian follows.

Real-world example

Mei inspects a 2 TB M.2 NVMe drive: one controller under a thermal pad, four NAND packages, one 2 GB DRAM chip and small power regulators. The controller tracks where every 4 KB of her data lives — a map of about 2 GB for 2 TB of flash — which is why the drive carries 2 GB of DRAM.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The host sends read and write commands over NVMe (PCIe) or SATA to the controller.
  2. Controller cores and hardware engines translate logical addresses to physical NAND locations using the FTL map.
  3. Writes land in a fast buffer (DRAM or an SLC cache), then are programmed across many dies in parallel.
  4. Every page passes through LDPC error correction and, usually, AES-256 encryption on its way to and from NAND.
  5. Background firmware runs garbage collection, wear levelling, data refresh and thermal management.
  6. Power circuits — and capacitors in enterprise drives — keep everything consistent if power fails.

Who uses it

SSD firmware and hardware engineers, PC builders, data-centre hardware engineers and technicians diagnosing slow or failing drives.

Key takeaway

Rule of thumb: a 4 KB page-mapped FTL needs about 1 GB of DRAM per 1 TB of flash (a 4-byte entry per 4 KB), which is why DRAM-less drives use HMB and huge drives use bigger mapping units.

Going deeper

  • Controllers typically combine several ARM Cortex-R real-time cores with fixed-function engines for LDPC, encryption and data movement; enterprise controllers add more cores and 16 or more NAND channels.
  • DRAM-less SSDs use NVMe's Host Memory Buffer, added in NVMe 1.2, borrowing typically tens of megabytes of host RAM to cache the hottest parts of the mapping table.
  • Very large QLC drives use mapping units (indirection units) of 16 KB or more instead of 4 KB, cutting DRAM needs fourfold or more but penalising small random writes.
  • Dynamic SLC caching writes incoming data at one bit per cell into free TLC/QLC blocks, then folds it into full-density blocks later; the cache shrinks as the drive fills.
  • PCIe Gen5 controllers can draw several watts and thermally throttle; many Gen5 M.2 drives ship with heatsinks, and some early Gen5 drives even used small fans.
  • Firmware matters: in 2023 Samsung released firmware fixes for 980 PRO and 990 PRO drives whose health readings were dropping abnormally fast.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Never updating SSD firmware: firmware bugs have caused data loss and premature wear, so check the vendor tool periodically.
  • Assuming DRAM-less always means slow: with HMB many DRAM-less Gen4 drives are fine for everyday use, though weaker under heavy mixed loads.
  • Believing the advertised speed lasts for any size of copy: SLC cache exhaustion and thermal throttling both cut sustained speed.

docs.title: Try it: Identify your SSD and its Host Memory Buffer request
docs.text:
# Linux (nvme-cli): model, firmware, HMB preferred/minimum size

docs.title: 3.7 The Flash Translation Layer: Garbage Collection, Wear Levelling, Over-provisioning and TRIM
docs.text:
Because flash cannot overwrite in place and wears out, every SSD runs a Flash Translation Layer (FTL) — firmware that pretends to be a simple disk. It writes new data to fresh pages, keeps a map of where everything really is, cleans up stale pages in the background and spreads wear evenly. Hidden spare space and the TRIM command help it work efficiently.

Life of a page under the FTL. Pages are never overwritten; they are invalidated, collected and erased in whole blocks.

Think of it like…

The FTL is a hotel receptionist: returning guests (data) never get their old room back; they get any clean room, the guest list is updated, and housekeeping (garbage collection) cleans vacated rooms — spare rooms (over-provisioning) make the job much easier.

Real-world example

Leo's 1 TB SSD is 90% full and he repeatedly re-saves a large video project. With little free space, the FTL must copy many still-valid pages out of each block before erasing it, so 10 GB written by Leo might cause around 25 GB of NAND writes — a write amplification factor of 2.5. Freeing space and letting TRIM run brings it closer to 1.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The host writes logical block address X; the FTL puts it in the next free page and updates the map entry for X.
  2. The page that held the old copy of X is marked invalid (stale).
  3. When free blocks run low, garbage collection picks blocks with mostly stale pages, copies their valid pages elsewhere and erases them.
  4. Wear levelling steers writes, and sometimes moves cold data, so all blocks age at a similar rate.
  5. TRIM / UNMAP / Deallocate tells the SSD which addresses the file system no longer uses, so GC can skip them.
  6. Write amplification = NAND writes ÷ host writes; over-provisioning and TRIM keep it low.

Who uses it

SSD firmware developers, storage performance engineers, database and file-system developers, and anyone sizing SSDs for write-heavy work.

Key takeaway

Memorise WAF = bytes written to NAND ÷ bytes written by the host: about 1 for sequential writes, and well above 3 for small random writes on a nearly full drive.

Going deeper

  • Page-level mapping keeps one entry per logical page (usually 4 KB) for the best random-write performance; early low-cost controllers used block or hybrid mapping to save RAM, with much worse random writes.
  • Greedy garbage collection picks blocks with the fewest valid pages; cost-benefit policies also weigh data age so cold blocks are cleaned less often, reducing copying.
  • Static wear levelling moves rarely changed data off lightly worn blocks so they can absorb new writes; dynamic wear levelling only chooses among blocks that are already free.
  • About 4 TiB (4.40 TB) of raw NAND sold as 3.84 TB leaves roughly 15% spare; sold as 3.2 TB 'mixed-use' it leaves about 37%, cutting WAF for random writes.
  • ATA TRIM, SCSI UNMAP and NVMe Deallocate are the same idea in three protocols; Linux can trim continuously with the discard mount option or periodically with fstrim, the usual desktop default.
  • NVMe reports host 'Data Units Written'; comparing it with media-write counters, such as the OCP datacenter log's physical media units written, reveals a drive's real write amplification.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Defragmenting an SSD: it adds writes for no benefit; Windows' Optimize Drives sends TRIM to SSDs instead.
  • Filling an SSD to 99%: garbage collection has little room, so speed and lifespan suffer; leave 10-20% free on client drives.
  • Expecting deleted files to be recoverable from an SSD: after TRIM the drive may return zeros, defeating most recovery tools.
  • Treating TRIM as secure deletion: it only marks blocks unused; use the drive's sanitise or crypto-erase commands instead.

docs.title: Try it: Check and run TRIM
docs.text:
# Linux
lsblk --discard                 # non-zero DISC-GRAN/DISC-MAX = TRIM supported
sudo fstrim -av                 # trim all mounted file systems that support it
systemctl status fstrim.timer   # weekly TRIM on most distributions

# Windows (admin)
fsutil behavior query DisableDeleteNotify   # 0 = TRIM enabled
Optimize-Volume -DriveLetter C -ReTrim -Verbose

Ubuntu enables fstrim.timer by default, trimming SSDs once a week. Mei runs Optimize-Volume -ReTrim after deleting 300 GB of old game installs. A benchmark preconditions an enterprise SSD with hours of random writes before recording its steady-state IOPS.

docs.title: 3.8 Endurance and Data Retention: P/E Cycles, TBW, DWPD and JESD218
docs.text:
Every flash cell wears a little each time it is erased, so SSDs carry an endurance rating: total terabytes written (TBW) or drive writes per day (DWPD) over the warranty. Separately, retention describes how long data survives without power. Worn cells hold their charge for less time, and heat speeds up the leakage.

JEDEC JESD218 client vs enterprise SSD classes

Client Enterprise Active use 8 h/day at 40°C 24 h/day at 55°C Power-off retention 1 year at 30°C 3 months at 40°C Max UBER ≤ 1 in 10^15 bits ≤ 1 in 10^16 bits Functional failures ≤ 3% ≤ 3% Test workload JESD219 client JESD219 enterprise

Retention figures apply at the end of rated life, not to a new drive.

Think of it like…

Like a rubber band: you can stretch it thousands of times, but it slowly loses its snap — and a worn band left in a hot car sags much faster than a new one.

Real-world example

Sara compares two drives. Drive A, 3.84 TB at 1 DWPD for five years, allows about 7 PB of writes (3.84 TB a day). Drive B, 3.2 TB at 3 DWPD, allows about 17.5 PB (9.6 TB a day). Her logging cluster writes 6 TB per drive per day, so she chooses Drive B despite its smaller capacity.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. P/E cycle rating: how many times each block can be erased and rewritten while still meeting specification.
  2. TBW: total host terabytes that may be written during the warranty.
  3. DWPD = TBW ÷ (capacity × 365 × warranty years) — how many full-drive writes per day the rating allows.
  4. Retention: how long data stays readable unpowered once the drive reaches rated wear, at a stated temperature.
  5. The drive reports wear, e.g., NVMe 'Percentage Used'; 100% means rated endurance is used up, not instant failure.
  6. While powered, firmware scans and rewrites ageing data in the background to fight charge loss.

Who uses it

Storage architects sizing drives, procurement teams, reliability engineers and anyone tempted to keep data on an SSD in a drawer.

Key takeaway

Learn the conversion: DWPD = TBW ÷ (capacity in TB × 365 × years); 1 DWPD on a 3.84 TB five-year drive is about 7 PB of writes.

Going deeper

  • JEDEC JESD218 defines how SSD endurance is rated and JESD219 defines the client and enterprise workloads used to test it; a TBW rating is valid only if retention and error-rate limits are still met afterwards.
  • Retention falls steeply as storage temperature rises, an Arrhenius effect: a worn drive kept warm can lose data far sooner than its rating, while cool storage extends retention.
  • A fresh SSD typically keeps data for many years unpowered; JESD218's one-year (client) and three-month (enterprise) figures describe drives at the end of rated wear, which is why worn drives make poor archives.
  • Data-centre classes: read-intensive about 1 DWPD, mixed-use about 3 DWPD, write-intensive 10 DWPD or more; very large QLC drives are often well under 1 DWPD and may quote separate sequential and random ratings.
  • Samsung's 990 PRO 2 TB is rated 1,200 TBW over five years — about 0.33 DWPD — which is still more than most home users write in decades.
  • NVMe's Percentage Used can exceed 100%; many drives keep working, but some switch to read-only mode at end of life to protect the data already stored.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating TBW as a cliff edge: drives usually outlive their rating, but the warranty ends and retention guarantees weaken.
  • Using an old SSD in a drawer as a long-term archive: worn, unpowered flash can lose data; use HDD, tape or refreshed copies.
  • Comparing DWPD across drives with different warranty lengths: convert both to TBW first.

docs.title: Try it: Convert TBW to DWPD and check real wear
docs.text:
def dwpd(tbw, cap_tb, years=5):
    return tbw / (cap_tb * 365 * years)

print(round(dwpd(1200, 2.0), 2))   # 2 TB consumer drive rated 1,200 TBW -> ~0.33
print(round(dwpd(7008, 3.84), 2))  # 3.84 TB data-centre drive -> 1.0

# Linux: see percentage_used and data_units_written
# sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0

docs.title: 3.9 Power-Loss Protection and Data Integrity
docs.text:
SSDs often tell the computer 'done' while new data still sits in a fast, volatile buffer. If power is cut at that moment, the data — or worse, the drive's own mapping tables — can be lost. Enterprise SSDs carry capacitors that keep them alive for a few milliseconds to flush everything safely; consumer drives rely on the operating system sending flush commands.

A power cut with power-loss protection. Capacitors give the controller just enough time to make acknowledged writes durable.

Think of it like…

It's like a waiter who says 'order placed!' before reaching the kitchen — fine unless he trips. Power-loss protection gives the waiter an emergency torch and just enough time to reach the kitchen.

Real-world example

Fictional Harbour Bank runs PostgreSQL. A power supply fails instantly during a storm; its enterprise NVMe drives use their capacitors to flush in-flight writes, so every committed transaction survives. A test server with consumer SSDs also survives because PostgreSQL issues flushes on commit — but it was running far slower, because each flush had to wait for NAND.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Host writes land in the SSD's DRAM or SRAM buffer and are acknowledged quickly.
  2. Without PLP, software must send FLUSH (or use FUA writes) to force data onto NAND; databases do this on every commit.
  3. Drives with PLP detect the supply voltage dropping and switch to energy stored in on-board capacitors.
  4. In those milliseconds the controller writes buffered data and mapping updates to NAND.
  5. At next power-up, firmware replays its journal and checks consistency before accepting I/O.

Who uses it

Database administrators, storage and server engineers, Ceph and hyperconverged storage operators, and embedded designers whose devices lose power abruptly.

Key takeaway

For databases, choose SSDs with full power-loss protection: they can safely acknowledge flushes from their buffer, giving much lower sync-write latency than consumer drives.

Going deeper

  • PLP hardware is usually a bank of tantalum or polymer capacitors, charged above the supply voltage to store enough energy for a full flush, sized with margin because capacitors lose capacity as they age.
  • Drives with full PLP can treat FLUSH as nearly free, cutting sync-write latency from milliseconds to tens of microseconds — the main reason databases and Ceph's write-ahead log favour enterprise SSDs.
  • Some client drives offer only protection for data at rest — guarding already-written data and mapping tables — not in-flight cached writes, so read the datasheet wording carefully.
  • NVMe exposes a Volatile Write Cache feature (ID 0x06) and a Force Unit Access bit; SATA uses FLUSH CACHE EXT; Linux's block layer issues these when file systems need ordering guarantees.
  • Losing power while programming an upper page can corrupt the already-written lower page sharing its word line in MLC/TLC NAND, a classic data-loss cause that PLP and careful firmware avoid.
  • End-to-end protection information (T10 PI, NVMe PI) adds 8 or more bytes of guard and reference tags per block so corruption anywhere between host and media is detected.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Disabling write barriers or flushes for speed on drives without PLP: a power cut can corrupt the file system or database.
  • Assuming a UPS replaces PLP: power-supply failures, cable pulls and server faults still cut drive power instantly.
  • Believing every 'enterprise-looking' M.2 drive has PLP: look for the capacitors and explicit datasheet wording.

docs.title: Try it: See whether your drive reports a volatile write cache (Linux)
docs.text:
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/write_cache        # 'write back' or 'write through'
sudo nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x06 -H     # Volatile Write Cache feature

docs.title: 3.10 Everyday Flash: eMMC, UFS, SD/microSD Express, CFexpress and USB Drives
docs.text:
Phones, tablets, cameras, game consoles and USB sticks all use NAND flash, packaged with their own small controllers. eMMC and UFS are chips soldered inside phones and low-cost laptops; SD and microSD cards and USB drives are removable. Newer formats borrow PCIe and NVMe from SSDs to go much faster.

Mobile and removable flash speeds. PCIe and faster M-PHY gears lifted phones and cards into SSD territory.

Think of it like…

Same flour, different bakeries: a phone gets a small dense loaf (UFS), a camera gets rolls you can swap (memory cards), and a USB stick is a sandwich to take away.

Real-world example

Aiko's new phone has 512 GB of UFS 4.1 storage. Her Nintendo Switch 2 needs a microSD Express card for games, so her old UHS-I card is now only good for screenshots. Her mirrorless camera records high-bitrate video to a CFexpress Type B card.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. eMMC: NAND and controller in one BGA package on an 8-bit parallel bus — half-duplex, up to about 400 MB/s.
  2. UFS: the same idea over serial MIPI M-PHY lanes, full duplex with command queuing — about 4 GB/s in UFS 4.x.
  3. SD/microSD: UHS-I bus up to 104 MB/s for most cards; SD Express adds a PCIe/NVMe mode.
  4. CFexpress: PCIe/NVMe cards for professional cameras (Type A and Type B).
  5. USB flash drives: a USB controller plus NAND, usually with no DRAM and simple firmware.
  6. Check speed-class logos (V30, V60, V90; A1, A2; E-classes) rather than headline 'up to' speeds.

Who uses it

Mobile and embedded engineers, camera operators and videographers, gamers, IT support staff and digital forensics examiners.

Key takeaway

Know the ladder: eMMC 5.1 ≈ 400 MB/s, UFS 4.x ≈ 4 GB/s, UFS 5.0 ≈ 10.8 GB/s target; microSD UHS-I 104 MB/s vs microSD Express ≈ 985 MB/s (PCIe Gen3) or up to 2 GB/s (Gen4).

Going deeper

  • eMMC 5.1 (JEDEC JESD84-B51, 2015) peaks with its HS400 mode at about 400 MB/s; it remains common in low-cost Chromebooks, TVs, cars and single-board computers.
  • UFS 4.0 (2022) uses MIPI M-PHY HS-Gear5 at 23.2 Gb/s per lane over two lanes; UFS 4.1 followed in late 2024, and UFS 5.0, reported published in early 2026, adds HS-Gear6 at up to 46.6 Gb/s per lane.
  • SD 7.0 (2018) added PCIe/NVMe 'SD Express' via a second pin row; SD 8.0 (2020) allowed PCIe Gen4 x2 for nearly 4 GB/s, and SD 9.1 (2023) raised microSD Express to 2 GB/s with E150-E600 speed classes.
  • Capacity families: SDHC up to 32 GB, SDXC up to 2 TB and SDUC up to 128 TB; 1 TB microSDXC cards are common, while SDUC cards remain rare.
  • Video speed classes guarantee minimum sustained writes (V30 = 30 MB/s, V60 = 60, V90 = 90); app classes guarantee random IOPS, A2 meaning at least 4,000 read and 2,000 write IOPS.
  • Nintendo's Switch 2 (2025) accepts only microSD Express cards for games; shipping cards use PCIe Gen3 x1, so they top out below the roughly 985 MB/s bus limit.
  • Apple's iPhones use Apple-designed NVMe-based storage rather than UFS, while most Android phones use UFS from Samsung, SK hynix, Kioxia, Micron or Sandisk.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Pairing a fast card with a slow reader: a microSD Express card falls back to UHS-I speeds in readers without PCIe support.
  • Trusting suspiciously cheap high-capacity USB sticks: fake-capacity devices report 2 TB but store a fraction, silently overwriting data.
  • Using ordinary cards for continuous recording in dashcams or CCTV: choose high-endurance cards rated for constant writing.

docs.title: 3.11 SSD Form Factors and PCIe Generations: M.2, U.2/U.3, EDSFF and Gen5/Gen6 Drives
docs.text:
SSDs come in several physical shapes. Laptops and desktops use thin M.2 'gum sticks'; servers used 2.5-inch U.2/U.3 drives and are moving to the purpose-built EDSFF family (E1.S, E1.L, E3.S, E3.L). Each PCIe generation roughly doubles bandwidth: a Gen5 x4 SSD reads about 14 GB/s, and the first Gen6 data-centre drives reach about 28 GB/s.

PCIe x4 bandwidth by generation. Each PCIe generation doubles the link rate; real drives reach a little below the link limit.

Think of it like…

M.2 is a shoebox sized to fit a laptop; EDSFF is a standard shipping container designed so a whole data-centre 'ship' can pack, cool and swap them easily.

Real-world example

Fictional Orbit Cloud is refreshing its AI storage servers. The old 2U servers had 24 front U.2 bays. The new design takes E3.S drives that hot-swap from the front, cool better and run PCIe Gen5 x4 at about 14 GB/s each, with Gen6 E3.S drives planned for the next refresh.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. M.2 cards are named by width and length — 2280 means 22 mm × 80 mm; M-key slots carry PCIe x4.
  2. U.2 (SFF-8639) is a 2.5-inch drive with PCIe x4; U.3 (SFF-TA-1001) lets one bay take SAS, SATA or NVMe.
  3. E1.S is a small 'ruler' for 1U servers, available in several thicknesses.
  4. E3.S and E3.L are 76 mm-tall drives for 2U servers, supporting x4 or x8, more power, and CXL devices too.
  5. E1.L and E3.L are long formats for maximum NAND per slot — 245.76 TB fits in E3.L.
  6. Approximate x4 link bandwidth: Gen3 3.9 GB/s, Gen4 7.9, Gen5 15.8, Gen6 about 30 GB/s, before protocol overhead.

Who uses it

PC builders, laptop designers, server and data-centre hardware engineers, and hyperscale platform teams.

Key takeaway

Decode an M.2 listing — '2280 M-key PCIe Gen4 x4 NVMe' gives size, connector key, PCIe generation, lane count and protocol; check all five before buying.

Going deeper

  • PCIe 6.0 (2022) doubles the rate to 64 GT/s using PAM4 signalling with fixed-size FLIT packets and lightweight forward error correction; PCIe 7.0 (128 GT/s) was released in 2025, so Gen7 SSDs are still ahead.
  • Micron's 9650, unveiled in July 2025 and reported in mass production in early 2026, was the first PCIe Gen6 data-centre SSD, quoting up to 28 GB/s reads and 5.5 million random-read IOPS in E1.S and E3.S.
  • Gen5 consumer drives such as Samsung's 9100 PRO (2025) read at about 14-15 GB/s; outside big file transfers most users notice little difference from a good Gen4 drive.
  • EDSFF sizes are SNIA SFF specifications: E1.S (SFF-TA-1006), E1.L (SFF-TA-1007) and E3 (SFF-TA-1008), all using the SFF-TA-1002 card-edge connector.
  • E3.S comes in 1T and 2T thicknesses with higher power budgets than M.2, roughly 25 W and 40 W, so Gen5 and Gen6 drives can run fast without throttling.
  • U.3 tri-mode backplanes let servers mix SAS, SATA and NVMe drives in the same bays via a tri-mode controller, easing transitions in enterprise servers.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming every M.2 slot supports NVMe: some older slots are SATA-only, and some share lanes with SATA ports or other slots.
  • Putting a Gen5 SSD in a Gen4 slot and expecting Gen5 speed: it works, but only at the slot's lower rate.
  • Ignoring cooling for Gen5 drives: without airflow or a heatsink they throttle heavily under sustained load.

docs.title: 3.12 Host-Guided Data Placement: ZNS, Flexible Data Placement and Open-Channel SSDs
docs.text:
A normal SSD hides flash's quirks but doesn't know which data will be deleted together, so it mixes them in the same blocks and later has to copy data during garbage collection. Zoned Namespaces (ZNS) and Flexible Data Placement (FDP) let the host group data with similar lifetimes, cutting write amplification, spare space and wear.

Conventional SSD vs ZNS vs FDP

Conventional ZNS FDP Host write rules Random anywhere Sequential within zones Random + optional hints Who does GC SSD Mostly the host SSD, guided by hints Old software works Yes No, must be zone-aware Yes Write amplification Higher on mixed data Near 1 Near 1 when used well Over-provisioning Highest Lowest Can be reduced NVMe work item Base spec TP 4053 (2020) TP 4146 (2022)

FDP keeps compatibility while capturing much of ZNS's write-amplification benefit.

Think of it like…

Instead of throwing all your groceries onto one fridge shelf and later picking out the expired items, you keep milk, vegetables and leftovers on separate shelves so each shelf can be cleared in one go.

Real-world example

Fictional streaming company Riverflix runs a large flash cache. It tags small-object writes and large-object writes with different FDP placement handles, so the SSD keeps them in separate blocks. When objects expire, whole blocks become invalid together, garbage collection has almost nothing to copy, and write amplification falls close to 1 — letting Riverflix use cheaper, lower-endurance drives.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. ZNS divides a namespace into zones that must be written sequentially and reset as a whole, mirroring NAND blocks.
  2. With ZNS, the host (file system or application) tracks write pointers and resets zones, taking over much of garbage collection.
  3. FDP keeps the normal random-write interface but lets the host attach a placement handle to each write.
  4. The SSD puts writes with the same handle into the same reclaim units, so data that dies together sits together.
  5. Hosts that ignore FDP still work unchanged — the main reason FDP is easier to adopt than ZNS.

Who uses it

Hyperscale storage engineers, database and cache developers, Linux kernel and file-system developers, and SSD firmware architects.

Key takeaway

Interview contrast: ZNS = the host must write sequentially and manage zones (large gains, large software changes); FDP = optional hints on a normal SSD (smaller gains to set up, fully backward compatible).

Going deeper

  • NVM Express ratified ZNS in 2020 (TP 4053) and it became the Zoned Namespace Command Set in NVMe 2.0; its zone model borrows from SMR hard drives' ZBC/ZAC standards.
  • ZNS adds Zone Append: many writers can append to one zone without coordinating offsets, and the drive returns the address where each write landed.
  • Linux supports zoned devices natively; f2fs and btrfs have zoned modes, zonefs exposes zones as files, and RocksDB's ZenFS plugin stores database files directly in zones.
  • FDP (TP 4146, ratified in late 2022) grew from Google and Meta proposals; it groups flash into reclaim units and reclaim groups addressed by placement handles carried in write commands.
  • Meta and Samsung published results showing Meta's CacheLib flash cache running with write amplification close to 1 using FDP, enabling cheaper drives in caching tiers.
  • Open-Channel SSDs (LightNVM, merged into Linux 4.4 in 2016 and removed in 2021) exposed raw flash geometry to the host; NVMe Streams (2017) offered hints but saw little use. Both informed ZNS and FDP.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming any application benefits from ZNS automatically: software must be zone-aware or run on a zoned file system.
  • Thinking wrong FDP hints corrupt data: hints only affect physical placement, so mistakes cost efficiency, never correctness.
  • Equating NVMe zones with SMR disk zones in speed: both need sequential writes, but SSD zones reset and read randomly far faster.

docs.title: Try it: Look for zoned block devices (Linux)
docs.text:
lsblk -o NAME,MODEL,ZONED,ZONE-SZ
cat /sys/block/*/queue/zoned   # none / host-aware / host-managed

docs.title: 3.13 Giant QLC SSDs for AI and Hyperscale: 122 TB, 245 TB and Beyond
docs.text:
AI training and inference need huge datasets close to the GPUs, and data centres are short of power and space. Very large QLC SSDs — 61 TB, 122 TB and now around 245 TB in one drive — pack petabytes into a few rack units, delivering far more read performance per watt than the many hard drives that would hold the same data.

Capacity per drive, 2026. QLC SSDs now exceed the largest hard drives several times over.

Think of it like…

Like replacing a car park full of small vans (hard drives) with a few enormous lorries that are also much faster to load and unload.

Real-world example

Fictional lab Nova AI needs 10 PB next to its GPU cluster. With 122.88 TB QLC SSDs that is about 82 drives — a handful of servers. Holding it on 30 TB hard drives would take over 330 disks and many more servers, and still read far more slowly.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start with dense QLC dies, often 2 Tb each, stacked 16-32 per package.
  2. Use a large indirection unit (16 KB or more) so mapping DRAM stays affordable.
  3. Package in E3.L, U.2 or E1.L for the most NAND per slot and good cooling.
  4. Tune firmware for large sequential writes and heavy reads; endurance is usually below 1 DWPD.
  5. Deploy for data lakes, training datasets, checkpoints and inference data tiers.

Who uses it

AI infrastructure architects, hyperscale and GPU-cloud storage teams, HPC centres, and all-flash storage vendors.

Key takeaway

Know the 2026 capacity points: 61.44 TB and 122.88 TB QLC are established; Kioxia's LC9 reached 245.76 TB and Sandisk announced a 256 TB UltraQLC drive.

Going deeper

  • Solidigm's D5-P5336 reached 61.44 TB in 2023 and 122.88 TB at the turn of 2025 using 192-layer QLC on PCIe 4.0 — proof that capacity, not interface speed, drives this market.
  • Kioxia's LC9, announced in July 2025, offers 245.76 TB in E3.L using 32-die stacks of 2 Tb BiCS8 QLC; a 122.88 TB version comes in the smaller E3.S format.
  • Sandisk unveiled a 256 TB UltraQLC U.2 SSD at FMS 2025 with its own controller, targeting the first half of 2026; check current shipment status before planning on it.
  • TrendForce reported nearline HDD lead times beyond 52 weeks in 2025, pushing some buyers to QLC; by mid-2026 enterprise SSDs reportedly absorbed nearly half of all NAND bits shipped.
  • Training checkpoints write terabytes in bursts, so AI storage systems often pair QLC capacity tiers with TLC or SLC write buffers to protect endurance and absorb peaks.
  • Everpure (Pure Storage) builds its own DirectFlash Modules from raw NAND, announcing 75 TB and 150 TB modules, instead of buying finished SSDs — a different route to the same density.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating a 245 TB QLC drive like a TLC database SSD: small random writes cause high write amplification and burn through its limited endurance.
  • Ignoring the blast radius: one failed 122 TB drive means a long rebuild, so use erasure coding and plan rebuild bandwidth.
  • Assuming flash now beats disk on cost: for cold bulk data, hard drives and tape remain much cheaper per terabyte.

docs.title: Try it: How many drives to hold 10 PB?
docs.text:
import math
need_pb = 10
for tb in (30.72, 61.44, 122.88, 245.76):
    print(f"{tb:>7} TB drives: {math.ceil(need_pb * 1000 / tb)}")

docs.title: 3.14 Who Makes Flash and SSDs: NAND Makers, Controller Vendors and Brands in 2026
docs.text:
Only a handful of companies make NAND flash chips: Samsung, SK hynix (with its Solidigm subsidiary), Kioxia and Sandisk (who share fabs), Micron and China's YMTC. Other companies design SSD controllers, such as Phison, Silicon Motion, Marvell and Maxio, and many brands assemble finished drives. In 2025-2026 AI demand made NAND scarce and prices rose sharply.

The flash supply chain. A few fabs feed many brands; big makers also build complete drives themselves.

Think of it like…

Like the coffee trade: a few growers (NAND fabs), a few roasters (controller makers) and hundreds of cafés selling the result under their own names.

Real-world example

Kenji compares three 2 TB budget SSDs from different brands and finds two use the same Phison controller and Kioxia NAND, differing mainly in firmware tuning and warranty. His company's servers, meanwhile, use Samsung and Solidigm drives whose controller, firmware and NAND all come from one maker.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. NAND makers fabricate wafers and sell dies, packages or finished SSDs.
  2. Controller vendors design controllers and reference firmware; brands buy controllers plus NAND.
  3. Vertically integrated makers build controller, firmware and NAND in-house for flagship drives.
  4. Brands such as Kingston, ADATA, Corsair and Teamgroup assemble drives from bought parts.
  5. Hyperscalers and server makers (Dell, HPE, Lenovo) qualify drives and often specify custom firmware.

Who uses it

Procurement teams, supply-chain analysts, hardware reviewers, investors and engineers choosing drives.

Key takeaway

Remember the recent changes: Kioxia listed in Tokyo (December 2024), Western Digital spun off Sandisk (February 2025), Micron ended its Crucial consumer brand (early 2026), and AI demand drove a NAND price surge.

Going deeper

  • TrendForce's Q2 2026 ranking of listed NAND makers by revenue put Samsung first at about 29%, SK hynix group (with Solidigm) second, Micron third, Kioxia fourth and Sandisk fifth; Counterpoint estimated YMTC at about 14%.
  • Kioxia and Sandisk jointly operate fabs at Yokkaichi and Kitakami in Japan, sharing wafer output while designing and selling their own SSDs separately.
  • Solidigm was formed when SK hynix bought Intel's NAND and SSD business (first closing in December 2021), inheriting Intel's floating-gate QLC designs and the Dalian fab in China.
  • Phison (Taiwan) supplies controllers to many retail brands and sells its own Pascari enterprise drives; Silicon Motion's SM2508 is a 6 nm PCIe Gen5 client controller.
  • China's ecosystem — YMTC for NAND, Maxio for controllers, Longsys-owned Lexar for drives — grew quickly; YMTC has been on the US Entity List since December 2022.
  • NAND revenue for the top makers jumped roughly 70-77% quarter-on-quarter in Q2 2026 as prices rose; Micron's December 2025 Crucial exit showed makers prioritising enterprise and AI customers.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming the same model name means the same hardware: brands sometimes change controllers or NAND mid-life, so check reviews for revisions.
  • Choosing by brand alone: the controller, NAND type, DRAM and warranty TBW matter more than the label.
  • Ignoring supply risk: during shortages, qualifying drives from more than one vendor keeps projects on schedule.

docs.title: Glossary of Terms

docs.text: 3-2-1-1-0 rule Backup guideline: three copies on two media types, one offsite, one immutable or offline, and zero errors in restore tests. 3D NAND Flash memory built as vertical stacks of hundreds of cell layers, raising density without shrinking each cell further.

docs.title: A
docs.text: Air gap Physical or logical separation of a data copy from any network, so attackers and ransomware cannot reach it.

docs.title: B
docs.text: Bandwidth (throughput) How much data moves per second, measured in MB/s or GB/s; equals IOPS multiplied by the I/O size. Bit rot Silent corruption of stored data over time from media decay or errors; detected by checksums and scrubbing. Block storage Storage addressed as numbered fixed-size blocks, such as a disk, LUN or cloud volume, organised by the host's file system.

docs.title: C
docs.text: Cache A small, fast memory or storage layer holding copies of frequently used data to hide the latency of slower layers. Ceph Open-source distributed storage system that provides block, file and object storage from clusters of commodity servers. Checkpoint A saved copy of a running job's state, such as AI model weights and optimiser state, used to resume after failures. CXL (Compute Express Link) Open interconnect on PCIe physical links that lets CPUs coherently attach extra memory and accelerators, including pooled and shared memory.

docs.title: D
docs.text: DAS (direct-attached storage) Storage connected directly to one computer, such as an internal SSD or a USB drive, with no network in between. DDR5 Fifth generation of double-data-rate SDRAM for PCs and servers, with two independent subchannels per module and on-die ECC. Deduplication Storing identical blocks or files only once and replacing repeats with references, saving capacity. DRAM Dynamic RAM: main memory that stores each bit as charge in a tiny capacitor and must be refreshed every few milliseconds. DWPD (drive writes per day) SSD endurance rating: how many times the full capacity can be written each day over the warranty period.

docs.title: E
docs.text: ECC (error-correcting code) Extra check bits that let memory or storage detect and correct bit errors automatically. Erasure coding Splitting data into fragments plus parity fragments across devices or nodes so it survives several failures with less overhead than full copies.

docs.title: F
docs.text: Fibre Channel Dedicated, lossless storage-networking technology used to build SANs, with 32, 64 and 128 Gb/s generations. File system Software that organises blocks into named files and directories with metadata, permissions and space allocation. Flash translation layer (FTL) SSD firmware that maps host logical addresses to physical NAND pages, hiding erase-before-write and wear.

docs.title: G
docs.text: Garbage collection SSD background process that copies valid pages out of partly stale blocks and erases them for reuse. GiB (gibibyte) Binary unit of 2^30 bytes (1,073,741,824); a decimal gigabyte (GB) is 10^9 bytes.

docs.title: H
docs.text: HAMR (heat-assisted magnetic recording) Hard-drive recording that briefly heats each spot with a laser so smaller, more stable magnetic grains can be written. HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) Stacked DRAM dies joined by through-silicon vias and placed beside a processor on a very wide bus, giving terabytes per second. HDD (hard disk drive) Storage device that records data magnetically on spinning platters read by heads on a moving actuator arm. Hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) Servers that combine compute, virtualisation and software-defined storage pooled from their local drives.

docs.title: I
docs.text: Immutable backup A backup copy that cannot be changed or deleted until its retention period ends, protecting against ransomware. IOPS Input/output operations per second: how many separate reads or writes a device or system completes each second. iSCSI Protocol carrying SCSI block commands over TCP/IP, letting ordinary Ethernet networks act as a SAN.

docs.title: K
docs.text: KV cache Stored attention keys and values from earlier tokens that let a language model generate new tokens without recomputing them.

docs.title: L
docs.text: Latency Time taken to complete one operation, from request to response, measured in nanoseconds, microseconds or milliseconds. LTO (Linear Tape-Open) Open magnetic-tape format family used for backup and archive, with each generation adding capacity. LUN (logical unit number) A virtual disk presented by a storage array to hosts over a SAN, identified by a number.

docs.title: M
docs.text: Memory hierarchy The layered arrangement of registers, caches, DRAM, SSDs, HDDs and tape that trades speed against capacity and cost.

docs.title: N
docs.text: NAND flash Non-volatile memory storing charge in cells arranged in strings; read and written in pages, erased in larger blocks. NAS (network-attached storage) A file server that shares folders over a network using NFS or SMB. NFS (Network File System) File-sharing protocol from the Unix world; current versions are NFSv3 and NFSv4.x, usually on TCP port 2049. Non-volatile memory Memory or storage that keeps data without power, such as flash, MRAM or magnetic disks. NUMA (non-uniform memory access) Design in which each CPU socket has local memory that is faster to reach than other sockets' memory. NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) Storage protocol designed for flash over PCIe, allowing up to about 64K I/O queues, each up to about 64K commands deep. NVMe-oF (NVMe over Fabrics) Extension of NVMe across networks such as RDMA Ethernet, InfiniBand, TCP and Fibre Channel.

docs.title: O
docs.text: Object storage Storage that keeps whole objects with keys and metadata in a flat namespace, accessed over HTTP APIs such as S3. Over-provisioning Spare NAND capacity hidden from the user that gives an SSD room for garbage collection and wear levelling.

docs.title: P
docs.text: Page cache Operating-system memory holding recently read or written file data so later access avoids the disk. Parallel file system Shared file system that stripes data across many servers so thousands of clients can read and write at once, such as Lustre. PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) A Kubernetes request for storage of a given size, access mode and class, fulfilled by a persistent volume.

docs.title: Q
docs.text: QLC (quad-level cell) NAND that stores four bits per cell: denser and cheaper per GB than TLC but slower to write and less durable. Queue depth Number of I/O requests outstanding at once; higher depths let SSDs work in parallel but can raise latency.

docs.title: R
docs.text: RAID Redundant Array of Independent Disks: combining drives for speed, redundancy or both, such as RAID 1, 5, 6 and 10. Refresh Periodic rewriting of DRAM rows (typically every 32-64 ms) so leaking capacitor charge does not lose data. Rowhammer Disturbance error in which repeatedly activating one DRAM row flips bits in neighbouring rows. RPO (recovery point objective) The maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured as time since the last good copy. RTO (recovery time objective) The maximum acceptable time to restore a service after an outage.

docs.title: S
docs.text: S3 API Amazon S3's HTTP interface for buckets and objects, now the common language of object storage. SAN (storage area network) A dedicated network giving servers shared block storage (LUNs) over Fibre Channel, iSCSI or NVMe-oF. SAS (Serial Attached SCSI) Enterprise drive interface carrying SCSI commands, supporting dual ports and expanders for many drives. SATA Serial ATA: the common consumer drive interface, limited to about 600 MB/s and, with AHCI, a single 32-command queue. SMART Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology: health and error counters reported by drives. SMB (Server Message Block) Windows file-sharing protocol, current dialect 3.1.1, usually on TCP port 445. Snapshot A point-in-time, usually space-efficient view of a volume or file system used for fast rollback — not a backup by itself. SRAM Static RAM built from six-transistor latches; fast and refresh-free, used for CPU caches but costly per bit. SSD (solid-state drive) Storage device built from flash memory and a controller, with no moving parts. Storage class (cloud) A price and performance tier in cloud object storage, such as S3 Standard, Standard-IA or Glacier Deep Archive.

docs.title: T
docs.text: TBW (terabytes written) SSD endurance rating: the total amount of host data that can be written over the drive's warranty. Tiering Automatically moving data between faster, costlier storage and slower, cheaper storage according to how often it is used. TRIM / UNMAP Commands telling an SSD or array which blocks no longer hold valid data, helping garbage collection and thin provisioning.

docs.title: V
docs.text: Volatile memory Memory that loses its contents when power is removed, such as DRAM and SRAM.

docs.title: W
docs.text: Wear levelling Spreading writes evenly across all flash blocks so no block wears out early. Write amplification Ratio of data physically written to flash versus data the host asked to write; lower is better for speed and endurance.

docs.title: Z
docs.text: ZFS (OpenZFS) Copy-on-write file system and volume manager with end-to-end checksums, snapshots, RAID-Z and self-healing.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Hard Drives, Tape, Optical & Archive Storage
docs.text: Most of the world's data still lives on spinning disks and magnetic tape. This chapter opens up the hard drive — platters, heads, seek times, CMR and SMR, HAMR and MAMR, helium and multi-actuator designs, reliability and the 2026 nearline market — then moves to tape, LTO-10 and tape libraries, optical discs, emerging glass, ceramic and DNA media, cold-storage tiers in the cloud, and the discipline of keeping data readable for decades.

docs.title: 4.1 Inside a Hard Drive: Platters, Heads, Actuator and Spindle
docs.text:
A hard disk drive (HDD) stores data as tiny magnetised regions on spinning disks called platters. Read/write heads float a few nanometres above the surface on a cushion of air or helium, swung across the disk by an arm called the actuator. A small controller board turns all this mechanics into a simple block device for the computer.

Parts of a hard disk drive. Mechanics and electronics work together to position a head within nanometres of a spinning disk.

Think of it like…

A record player where the needle never touches the record, the record spins up to 120 times a second, and the needle can both read and rewrite the grooves.

Real-world example

Jonas, a student technician, opens a dead 4 TB desktop drive in class: two platters, four heads on one actuator arm driven by a voice-coil motor, a spindle motor, and a circuit board with the controller, a DRAM cache and a motor driver. The platters spun at 5,400 rpm — 90 rotations every second.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Platters coated with a thin magnetic layer spin on a spindle motor at 5,400-7,200 rpm (up to 15,000 in old performance drives).
  2. Each platter surface has its own head on a slider that flies a few nanometres above it.
  3. A voice-coil actuator swings all the heads together to the right track, guided by servo marks on the disk.
  4. Writing: the head's write pole magnetises tiny regions in one of two directions.
  5. Reading: a magnetoresistive (TMR) sensor detects those directions as changes in electrical resistance.
  6. The controller, cache and firmware handle error correction, defect remapping and the SATA or SAS interface.

Who uses it

Data-centre technicians, storage engineers, data-recovery specialists and anyone building NAS or backup systems.

Key takeaway

Learn the parts list — platters, spindle motor, heads and sliders, actuator arm and voice-coil motor, servo, controller and cache — and remember the heads never touch the platters in normal operation.

Going deeper

  • Platter substrates are aluminium alloy or glass; glass is stiffer and smoother, allowing thinner disks — Toshiba plans glass platters to fit twelve disks in a 40 TB-class drive in 2027.
  • Thermal fly-height control heats a tiny element in the slider so the head bulges toward the disk only while reading or writing, keeping head-to-media spacing at just a few nanometres.
  • Modern readers use tunnelling magnetoresistance; two-dimensional magnetic recording (TDMR) adds multiple reader sensors per head so narrower, more tightly packed tracks can be read reliably.
  • Servo patterns written at the factory sit in wedges around each surface; the drive reads them many thousands of times per second to keep the head centred on tracks only tens of nanometres wide.
  • Most high-capacity drives add micro-actuators — piezoelectric elements near the head — for fine positioning on top of the coarse voice-coil motor, known as dual- or triple-stage actuation.
  • Load/unload ramps park the heads off the platters when idle or powered off; drives specify a maximum number of load/unload cycles, often hundreds of thousands.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Opening a drive outside a cleanroom to 'fix' it: a dust particle is far larger than the flying height and can crash the heads.
  • Thinking hard drives are obsolete: in 2026 they still hold most of the data in hyperscale clouds, at far lower cost per terabyte than flash.
  • Moving or knocking a running drive: shocks during operation can make the heads strike the platter.

docs.title: Try it: Spot spinning disks and their speed
docs.text:
# Linux: ROTA=1 means a rotating hard drive
lsblk -d -o NAME,MODEL,ROTA,SIZE

# Windows PowerShell
Get-PhysicalDisk | Select-Object FriendlyName, MediaType, SpindleSpeed, Size

A NAS owner notices a faint whine from an ageing drive, often a sign of spindle-bearing wear. Each of the ten platters in a nearline drive has two heads, one per surface — twenty in total. TMR readers replaced older GMR sensors as bits shrank in the mid-2000s. Actuator arm and voice-coil motorHDD makers · Component · Current · Beginner Pivoting arm moved by an electromagnetic voice-coil motor, swinging all heads across the platters together. During a random-read test, Jonas hears the actuator's rapid clicking as it seeks between tracks. Micro-actuatorHigh-capacity HDDs · Technology · Current · Advanced Piezoelectric element near the head adding fine, fast position corrections on top of the voice-coil motor. Dual-stage actuation lets a 30 TB drive stay centred on tracks far narrower than a human hair. Servo wedgesHDD track-following system · Concept · Current · Intermediate Factory-written position markers around each surface that the drive reads continuously to keep heads on track. If servo information is damaged, the drive cannot find tracks and becomes unreadable without lab recovery. Thermal fly-height control (TFC)HDD head technology · Technology · Current · Advanced Small heater in the slider that lowers the head toward the disk only during reads and writes. TFC lets a drive fly the head higher while seeking and closer while writing, protecting it from contact. Two-dimensional magnetic recording (TDMR)Seagate, Western Digital · Technology · Current · Advanced Heads with multiple read sensors whose combined signals help read tightly packed tracks despite interference. TDMR helped drive makers squeeze more tracks per inch before energy-assisted recording arrived. Load/unload rampHDD makers · Component · Current · Intermediate Plastic ramp at the platter edge where heads park when idle, avoiding contact with the disk surface. Aggressive power saving on a home server drives the load/unload counter up quickly — worth watching in SMART data. Drive cache (DRAM buffer)HDD makers · Component · Current · Beginner DRAM on the drive's circuit board, often 256-512 MB on large drives, buffering reads, writes and command queues. A large drive's cache absorbs short bursts of small writes, then writes them to platters in an efficient order. Defect management and reallocationHDD firmware · Software · Current · Intermediate Firmware that maps bad sectors to spare sectors, invisible to the host apart from SMART counters. Jonas sees 'Reallocated Sectors Count: 8' on an old drive — the firmware has already swapped out eight bad sectors. Advanced Format (512e / 4Kn)IDEMA and HDD makers (transition from 2010) · Format · Current · Intermediate 4,096-byte physical sectors for better error correction; 512e drives emulate 512-byte sectors for older software. Misaligned partitions on 512e drives once caused slow writes until tools began aligning partitions to 1 MiB.

docs.title: 4.2 HDD Performance: RPM, Seek Time, Rotational Latency and Zoned Recording
docs.text:
A hard drive must physically move its heads and wait for the right spot to spin round, so each random access takes milliseconds — around a hundred times slower than an SSD. Once positioned, though, it streams data quickly. So HDDs are good at large sequential reads and writes and poor at small random ones.

Where a random HDD read spends its time. Mechanical seek and rotation dominate; the data transfer itself is tiny.

Think of it like…

Like finding a song on a vinyl record: moving the needle to the right place (seek) and waiting for the song's start to come round (rotational latency) take far longer than actually playing it.

Real-world example

Fatima's 7,200 rpm NAS drive averages about 8 ms to seek plus 4.17 ms of rotational latency — roughly 12 ms per random read, or about 80 reads per second. Copying one 50 GB video, though, runs at over 250 MB/s because the head simply follows the track.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Seek: the actuator moves the heads to the target track — about 1 ms to a neighbouring track, around 8 ms on average.
  2. Rotational latency: wait for the sector to arrive under the head — on average half a revolution.
  3. Transfer: read or write at the media rate, faster on outer tracks than inner ones.
  4. Command queuing (NCQ or SAS tagged queuing) lets the drive reorder requests to shorten head travel.
  5. For random work, throughput = IOPS × request size; big sequential streams reach the media rate.

Who uses it

Storage administrators, performance engineers, NAS builders and anyone sizing disk arrays for databases, video or backups.

Key takeaway

Memorise: average rotational latency in ms = 30,000 ÷ rpm — 7,200 rpm = 4.17 ms, 10,000 rpm = 3 ms, 15,000 rpm = 2 ms; one HDD gives roughly 75-200 random IOPS.

Going deeper

  • Zoned bit recording puts more sectors on longer outer tracks, so a large drive's sequential speed may fall from roughly 280 MB/s at the outer edge to about half at the inner edge.
  • SATA's Native Command Queuing holds up to 32 commands and SAS supports much deeper queues; firmware reorders them by position, so random IOPS rise noticeably at higher queue depths.
  • 10,000 and 15,000 rpm 2.5-inch SAS 'performance' drives have largely been replaced by SSDs; 2026 data-centre HDDs are almost all 7,200 rpm nearline drives.
  • IOPS per terabyte is HDD's core problem: a 30 TB drive delivers about the same ~100-200 IOPS as an 8 TB drive, so each terabyte gets far fewer IOPS as capacity grows.
  • Short-stroking — using only the outer tracks — and placing hot data at the outer edge were classic tricks that cut seek distance and raised speed at the cost of capacity.
  • Random 4 KB throughput is tiny: 150 IOPS × 4 KB ≈ 0.6 MB/s, compared with 250+ MB/s sequential — over 400 times less from the same drive.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Quoting a sequential MB/s figure for a database: random IOPS, not sequential speed, limit HDDs.
  • Assuming a bigger hard drive is faster per terabyte: capacity grows much faster than IOPS, so IOPS per TB falls.
  • Running heavy random workloads on SMR or 5,400 rpm drives: use CMR 7,200 rpm drives or SSDs instead.

docs.title: Try it: Estimate random IOPS from RPM and seek time
docs.text:
typical_seek_ms = {5400: 11.0, 7200: 8.5, 10000: 4.5, 15000: 3.5}
for rpm, seek in typical_seek_ms.items():
    rot = 30000 / rpm                 # half a revolution, in ms
    iops = 1000 / (seek + rot)
    print(f"{rpm:>5} rpm: {rot:.2f} ms rotational, ~{iops:.0f} random IOPS")

docs.text: Name What it does Example Seek timeHDD datasheet parameter · Metric · Current · Beginner Time for the actuator to move the heads to the target track; around 8 ms average on 7,200 rpm drives. A datasheet lists 8.5 ms average read seek, so Fatima knows random reads cost at least that much. At 5,400 rpm the average wait is 5.56 ms; at 15,000 rpm only 2 ms. A 12-drive array of 7,200 rpm disks gives roughly 1,500-2,000 random read IOPS in total. Copying a 50 GB video file runs at around 270 MB/s, close to the drive's rated maximum. A benchmark graph of a drive shows speed sloping down from outer to inner tracks.
