Performance HDD (10K / 15K SAS)Seagate, Western Digital, Toshiba · Device · Legacy · Intermediate Fast-spinning small-capacity enterprise disks once used for databases, now almost entirely replaced by SSDs. An old SAN still running 15,000 rpm drives is migrated to flash, shrinking from several shelves to one. Nearline HDDSeagate Exos, WD Ultrastar, Toshiba MG · Device · Current · Beginner High-capacity 7,200 rpm 3.5-inch drive for always-on bulk data; the bulk of HDD capacity shipped in 2026. Cloud object storage keeps most customer data on nearline drives behind an SSD caching layer.

docs.title: 4.3 Recording Methods: Perpendicular (CMR) and Shingled (SMR)
docs.text:
Modern drives record bits standing upright in the magnetic layer — perpendicular recording — which is what 'CMR' (conventional magnetic recording) means today. SMR overlaps tracks like roof shingles to squeeze in more data, but rewriting one track disturbs the next, so data must be written sequentially in zones.

CMR vs SMR

CMR SMR Track layout Separate tracks with gaps Overlapping, shingled tracks Random overwrite In place Rewrite the band or zone Capacity Baseline Roughly 10-20% more Sustained random writes Consistent Can collapse when cache fills Best for RAID, NAS, databases Archives, append-only stores Standards Normal block commands ZBC (SCSI) / ZAC (ATA)

SMR gains capacity by giving up cheap in-place rewrites.

Think of it like…

SMR is like laying roof shingles: overlapping them fits more on the roof, but replacing one in the middle means lifting and re-laying all the ones on top of it.

Real-world example

Owen builds a home ZFS NAS with cheap 8 TB drives. When one fails, the replacement turns out to be drive-managed SMR, and the rebuild crawls for days because its shingled bands cannot absorb the flood of random writes. He returns it for a CMR NAS drive, and the next rebuild finishes overnight.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Longitudinal recording (bits lying flat) hit its limits in the mid-2000s; perpendicular recording stood bits upright for higher density.
  2. CMR writes tracks side by side with small gaps, so any sector can be rewritten in place.
  3. SMR's wide write head overlaps the previous track, leaving a narrower readable strip and adding capacity.
  4. Rewriting a shingled track means rewriting every following track in its band, so data is written in zones.
  5. Drive-managed SMR hides this with a cache area and background clean-up; host-managed SMR exposes zones to software.

Who uses it

Hyperscale storage engineers, NAS builders, backup-appliance designers and anyone buying drives for RAID or ZFS.

Key takeaway

For RAID and ZFS NAS use CMR drives; host-managed SMR shines only with zone-aware software at scale, such as large append-only object stores.

Going deeper

  • Toshiba shipped the first perpendicular-recording hard drive in 2005; within a few years almost every drive used it, and 'CMR' became the name for non-shingled perpendicular recording.
  • Host-managed SMR follows the INCITS T10 ZBC and T13 ZAC standards: mostly sequential-write-required zones, typically 256 MB, each with a write pointer, plus a few conventional zones for metadata.
  • Host-aware SMR accepts random writes like drive-managed SMR but also reports its zones, so zone-aware software can avoid the slow paths.
  • Western Digital's UltraSMR adds stronger error correction and uses its OptiNAND flash to boost capacity; its 40 TB ePMR/UltraSMR platform began shipping in mid-2026.
  • Drive-managed SMR drives keep a conventional 'media cache' region to absorb random writes and clean it into shingled bands while idle; sustained random writes larger than the cache cause steep slowdowns.
  • WD expects UltraSMR to reach roughly 60% of its nearline exabyte shipments by the end of its fiscal 2027, showing hyperscalers now use shingled recording at scale.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming 'PMR' on a datasheet means not shingled: SMR drives also record perpendicularly, so look for an explicit CMR statement.
  • Rebuilding RAID or ZFS onto drive-managed SMR disks: rebuilds can slow drastically or even time out.
  • Thinking SMR drives are unreliable: they are reliable; the problem is their write behaviour under the wrong workload.

docs.title: Try it: Check whether a drive reports zones (Linux)
docs.text:
cat /sys/block/sda/queue/zoned     # none / host-aware / host-managed
sudo smartctl -i /dev/sda | grep -iE 'model|capacity'
# Drive-managed SMR still shows 'none' - check the model's datasheet

Owen checks the datasheet says CMR before buying drives for his ZFS pool. SMR (shingled magnetic recording)All HDD makers · Technology · Current · Beginner Overlapping tracks like roof shingles to gain capacity, at the cost of slow in-place rewrites. A cloud archive writes large immutable objects sequentially, perfect for SMR's capacity boost. Drive-managed SMR (DM-SMR)Consumer and some NAS drives · Technology · Current · Intermediate SMR drive that hides shingling from the host using a cache region and background clean-up; works anywhere but can stall. A cheap external backup drive copies photos fine but slows to a crawl during a big random-write job. Host-managed SMR (HM-SMR)Nearline drives for hyperscalers · Technology · Current · Advanced SMR drive exposing sequential-write zones that the host must respect; highest capacity, needs zone-aware software. A hyperscaler's object store writes each shard sequentially into HM-SMR zones and resets zones after compaction. Host-aware SMRSome SMR drives · Technology · Current · Advanced Hybrid SMR mode that reports zones like host-managed SMR but still accepts random writes like drive-managed SMR. Software unaware of zones still works on host-aware drives, while zone-aware software gets full speed. ZBC / ZACINCITS T10 (ZBC, SCSI) and T13 (ZAC, ATA) · Standard · Current · Advanced Standards defining zone types, write pointers and zone commands for zoned hard drives over SAS and SATA. Linux's zoned block layer uses ZBC commands to report and reset zones on a SAS SMR drive. Media cacheSMR drive firmware · Component · Current · Advanced Conventionally recorded area on a drive-managed SMR disk that absorbs random writes before they are moved into shingled bands. A DM-SMR drive accepts writes quickly until its media cache fills, then performance drops sharply. UltraSMRWestern Digital · Technology · Current · Advanced WD's high-capacity shingled recording with enhanced error correction, used in its biggest hyperscale drives. WD's 40 TB nearline platform combines ePMR heads with UltraSMR to reach its capacity. 2020 SMR disclosure controversyNAS-drive market event · Concept · Legacy · Beginner Discovery that some NAS-marketed drives used drive-managed SMR without saying so, prompting clearer labelling. After 2020, Western Digital marked CMR NAS drives as Red Plus and Red Pro, keeping plain WD Red for SMR. Areal densityHDD industry measure · Metric · Current · Intermediate Bits stored per square inch of platter; raising it is the main way drives gain capacity without adding platters. Seagate's Mozaic 4+ reaches 44 TB with the same disks and heads as earlier 30 TB-class drives by raising areal density.

docs.title: 4.4 Energy-Assisted Recording: HAMR, MAMR and ePMR
docs.text:
Smaller magnetic grains fit more bits per square inch, but very small grains can flip on their own at room temperature. Grains made of 'harder' magnetic material stay stable, but ordinary write heads cannot switch them. Energy-assisted recording adds a brief burst of energy — heat from a laser (HAMR) or microwave-frequency or current effects (MAMR, ePMR) — to help the head write, then the bit settles into a stable state.

How a HAMR head writes a bit. Heat makes the hard media briefly writable; cooling locks the bit in place.

Think of it like…

Like writing in candle wax: hard wax holds an impression well but resists your stylus; warm it for a moment and it takes the shape easily, then hardens again.

Real-world example

Fictional cloud provider Cirrus deploys HAMR drives. A tiny laser on each head heats a nanometre-scale spot of platter for about a nanosecond while writing; the platter as a whole stays cool. Cirrus now fits up to 44 TB in a 3.5-inch slot that held 20 TB a few years earlier.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Shrinking grains raises density but risks thermal instability — the superparamagnetic limit.
  2. Use high-anisotropy media, such as iron-platinum for HAMR, whose small grains stay stable.
  3. HAMR: a laser and near-field transducer heat a tiny spot so the head can switch it; it cools in about a nanosecond.
  4. MAMR: a spin-torque oscillator in the head adds a microwave-frequency field to help flip grains; Toshiba's FC-MAMR variant boosts the write field.
  5. ePMR (Western Digital): a bias current on the write pole makes writing more consistent, without laser or microwaves.
  6. Roadmaps: 44 TB HAMR drives in 2026, about 50 TB next, with 80-100 TB talked about around 2030.

Who uses it

Recording physicists, head and media engineers, hyperscale procurement teams and industry analysts.

Key takeaway

Remember the magnetic recording trilemma — small grains (density) vs thermal stability vs writability — and that energy assistance is how the industry breaks it.

Going deeper

  • Seagate's Mozaic 3+ platform (2024) combined iron-platinum superlattice media, a plasmonic writer with a nanophotonic laser, a seventh-generation spintronic reader and a 12 nm controller, at about 3 TB per platter.
  • Seagate said in March 2026 that Mozaic 4+, supporting up to 44 TB with the same number of disks and heads, was qualified at two hyperscalers; Mozaic 5 targets about 50 TB, with qualification planned for late 2027.
  • Western Digital reached 40 TB in 2026 with ePMR plus UltraSMR, and planned its first HAMR drive, 44 TB, for volume shipments in the first half of 2027, with 80-100 TB goals around 2030.
  • Toshiba began shipping flux-control MAMR with its 18 TB MG09 in 2021; its roadmap pairs MAMR with twelve glass platters for 40 TB-class drives in 2027 while developing HAMR in parallel.
  • Heated-dot magnetic recording — HAMR on bit-patterned media where each bit is a pre-formed magnetic island — is the next step vendors describe for after 2030.
  • Early HAMR concerns focused on laser and near-field transducer lifetime and head contamination; Seagate reports hyperscale reliability comparable to conventional drives, a vendor claim worth checking against field data.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking HAMR heats the whole platter: only a nanometre-scale spot is heated, for about a nanosecond, during writing.
  • Assuming HAMR drives need special interfaces: to the host they are ordinary SATA or SAS drives.
  • Treating vendor roadmaps as delivery dates: HAMR was promised for over a decade before shipping in volume.

docs.title: Try it: Drive capacity = platters × capacity per platter
docs.text:
for name, platters, tb_per_platter in [
    ('2020 ePMR/MAMR drive', 9, 2.0),
    ('Mozaic 3+ class', 10, 3.0),
    ('Mozaic 4+ class', 10, 4.4),
]:
    print(f"{name}: ~{platters * tb_per_platter:.0f} TB")

docs.title: 4.5 Helium-Sealed and Multi-Actuator Drives
docs.text:
Two tricks keep big hard drives practical. Filling a sealed case with helium — far thinner than air — cuts turbulence and drag, so more, thinner platters fit and the drive uses less power. Multi-actuator drives split the heads into two independently moving groups, giving roughly double the performance from one drive.

Air-filled vs helium-filled drives

Air-filled Helium-filled Gas density 1× (air) About 1/7 of air Platters (3.5-inch) Typically up to 5-6 9-11 (12 planned) Power per TB Higher Lower Enclosure Breather filter Hermetically sealed Typical 2026 use Smaller desktop and NAS drives All high-capacity nearline

Helium made 10-platter drives possible.

Think of it like…

Helium is like swimming in thinner water so more swimmers fit in each lane; dual actuators are like two librarians fetching books from the same bookcase instead of one.

Real-world example

Fictional backup firm Vaultline replaces 10 TB air-filled drives with 24 TB helium drives, more than doubling capacity per slot while power per terabyte falls. For a busy analytics tier it tests dual-actuator drives, which appear to the server as two logical units and roughly double throughput per slot.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Helium has about one-seventh the density of air, so spinning platters face far less drag and flutter.
  2. Calmer gas lets heads track more precisely and allows thinner, more tightly stacked platters.
  3. Helium escapes through ordinary seals, so drives use hermetically sealed, welded enclosures.
  4. Multi-actuator drives put two actuators on one pivot, each serving half of the platters.
  5. The host sees two logical units (SAS) or two halves of the address range (SATA) and must spread I/O across both.

Who uses it

Data-centre and hyperscale storage engineers, backup-appliance designers and anyone planning dense storage racks.

Key takeaway

Remember HGST's 6 TB Ultrastar He6 (2013) as the first helium drive, and that virtually all high-capacity nearline drives are now helium-filled.

Going deeper

  • HGST, then part of Western Digital, launched the first helium drive — the 6 TB Ultrastar He6 — in 2013 using its HelioSeal process; Seagate and Toshiba followed within a few years.
  • Helium drives report gas level through a SMART attribute (often called helium condition), because a slow leak eventually raises drag and disturbs head flying.
  • Platter counts rose from seven to nine, ten and eleven; Toshiba plans twelve-disk drives with thinner glass platters, adding capacity without new recording physics.
  • Seagate's Mach.2 dual-actuator drives (Exos 2X14 and 2X18) roughly doubled per-drive throughput and random IOPS; SATA versions split the address range in half, so software must use both halves.
  • WD's OptiNAND (2021) embeds a small flash device in the drive to hold metadata and positioning data, freeing platter space and protecting cached writes during power loss.
  • Multi-actuator designs restore IOPS per terabyte as capacities pass 30-40 TB, which matters to hyperscalers whose service levels depend on per-drive performance.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating a dual-actuator SATA drive as one fast disk: without spreading I/O over both halves you get single-actuator speed.
  • Ignoring the helium-level SMART attribute: a falling value is an early warning to replace the drive.
  • Assuming helium makes drives fragile: sealed helium drives have shown reliability comparable to or better than air drives.

docs.title: Try it: See a dual-actuator SAS drive's two logical units (Linux)
docs.text:
lsblk -o NAME,HCTL,MODEL,SIZE
# A dual-actuator SAS drive appears twice, with LUN 0 and LUN 1 in the HCTL column

docs.title: 4.6 HDD Reliability, Drive Classes and Failure Modes
docs.text:
Hard drives wear out mechanically and occasionally develop unreadable sectors. Makers rate them with MTBF or AFR figures and annual workload limits, and build different classes — desktop, NAS, surveillance, enterprise — for different duty cycles. Large real-world studies, such as Backblaze's quarterly reports, typically show annual failure rates of around 1-2%.

Typical hard drive classes

Desktop NAS Enterprise nearline Duty cycle Part-time 24×7 24×7 Workload rating ~55 TB/year ~180-300 TB/year ~550 TB/year MTBF rating Often not stated ~1-1.2 M hours ~2.5 M hours Vibration handling Basic RV sensors on larger models RV sensors, any bay count Warranty 2-3 years 3-5 years 5 years Examples BarraCuda, WD Blue IronWolf, WD Red Plus, N300 Exos, Ultrastar, MG

Ratings vary by model; these are typical figures for each class.

Think of it like…

Like vehicle classes: a city hatchback, a delivery van and a long-haul lorry all have engines, but each is built and warrantied for a very different amount of driving.

Real-world example

Grace runs a 12-bay NAS for a fictional design studio. Her old desktop drives were rated for about 55 TB of workload a year and part-time use, but nightly backups and monthly scrubs push 150 TB a year. She switches to NAS-class drives rated about 180 TB a year for 24×7 use, with vibration sensors and RAID-friendly error recovery.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose a drive class for the duty cycle (hours per day), workload (TB per year), bay count and vibration.
  2. Check AFR or MTBF, warranty years and the unrecoverable read error rate (for example, 1 in 10^15 bits).
  3. Monitor SMART attributes such as reallocated and pending sectors and track them over time.
  4. Replace drives with growing reallocated or pending counts, or falling helium levels, before they fail.
  5. Expect a 'bathtub curve': some early failures, a long flat period, then rising wear-out after about five years.

Who uses it

System administrators, NAS owners, data-centre operations teams and reliability engineers.

Key takeaway

Convert MTBF to annual failure rate: AFR ≈ 8,760 ÷ MTBF hours — 2.5 million hours ≈ 0.35% a year on paper; real-world AFR is usually higher.

Going deeper

  • Backblaze publishes quarterly and annual failure statistics for hundreds of thousands of drives; its fleet-wide annualised failure rate has typically been around 1-2%, with large differences between models.
  • Workload ratings count all data read and written per year; exceeding them does not cause instant failure, but it breaks the assumptions behind the quoted AFR and may affect warranty claims.
  • Rotational vibration from neighbouring drives pushes heads off track; enterprise and larger NAS drives use vibration sensors and feed-forward control to compensate in dense chassis.
  • Time-limited error recovery (TLER, ERC or CCTL) makes NAS and enterprise drives give up on a bad sector after about seven seconds, letting the RAID layer rebuild the data instead of dropping the drive.
  • Common failure modes are head degradation or crashes, growing media defects, spindle-bearing wear, circuit-board failure and, for helium drives, slow gas loss.
  • A pending sector is unreadable but not yet remapped; when it is rewritten the drive tests it and reallocates it if needed, which is why scrubs and rebuilds often surface these sectors.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reading MTBF as lifespan: 2.5 million hours does not mean a drive lasts 285 years; it describes failure rate across a population.
  • Using desktop drives in multi-bay RAID: without TLER and vibration tolerance they drop out of arrays and slow everything down.
  • Waiting for SMART to say 'FAILED': many drives fail with only subtle attribute changes, so trend raw values and keep backups.

docs.title: Try it: Check the SMART attributes that predict trouble (Linux, smartmontools)
docs.text: sudo smartctl -a /dev/sda | grep -E 'Reallocated|Pending|Offline_Uncorrectable|Power_On|Load_Cycle'

docs.text: Name What it does Example MTBF (mean time between failures)HDD datasheets · Metric · Current · Beginner Statistical failure rate for a large population during service life, expressed in hours; not an individual drive's lifespan. An enterprise drive's 2.5 million-hour MTBF predicts about 35 failures a year among 10,000 drives. AFR (annualised failure rate)HDD datasheets and field studies · Metric · Current · Beginner Percentage of drives expected or observed to fail per year; easier to reason about than MTBF. Backblaze reports AFR by drive model so buyers can compare real-world reliability. Grace's nightly backups and scrubs total 150 TB a year, so she needs drives rated above that. A drive rated 1 in 10^15 bits may, on average, hit one unreadable sector per roughly 125 TB read. A laptop drive dropped while running suffers a head crash and needs a cleanroom data-recovery service. A shopping centre's video recorder uses surveillance drives that write 32 camera streams around the clock.

docs.title: 4.7 HDD Vendors, Product Lines and the Nearline Market in 2026
docs.text:
Only three companies still make hard drives: Seagate, Western Digital and Toshiba. Most drives now go to cloud and AI data centres as high-capacity 'nearline' drives. In 2025-2026, demand outran supply: lead times for the biggest drives stretched beyond a year and prices rose.

Hard drive milestones that shaped 2026. Capacity leaps came from new recording methods and helium.

Think of it like…

Like the airliner market: a few makers, enormous factories, long order books and customers booking capacity years ahead.

Real-world example

Fictional start-up DataHarbor wants 2 PB of nearline capacity in 2026 and learns that 30 TB-plus models carry lead times of over a year because hyperscalers have reserved output. It buys 24 TB drives through distributors, puts its hot tier on QLC SSDs and signs a supply agreement for 2027.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. 1980s-2000s: dozens of HDD makers consolidate through mergers and exits.
  2. 2011-2012: Seagate buys Samsung's HDD business; Western Digital buys HGST, and Toshiba takes some 3.5-inch assets.
  3. 2010s-2020s: laptops and desktops switch to SSDs while nearline exabytes keep growing.
  4. 2024: Seagate ships its first Mozaic 3+ HAMR drives; WD ships 32 TB UltraSMR drives.
  5. 2025-2026: AI data growth causes shortages; makers sell out 2026 output; WD becomes HDD-only after spinning off Sandisk.
  6. 2026-2027: 40-44 TB drives ship; WD HAMR and Toshiba 40 TB-class drives are planned for 2027.

Who uses it

Procurement and supply-chain teams, data-centre planners, investors, analysts and storage reviewers.

Key takeaway

Remember the three makers and their enterprise lines — Seagate Exos, WD Ultrastar, Toshiba MG — and that nearline drives now account for most HDD exabytes and revenue.

Going deeper

  • TrendForce reported in September 2025 that nearline HDD lead times had grown from a few weeks to over 52 weeks, because makers had not added capacity while AI-driven storage demand surged.
  • Both Seagate and Western Digital said nearline capacity was allocated through 2026, with customers negotiating into 2027 and beyond; WD raised HDD prices citing unprecedented demand.
  • Seagate reported that HAMR made up roughly 40% of its nearline exabyte shipment run rate by the end of its fiscal 2026, and expected Mozaic 4 to dominate HAMR exabytes by late 2026.
  • Western Digital completed the Sandisk separation in February 2025, leaving WD as a hard-drive company whose revenue now comes overwhelmingly from cloud customers.
  • Client HDD shipments for PCs have fallen for more than a decade, but rising nearline capacity per drive has kept total HDD exabytes shipped growing.
  • Toshiba's storage business, part of Toshiba Electronic Devices & Storage, sells MG-series nearline drives and N300 and X300 consumer drives, and is the smallest of the three makers.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Judging the data-centre market by retail prices: the 2026 shortage hit high-capacity nearline drives hardest.
  • Declaring the hard drive dead: hyperscalers still keep most of their capacity on HDD because cost per terabyte remains far below flash.
  • Confusing Western Digital and Sandisk after 2025: they are separate companies — WD makes hard drives, Sandisk makes flash.

docs.title: 4.8 How Magnetic Tape Works
docs.text:
Tape stores data on a long, thin ribbon — about a kilometre of it per cartridge — coated with magnetic particles. A drive pulls the tape past a fixed head that writes dozens of parallel tracks at once, running end to end and back many times. Finding one file is slow, but streaming is fast, cost per terabyte is very low, and a cartridge on a shelf uses no power.

Writing data to tape. The drive verifies every block as it writes and reverses direction at each end of the tape.

Think of it like…

Like a very long scroll: finding one paragraph means unrolling to it, but reading straight through is quick, and rolled-up scrolls sit safely on a shelf for decades.

Real-world example

Fictional broadcaster ArcTV archives finished programmes every night. One LTO-9 drive streams at up to 400 MB/s, so filling an 18 TB cartridge takes about 12.5 hours. Restoring a single clip takes a minute or two: the library robot loads the cartridge and the drive winds to the right spot.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The drive compresses data (if compressible), can encrypt it, and adds error-correction codes.
  2. The head writes a group of tracks simultaneously as the tape moves past at several metres per second.
  3. At the end of the tape the head steps sideways and writes the next 'wrap' in the reverse direction — linear serpentine recording.
  4. Factory-written servo bands keep the head aligned with tracks only micrometres wide.
  5. Read-after-write checks verify every block as it is written; bad blocks are rewritten further along.
  6. A chip in the cartridge (cartridge memory) stores its directory and usage history.

Who uses it

Backup and archive administrators, broadcast and media archivists, HPC centres, hyperscale cloud operators and research institutions.

Key takeaway

Remember tape's trade-off: slow time to first byte (often a minute or more) but fast streaming, the lowest cost per terabyte, and a natural air gap.

Going deeper

  • Modern LTO and enterprise tapes use barium ferrite particles; Fujifilm and IBM demonstrated strontium ferrite media in 2020 at an areal density that implied roughly 580 TB per cartridge.
  • Tape drives must stream: if the host cannot supply data fast enough, the drive stops, backs up and restarts ('shoe-shining'); speed matching slows the tape to reduce this.
  • Tape makers quote bit error rates around 1 in 10^19 to 10^20 bits for modern LTO, several orders of magnitude better than the 1 in 10^15 typical of hard-drive specifications.
  • Media makers rate modern tape for around 30 years of archival life when stored in controlled conditions, roughly 16-25°C and 20-50% relative humidity.
  • Time to first byte includes the robot fetching the cartridge, loading and threading, then winding to the data — often a minute or more in total.
  • A cartridge on a shelf draws no power, so tape's energy use and carbon per stored terabyte are far below spinning disk — a growing argument for cold data.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using tape like a disk for random access: restoring millions of small files one by one is painfully slow, so batch and stage restores.
  • Underfeeding a tape drive: slow sources cause shoe-shining that wears tape and heads; stage data on disk first.
  • Budgeting with 'compressed' capacity: video and already-compressed files store only at native capacity.

mt -f /dev/nst0 status     # drive and position status

# Without a drive, try: man mt

docs.title: 4.9 LTO Generations: LTO-9, LTO-10 and the Roadmap
docs.text:
Linear Tape-Open (LTO) is the open, multi-vendor tape format used by most organisations. A new generation arrives every few years with more capacity. LTO-9 holds 18 TB native; LTO-10 launched in 2025 at 30 TB, with a 40 TB cartridge following in 2026 — but LTO-10 drives cannot read older generations.

LTO native capacity by generation. Capacity has grown about 27-fold since LTO-5.

Think of it like…

Like successive editions of a standard shipping container that each hold more cargo — except LTO-10 changed the door design, so old containers no longer fit the new cranes.

Real-world example

Fictional genomics lab GenomeX has 3 PB on LTO-8 and LTO-9 tapes. Moving to LTO-10, it keeps two LTO-9 drives in the library to read old tapes, buys LTO-10 drives for new data, and schedules migration of its LTO-8 tapes while LTO-9 drives are still easy to buy.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The LTO Program (HPE, IBM and Quantum) defines each generation and licenses manufacturers.
  2. Each generation raises native capacity; transfer speed reached 400 MB/s native with LTO-9.
  3. Up to LTO-9, drives handled at least one older generation: LTO-9 reads and writes LTO-8.
  4. LTO-10 drives use a new servo format and head design and accept only LTO-10 media.
  5. WORM cartridges, AES-256 encryption and LTFS are supported across modern generations.
  6. The updated roadmap extends to Generation 14, at up to 913 TB per cartridge.

Who uses it

Backup administrators, archive managers, media and entertainment, HPC and life-science data managers, and cloud providers.

Key takeaway

Memorise native capacities — LTO-7 6 TB, LTO-8 12 TB, LTO-9 18 TB, LTO-10 30 TB (40 TB cartridge in 2026) — and that LTO-10 broke backward compatibility.

Going deeper

  • LTO-9 stores 18 TB native (45 TB at 2.5:1) at up to 400 MB/s and requires a one-time media optimisation when each new cartridge is first loaded, which can take tens of minutes or longer.
  • LTO-10 launched in 2025 at 30 TB native, kept the 400 MB/s rate, removed the media-calibration step and introduced a revised servo format and head design.
  • The 40 TB LTO-10 cartridge, shipping from early 2026, uses a thinner, smoother aramid base film so more tape fits in the standard shell; it works in existing LTO-10 drives.
  • LTO-10 drives cannot read or write LTO-9 or older cartridges, ending the long tradition of reading back one or two generations, so sites must keep older drives or migrate archives.
  • LTO Program figures show record shipments of 176.5 EB (compressed) in 2024, a dip to 160.3 EB in 2025, then a 57% year-on-year rise in Q1 2026 as LTO-10 ramped.
  • LTO media comes from Fujifilm and Sony, while current LTO drives are largely manufactured by IBM and sold under many brands, including HPE, Quantum and Dell.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Retiring every LTO-9 drive when moving to LTO-10: older archives become unreadable without a migration plan.
  • Budgeting with compressed capacity: plan on native capacity unless your data is proven to compress.
  • Forgetting LTO-9's first-load media optimisation: new cartridges can delay backup windows while they calibrate.

docs.title: Try it: How long does it take to fill a tape?
docs.text:
rate_mb_s = 400   # LTO-9 and LTO-10 native speed
for gen, tb in [('LTO-9', 18), ('LTO-10', 30), ('LTO-10 40 TB', 40)]:
    hours = tb * 1e6 / rate_mb_s / 3600
    print(f"{gen}: {tb} TB native, ~{hours:.1f} h at full speed")

docs.title: 4.10 Enterprise Tape, LTFS, Tape Libraries and the Air Gap
docs.text:
Organisations rarely handle tapes by hand. Robotic tape libraries hold thousands of cartridges and many drives; backup software, archive managers or LTFS decide what goes where; and tapes not in a drive are physically disconnected — an 'air gap' that ransomware cannot reach. IBM also sells its own enterprise tape format with higher capacity than LTO.

A tape library system. Software decides what to write; robots and drives do the physical work.

Think of it like…

A tape library is an automated warehouse: robots fetch the right box from the shelves and put it on the loading dock (drive), and boxes on the shelves are out of reach of burglars on the network.

Real-world example

Fictional insurer Meridian keeps 30 days of backups on disk and copies weekly backups to an LTO library at a second site; each week some cartridges are ejected and stored in a vault. When ransomware encrypts its disk backups, the vaulted tapes are untouched, and Meridian restores its core systems from them.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Backup or archive software writes data to tape through the library's drives.
  2. The library robot moves cartridges between storage slots, drives and import/export slots, reading barcodes.
  3. LTFS formats a tape with an index partition and a data partition so it looks like a drive with files and folders.
  4. Cartridges can be ejected and vaulted off-site, or kept in the library but logically offline.
  5. Libraries scale from a few dozen slots to tens of thousands by adding frames.
  6. Cloud providers are widely reported to run large tape libraries behind their deepest archive tiers.

Who uses it

Backup engineers, archive and records managers, ransomware-recovery teams, media archivists and cloud infrastructure teams.

Key takeaway

Interview point: tape gives a true air gap and WORM immutability at the lowest cost per terabyte, which is why it appears as the offline copy in 3-2-1-1-0 backup plans.

Going deeper

  • IBM's enterprise TS1170 drive (2023) stores 50 TB native on 3592 JF cartridges at up to 400 MB/s; the IBM-only 3592 line stays ahead of LTO on capacity per cartridge.
  • LTFS arrived with LTO-5 in 2010 and became ISO/IEC 20919:2016; its separate index partition lets software list files without reading the whole tape, making cartridges portable between systems.
  • Large library families include IBM TS4500 and Diamondback, Spectra Logic TFinity, and Quantum Scalar i6 and i7; the biggest systems reach hundreds of petabytes or more.
  • Air-gap strength varies: ejected, vaulted cartridges are strongest; a logical air gap — tapes inside the library but not mounted or reachable — is cheaper but depends on the library's own security.
  • Writing two copies to tapes in different libraries or sites, or using RAIT (striping with parity across drives), protects against losing a single cartridge.
  • Hierarchical storage management moves cold files from disk to tape automatically, leaving small stubs so users still see the files and trigger a recall when they open one.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Keeping every tape permanently in a networked library: an attacker with admin access can still erase them, so vault some copies.
  • Never testing restores: unread tapes may be unreadable or incomplete, so schedule regular restore tests.
  • Keeping 30-year archives only in one backup product's proprietary tape format: prefer LTFS or documented formats.

docs.title: Try it: Use a tape like a USB drive with LTFS (needs an LTO drive)
docs.text:
sudo mkltfs -d /dev/sg2           # formats (erases) the loaded cartridge
sudo ltfs -o devname=/dev/sg2 /mnt/ltfs
ls /mnt/ltfs && cp -r ~/project /mnt/ltfs/
sudo umount /mnt/ltfs             # writes the index back to tape

docs.title: 4.11 Optical Discs: CD, DVD, Blu-ray, M-DISC and Archival Disc
docs.text:
Optical discs store data as tiny marks read by a laser. Pressed discs (music and films) have moulded pits; recordable discs have a dye or inorganic layer that the burner's laser changes. Shorter laser wavelengths read smaller marks: CD uses infrared, DVD red and Blu-ray blue-violet light. In 2026 optical is a niche archive medium, and recordable media supply is shrinking.

CD vs DVD vs Blu-ray

CD DVD Blu-ray Laser wavelength 780 nm (infrared) 650 nm (red) 405 nm (blue-violet) Lens NA 0.45 0.60 0.85 Track pitch 1.6 µm 0.74 µm 0.32 µm Capacity per layer 700 MB 4.7 GB 25 GB Launched 1982 1996 2006

Shorter wavelengths and stronger lenses shrink the laser spot, packing tracks tighter.

Think of it like…

Like Braille read by light: the laser 'feels' marks as changes in reflected light, and a finer fingertip — a shorter wavelength — can read smaller dots.

Real-world example

A fictional city archive keeps meeting recordings on 100 GB M-DISC BD-R discs as a third copy. When Sony stopped making recordable Blu-ray media in 2025, the archivist checked remaining suppliers, kept verifying discs yearly with checksums and began planning migration of the collection to LTO tape.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A laser focuses through the disc's clear layer onto a reflective data layer spinning above it.
  2. Pits and lands (pressed) or burned marks (recordable) change reflectivity; transitions encode bits.
  3. Shorter wavelength plus a stronger lens means a smaller spot: 780 nm for CD, 650 nm for DVD, 405 nm for Blu-ray.
  4. Extra layers (dual-layer DVD, triple- and quad-layer BDXL) multiply capacity per disc.
  5. Recordable types are write-once (-R) or rewritable (-RW/RE) phase-change discs.

Who uses it

Archivists, libraries, legal and medical records departments, media distributors and digital preservation specialists.

Key takeaway

Know the capacities — CD 700 MB, DVD 4.7 GB (8.5 GB dual-layer), Blu-ray 25 GB per layer, BDXL 100-128 GB — and that M-DISC uses an inorganic layer for longer life.

Going deeper

  • Write-once discs use organic dyes (CD-R, DVD±R) or inorganic recording layers (many BD-R and all M-DISC); organic dyes are sensitive to light, heat and humidity, so lifetimes vary widely by brand and storage.
  • M-DISC, developed by Millenniata around 2009 and now sold by Verbatim, uses a stone-like inorganic layer; vendors claim centuries of life, and early independent stress tests found it outlasted dye-based discs.
  • ISO/IEC 16963 defines accelerated-ageing test methods for estimating the archival life of recordable optical discs; results depend heavily on storage temperature and humidity.
  • Sony and Panasonic announced the Archival Disc format in 2014 for 300 GB to 1 TB per disc, and Sony's Optical Disc Archive cartridges packed many discs together for broadcasters.
  • Sony ended production of recordable Blu-ray, MiniDisc and MiniDV media in February 2025, citing losses in its storage-media business, leaving fewer suppliers for archive-grade discs.
  • Facebook built a Blu-ray cold-storage rack prototype around 2014 holding about 10,000 discs (roughly 1 PB), showing optical's appeal for low-power cold data.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Trusting cheap dye discs for decades: verify them regularly and migrate; store them cool, dark and upright in cases.
  • Using solvent markers or adhesive labels: they can damage the data layer or unbalance the disc at high speed.
  • Assuming drives will always be available: keep a working drive and plan migration as optical hardware vanishes from new PCs.

docs.title: Try it: Check a burned disc's media and verify its files (Linux)
docs.text:
dvd+rw-mediainfo /dev/sr0            # media type, layers, recorded size
cd /media/$USER/ARCHIVE_DISC && sha256sum -c --quiet MANIFEST.sha256

docs.title: 4.12 Emerging Archive Media: Glass, Ceramic, DNA and Film
docs.text:
Researchers want archive media that last centuries, need no power and never require migration. Leading candidates include data written into glass with lasers (Microsoft's Project Silica), laser-etched ceramic layers (Cerabyte), synthetic DNA, and data printed on photographic film (Piql). In 2026 most are still in research or pilot stages.

Three candidate archive media

Glass (Silica) Ceramic (Cerabyte) DNA Write method Femtosecond-laser voxels Laser holes in ceramic film Chemical or enzymatic synthesis Read method Microscopy + ML High-speed camera DNA sequencing Claimed life 10,000+ years (lab ageing) Thousands of years (vendor) Centuries if cool and dry 2026 status Research phase complete Pilot systems First commercial offers planned Key players Microsoft Research Cerabyte Biomemory, Atlas Data Storage

All promise very long life; none yet matches tape on speed, cost and maturity.

Think of it like…

Like carving records into stone instead of writing them on paper: slower to write, but they survive fire, flood and time.

Real-world example

Fictional national library Aurora tests three 'forever' options: Piql film stored in an Arctic vault, a glass-storage research partnership and a DNA storage pilot. It keeps LTO tape as its working archive and treats the new media only as an extra insurance copy.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Glass: femtosecond lasers write tiny 3D marks (voxels) inside glass; microscopes and machine learning read them.
  2. Ceramic: lasers make nanoscale holes in a thin ceramic coating on glass; high-speed cameras read them.
  3. DNA: bits map to the bases A, C, G and T; DNA is synthesised, stored dry and read by sequencing.
  4. Film: data is printed as dense 2D codes on photosensitive film and read back by scanning.
  5. All aim for write-once, centuries-long life with zero power while in storage.

Who uses it

Archivists, cultural-heritage institutions, hyperscale research teams, synthetic-biology companies and storage researchers.

Key takeaway

Compare archive media on four axes — write speed, read latency, cost per TB and proven longevity; new media usually win on longevity and lose on speed and cost.

Going deeper

  • Microsoft's February 2026 Nature paper moved Project Silica from costly fused silica to cheap borosilicate glass, storing 2.02 TB on a 120 mm square, 2 mm plate (4.8 TB on fused silica), with ageing tests suggesting 10,000+ years.
  • Silica writes slowly — about 66 Mbit/s using four laser beams in the 2026 work, versus LTO's 400 MB/s — and Microsoft said the research phase was complete without announcing a product.
  • Cerabyte (Germany) coats thin glass with a ceramic layer about 10 nm thick and writes with femtosecond lasers; backers include Western Digital, Everpure (Pure Storage) and In-Q-Tel, and its first pilot targets about 1 PB per rack.
  • DNA's theoretical density is enormous — a 2017 'DNA Fountain' study estimated about 215 PB per gram — but synthesis cost and speed remain the barriers; SNIA's DNA Data Storage Alliance works on standards.
  • Atlas Data Storage spun out of Twist Bioscience in 2025 with $155 million in seed funding; Biomemory acquired Catalog's assets in March 2026 and aimed for first commercial products in the second half of 2026.
  • Piql writes data as dense visual codes on photosensitive film; the Arctic World Archive in a Svalbard mine, opened in 2017, stores such reels, including GitHub's 2020 Arctic Code Vault.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating lab longevity claims as proven: accelerated ageing assumes particular failure mechanisms, and real centuries remain untested.
  • Forgetting the reader: media that outlive their drives and software still need documented formats and available readers.
  • Planning budgets around emerging-media dates: most are pilots, so keep tape, disk or cloud as the production archive.

docs.title: 4.13 Cold Storage Tiers in the Cloud
docs.text:
Cloud providers sell archive tiers that are extremely cheap to keep data in — around $1 per terabyte per month — but charge to get it back, may make you wait hours, and bill a minimum storage period. Behind the scenes they use dense hard drives, tape and careful scheduling.

Storage price per TB-month (US list prices, approx., 2026). Archive tiers cost about 1/20th of standard storage — before retrieval fees.

Think of it like…

Like a self-storage unit far out of town: the monthly rent is tiny, but getting a box back means booking a delivery, paying a fee and waiting.

Real-world example

Fictional Westbrook Hospital must keep 400 TB of old scans for ten years. In S3 Glacier Deep Archive at about $0.00099 per GB-month, that costs roughly $396 a month. When a legal case needs 10 TB back, the standard retrieval fee is about $200, plus any network egress, and the data arrives within 12 hours.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose a tier by how often and how quickly you will need the data (hot, cool, cold, archive).
  2. Upload objects directly to the tier, or let lifecycle rules move them after a number of days.
  3. Pay a low per-GB monthly price but respect minimum storage durations (30, 90, 180 or 365 days).
  4. For offline archive tiers, request a restore (rehydration) and wait from minutes to about two days.
  5. Pay per-GB retrieval and per-request fees, plus egress if data leaves the cloud.

Who uses it

Cloud architects, FinOps teams, backup and compliance managers, and research data managers.

Key takeaway

Model total cost = storage + retrieval + requests + egress + early-deletion charges; archive tiers are cheap only if you rarely read the data.

Going deeper

  • AWS offers S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (milliseconds, 90-day minimum), Flexible Retrieval (minutes to hours, 90-day minimum) and Deep Archive (standard restores within 12 hours, bulk within 48, 180-day minimum).
  • Azure Blob Storage has Hot, Cool (30-day minimum), Cold (90-day) and Archive (180-day) tiers; Archive blobs are offline and must be rehydrated, which can take up to about 15 hours at standard priority.
  • Google Cloud Storage's Nearline (30-day), Coldline (90-day) and Archive (365-day) classes all return data in milliseconds; the trade-off is retrieval fees and minimum durations rather than waiting.
  • Azure introduced a 128 KiB minimum billable object size for its cold tiers, applying to new storage accounts from July 2026, so small files should be bundled before archiving.
  • S3's Glacier classes add about 40 KB of metadata per object, partly billed at Standard rates, so millions of tiny files cost more than expected; bundle them into tar or zip archives.
  • Providers do not publish their exact media, but tape and dense hard drives with power-managed scheduling are widely believed to sit behind the deepest tiers.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Archiving data you will read often: retrieval and egress fees can exceed what you saved on storage.
  • Deleting or moving objects early: minimum-duration charges still apply for the remaining days.
  • Treating 'archive' as 'backup': without versioning, Object Lock or a separate account, an error or attacker can still delete it.

docs.title: Try it: Archive and restore an object in S3 Glacier Deep Archive (AWS CLI, your own bucket)
docs.text:
aws s3 cp scans.tar s3://my-archive-bucket/ --storage-class DEEP_ARCHIVE

aws s3api restore-object --bucket my-archive-bucket --key scans.tar \
  --restore-request '{"Days":7,"GlacierJobParameters":{"Tier":"Standard"}}'

aws s3api head-object --bucket my-archive-bucket --key scans.tar   # shows restore status

docs.title: 4.14 Media Lifetimes, Migration and Digital Preservation
docs.text:
No storage medium lasts forever, and the drives, file formats and software needed to read data become obsolete even faster. Digital preservation is the discipline of keeping data readable and trustworthy for decades: several copies, regular integrity checks (fixity), planned migration to new media and formats, and good documentation.

The digital preservation cycle. Preservation is a loop of checking and moving data, not a one-off copy.

Think of it like…

Like caring for a historic building: you don't just lock the door — you inspect it regularly, repair damage early, keep the blueprints and move precious items before the roof fails.

Real-world example

Fictional museum Lumen Heritage holds 200 TB of digitised art. It keeps three copies (local disk, LTO tape and a cloud archive), recalculates SHA-256 checksums of every file yearly, stores images as TIFF and documents as PDF/A, and budgets its next tape migration before LTO-9 drives become scarce.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Ingest: record checksums plus technical and descriptive metadata when data arrives.
  2. Store several copies on different media types and in different locations.
  3. Run fixity checks on a schedule and repair any corrupted copy from a good one.
  4. Watch for obsolescence of media, drives and file formats.
  5. Migrate to new media every few years and normalise files to open formats.
  6. Document everything so future staff can understand and verify the collection.

Who uses it

Digital archivists, librarians, records managers, research data stewards and compliance officers in regulated industries.

Key takeaway

Media lifetime is rarely the real limit — drive and format obsolescence usually come first — so schedule migrations instead of waiting for media to fail.

Going deeper

  • The OAIS reference model (ISO 14721) defines the vocabulary of preservation — submission, archival and dissemination information packages — and the functions an archive must perform.
  • The NDSA Levels of Digital Preservation (version 2.0, 2019) give a practical matrix from level 1 to 4 across storage, integrity, control, metadata and content.
  • Rough practical lifetimes depend heavily on conditions: hard drives about five years in service, SSDs similar but needing power for retention, LTO tape rated around 30 years, and quality recordable discs years to decades.
  • Prefer open, well-documented formats such as PDF/A (ISO 19005), TIFF, PNG, FLAC, CSV and plain text; the Library of Congress publishes a Recommended Formats Statement to guide choices.
  • BagIt (RFC 8493) packages files with checksum manifests so transfers can be verified, and PREMIS is the standard data dictionary for recording preservation events and metadata.
  • LOCKSS ('Lots Of Copies Keep Stuff Safe'), started at Stanford in 1999, keeps many independent copies that audit each other — the principle behind geographically separated replicas.
  • Emulation, running old software on emulated hardware, complements migration for complex objects such as games, interactive art and legacy databases.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Storing one 'archival-grade' copy and forgetting it: one copy is no copy, so keep several independent copies and check them.
  • Checking only that files exist: verify content with checksums, because silent corruption leaves damaged files in place.
  • Waiting until old drives fail before migrating: by then replacement readers may be scarce and expensive.

docs.title: Try it: Create and verify a fixity manifest (Linux)
docs.text:
find /archive/collection1 -type f -exec sha256sum {} + > manifest.sha256
# ...months later
sha256sum -c --quiet manifest.sha256 && echo 'All files intact'

# Or package with BagIt (pip install bagit)
bagit.py --sha256 /archive/collection1

docs.title: How to read this guide
docs.text: Each topic follows the same simple pattern, so you can jump to any page and understand it without reading the rest first.

docs.title: How each topic is built
docs.text:
In plain English A jargon-free explanation of what the topic is. Think of it like… An everyday analogy that makes the idea click. Real-world example A short realistic story or worked example showing it in action. How it works The key steps, in order. Who uses it The people, jobs and industries that rely on it. Key takeaway The single most important thing to remember.

Many topics include a Try it box with a safe command or snippet. Then a table lists the most important entries — with what each one does and a concrete example.

docs.title: About this guide
docs.text: This guide is for students and self-learners. docs.title: Chapter 1: Memory & Storage Foundations
docs.text: Before studying chips, drives and file systems, you need the big picture: what separates memory from storage, how bits and bytes are counted (and why a 1 TB drive shows 931 GB), and how a pyramid of caches, DRAM, SSDs, disks and tape trades speed for capacity. This chapter explains the key metrics, how bits are physically stored, addressing and virtual memory, the history from punched cards to HBM, the journey of a saved file, reliability basics, and who makes and standardises it all.

docs.title: 1.1 Memory vs Storage — The Desk and the Filing Cabinet
docs.text:
Memory (RAM) is the computer's fast, temporary workspace that holds whatever the processor is using right now. Storage (an SSD, hard drive or cloud bucket) is the slower, permanent place that keeps files when the power is off. Programs and files are copied from storage into memory to be used, and saved back to storage to be kept.

Memory vs storage at a glance

Memory (DRAM) Storage (SSD / HDD) Keeps data without power No — volatile Yes — persistent Smallest access 1 byte (64-byte line) 4 KiB block Typical read latency ~100 ns ~80 µs SSD, ~8 ms HDD Typical PC capacity (2026) 16-64 GB 0.5-4 TB Rough cost dollars per GB cents per GB How software reaches it CPU load / store OS I/O request + driver

Every row is a trade-off: speed and byte access cost money and need constant power.

Think of it like…

Memory is your desk: small, everything within reach, but cleared every night. Storage is the filing cabinet down the corridor: huge and long-lasting, but you have to walk over to fetch or file anything.

Real-world example

Aisha's laptop has 16 GB of RAM and a 1 TB SSD. When she opens a 200 MB video project, the editor copies it from the SSD into RAM, where every edit takes nanoseconds. Her battery dies before she presses Save: the unsaved edits in RAM vanish, but yesterday's saved version on the SSD survives. With 30 browser tabs open, Windows starts pushing idle RAM pages to the SSD's page file and everything slows down.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Programs and data live permanently on storage (SSD, HDD, network or cloud) as files.
  2. When you launch something, the operating system copies the parts it needs from storage into RAM.
  3. The CPU reads and writes RAM directly, byte by byte, with load and store instructions — billions of times per second.
  4. Storage is reached through I/O requests for whole blocks (usually 4 KiB) handled by drivers and a drive controller.
  5. Saving copies changed data from RAM back to storage so it survives a power cut or reboot.

Who uses it

Everyone who buys, builds, supports or programs computers — from help-desk technicians sizing a laptop to cloud architects choosing instance memory and disk types.

Key takeaway

Memorise the four contrasts: memory is volatile, byte-addressable, nanosecond-fast and costly per GB; storage is persistent, block-addressable, micro-to-millisecond and cheap per GB.

Going deeper

  • The CPU reaches RAM through its integrated memory controller with ordinary instructions; storage sits behind an I/O interface (NVMe, SATA, USB) and a driver, so each access costs thousands to millions of CPU cycles.
  • Textbooks call RAM primary storage, internal drives secondary storage, robotic tape or disc libraries tertiary storage, and media you unplug and shelve off-line storage.
  • The speed gap is huge: a DRAM read takes roughly 100 ns, an NVMe SSD read 50-100 µs and a hard-drive read 5-10 ms — about a thousand and a hundred thousand times slower.
  • Operating systems use storage as overflow for RAM (Linux swap, Windows pagefile.sys, macOS swapfiles); it keeps programs alive but makes them sluggish when it happens constantly.
  • Phones and Apple-silicon Macs advertise RAM and storage separately (for example 12 GB + 256 GB); the bigger number is always flash storage, not memory.
  • The boundary is blurring: Intel Optane persistent memory (discontinued) was byte-addressable yet non-volatile, and CXL lets servers attach extra memory over a PCIe-style link.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling a phone's 256 GB of flash its 'memory': that is storage; its RAM is usually 8-16 GB.
  • Thinking more free disk space makes a slow PC faster: if apps are starved of RAM, adding memory helps far more than deleting files.
  • Believing typed data is safe: until it is saved and flushed to storage, a crash or power cut loses it.

docs.title: Try it: See how much memory and storage your own machine has
docs.text:
# Linux
free -h          # RAM and swap
df -h /          # storage behind the root file system
lsblk            # physical drives and partitions

# Windows PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object TotalPhysicalMemory
Get-Volume

A 2026 student laptop typically ships with 16 GB; video editors and developers often choose 32 GB or more. Leo's desktop boots from a 1 TB NVMe SSD and keeps photo archives on a 4 TB hard drive. Primary, secondary and tertiary storageClassic computer-architecture terms · Concept · Beginner Primary = memory the CPU addresses directly; secondary = internal drives; tertiary = robotic libraries of tape or discs. A bank's server holds today's transactions in RAM, last year's on SSD arrays and ten-year-old records in a tape library. Linux mounts /run and often /tmp as tmpfs, so temporary files never wear the SSD and vanish at shutdown. SAP HANA servers once used Optane PMem so in-memory databases restarted in minutes instead of reloading from disk. Architects designing a 2027 analytics platform evaluate CXL memory expanders as a cheaper tier between DRAM and NVMe SSDs. Memory sizing rule of thumbCommon IT practice · Concept · Beginner Size RAM for the working sets of everything running at once, then add headroom; size storage for data plus growth and backups. Ravi's help desk specifies 16 GB for office laptops and 32 GB for developers running containers and an IDE together.

docs.title: 1.2 Bits, Bytes and Units — Why a 1 TB Drive Shows 931 GB
docs.text:
A bit is a single 0 or 1; eight bits make a byte, enough for one letter. Bigger amounts use prefixes, but there are two systems: decimal (kilo = 1,000) used by drive makers and networks, and binary (kibi = 1,024) used for RAM and by Windows. The mismatch is why a new '1 TB' drive appears as about 931 GB.

How far binary units drift from decimal. The gap grows with each prefix step: about 7% at giga, 10% at tera and 13% at peta.

Think of it like…

It is like a 'dozen' that sometimes means 12 and sometimes 13: for one egg box the difference is small, but for a warehouse of boxes the gap becomes a whole pallet.

Real-world example

Jonas buys a '2 TB' external SSD for his gaming library. Windows shows 1.81 TB. The drive really holds 2,000,000,000,000 bytes; Windows divides by 1,099,511,627,776 (2^40) and labels the result 'TB' although it means TiB. Nothing is missing — and his '1 Gbps' internet line downloads at about 117 MB/s, because network speeds count bits, not bytes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start with bits (b): one 0 or 1. Group 8 bits into a byte (B); 4 bits is a nibble.
  2. Decimal SI prefixes multiply by 1,000: kB, MB, GB, TB, PB (drives, networks, macOS).
  3. Binary IEC prefixes multiply by 1,024: KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB (RAM, Windows, many Linux tools).
  4. Convert drive sizes: bytes ÷ 1,073,741,824 = GiB; so 10^12 bytes ÷ 2^30 ≈ 931.3 GiB.
  5. Convert speeds: divide bits per second by 8 to get bytes per second, then allow for protocol overhead.

Who uses it

Help-desk staff explaining 'missing' space, buyers comparing drives, network and storage engineers sizing links and arrays, and anyone sitting a CompTIA A+ exam.

Key takeaway

Memorise: 1 TB = 931 GiB, 1 GB = 0.931 GiB, and lowercase b = bits, uppercase B = bytes; a 1 Gb/s link moves at most 125 MB/s.

Going deeper

  • The IEC introduced binary prefixes (kibi, mebi, gibi, tebi) in 1998; they now live in the IEC 80000-13 standard, while SI defines kilo, mega and giga strictly as powers of ten.
  • JEDEC's memory standards still use 'GB' to mean 2^30 bytes for RAM chips and modules, so a 16 GB DIMM really holds 16 GiB — RAM marketing is binary, drive marketing is decimal.
  • Windows File Explorer divides by powers of 1,024 but prints KB, MB, GB and TB; macOS switched to decimal units in version 10.6 (2009), so the same drive shows its full labelled size on a Mac.
  • Formatted capacity is a little smaller again: partition tables, recovery partitions, file-system metadata and reserved blocks take space before you store anything.
  • Memory and interface speeds are often given in transfers per second: DDR5-6400 means 6,400 MT/s; on a 64-bit (8-byte) channel that is 6,400 × 8 = 51.2 GB/s peak.
  • In 2022 the General Conference on Weights and Measures added ronna (10^27) and quetta (10^30), the first new SI prefixes since 1991, partly because of growing global data volumes.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Returning a drive as 'short': a 1 TB drive showing 931 GB in Windows is complete; the units differ, not the bytes.
  • Mixing Mb and MB: a '500 Mbps' broadband plan peaks near 62 MB/s, not 500 MB/s.
  • Assuming every tool uses the same units: df -h, ls -lh, Explorer and Finder may disagree on the same file by several percent.

docs.title: Key memory types, devices, interfaces, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example Bit (b)Claude Shannon popularised the term, 1948 · Concept · Beginner The smallest unit of information: a single 0 or 1, stored as a charge, magnetic direction, pit or resistance. A 1 Gb DRAM chip from 2008 holds 1,073,741,824 bits — one tiny capacitor for each. Byte (B)IBM System/360 made 8-bit bytes standard, 1964 · Concept · Beginner Eight bits; enough to store one English letter in ASCII, and the unit computers use to address memory. The word 'storage' saved as plain ASCII text takes 7 bytes, or 56 bits. NibbleInformal computing term · Concept · Beginner Half a byte (4 bits), exactly one hexadecimal digit from 0 to F. The byte 0x3F is two nibbles: 3 (0011) and F (1111). SI decimal prefixesBIPM — International System of Units · Standard · Current · Beginner kilo = 10^3, mega = 10^6, giga = 10^9, tera = 10^12, peta = 10^15; used for drives and network speeds. Seagate labels a hard drive '24 TB' because it stores 24 × 10^12 bytes. IEC binary prefixes (KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB)IEC 80000-13 (introduced 1998) · Standard · Current · Beginner Unambiguous binary units: kibi = 2^10, mebi = 2^20, gibi = 2^30, tebi = 2^40 bytes. Linux's free -h and Kubernetes memory limits such as '512Mi' use binary units. JEDEC memory-size conventionJEDEC JESD100B.01 · Standard · Current · Intermediate Memory standards keep 'K', 'M' and 'G' as powers of two for RAM capacities, by long-standing custom. A '32 GB' DDR5 module holds 34,359,738,368 bytes, exactly 32 GiB. Decimal drive labellingDrive manufacturers, IDEMA practice · Concept · Current · Beginner Drive capacities are printed in decimal units, so the binary number shown by Windows always looks smaller. A '4 TB' hard drive appears as 3.63 TB in Windows Explorer. Windows size displayMicrosoft Windows File Explorer · Software · Current · Beginner Explorer calculates sizes in powers of 1,024 but labels them KB, MB, GB, TB — really KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB. A 1,000,000-byte file shows as '976 KB' in Explorer's Properties dialog. macOS size displayApple, decimal units since Mac OS X 10.6 (2009) · Software · Current · Beginner Finder uses decimal units, so drive capacities match the number on the box. The same 1 TB SSD shows as 1 TB on a Mac but 931 GB on a Windows PC. Bits per second vs bytes per secondNetworking and storage convention · Metric · Beginner Links are rated in bits per second (Mb/s, Gb/s); file transfers report bytes per second (MB/s) — divide by eight. A 10 Gb/s Ethernet link moves at most 1.25 GB/s before protocol overhead. Transfers per second (MT/s, GT/s)JEDEC and PCI-SIG usage · Metric · Current · Intermediate How many data transfers per second an interface makes; multiply by bus width in bytes for bandwidth. DDR5-5600 performs 5,600 million transfers per second, giving 44.8 GB/s per 64-bit channel. Formatted vs raw capacityFile systems and partitioning · Concept · Beginner Usable space is less than raw capacity after partitions, file-system metadata, reserved blocks and recovery images. A '512 GB' laptop SSD shows about 476 GiB, then roughly 455 GiB free once Windows and its recovery partition are installed. Ronna and quettaCGPM 2022 (27th General Conference on Weights and Measures) · Standard · Emerging · Beginner The newest SI prefixes: ronna = 10^27 and quetta = 10^30, with symbols R and Q. Analysts discussing yearly global data creation, measured in zettabytes, now have prefixes for far larger totals.

docs.title: 1.3 The Memory Hierarchy and Real Latencies
docs.text:
Computers stack several kinds of memory and storage in a pyramid: a few tiny, ultra-fast registers and caches at the top, gigabytes of DRAM in the middle, and terabytes of SSD, hard disk and tape at the bottom. Each step down is bigger and cheaper per byte but slower. Because programs reuse recent data and nearby data, the small fast layers catch most requests.

Typical access latency, register to tape. Log scale: each tier is roughly 3x to 1,000x slower than the one above it (approximate 2026 values).

Think of it like…

Think of a chef: spices in hand (registers), the chopping board (L1 cache), the counter (L2/L3), the fridge (DRAM), the cellar (SSD), and a warehouse across town (tape). Good chefs keep what they use most within arm's reach.

Real-world example

When Mei's photo app applies a filter, pixel values sit in registers and the L1 cache for a few nanoseconds each. The rest of the 48-megapixel image streams from DRAM at about 100 ns per new cache line. Opening another photo from the NVMe SSD costs around 80 µs per read — 800 times a DRAM access — and an old album on her NAS hard drive costs milliseconds per seek.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The CPU first looks in its registers, then L1 cache (about 1 ns).
  2. On a miss it checks L2 (~4 ns), then the shared L3 or last-level cache (~10-20 ns).
  3. Still missing? The memory controller fetches a 64-byte line from DRAM (~80-120 ns).
  4. If the data is not in RAM at all, the OS issues a storage read: ~50-100 µs on NVMe, 5-10 ms on a hard drive.
  5. Copies are kept in the faster levels, betting that the data — or its neighbours — will be needed again soon.

Who uses it

Software engineers tuning performance, system architects choosing hardware tiers, database and cloud engineers, and every computer-architecture student.

Key takeaway

Scale it to human time for interviews: if an L1 hit took 1 second, a DRAM access would take about 2 minutes, an SSD read about a day, and a hard-drive seek roughly three months.

Going deeper

  • Caches work because of locality: temporal (recently used data is reused soon) and spatial (neighbouring addresses are used together), which is why caches move whole 64-byte lines rather than single bytes.
  • Average memory access time (AMAT) = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty; with a 1 ns L1, 5% misses and a 20 ns penalty, AMAT is 2 ns.
  • Bandwidth also falls down the pyramid: L1 serves well over 100 GB/s per core, dual-channel DDR5-6000 about 96 GB/s, a PCIe 5.0 x4 SSD roughly 14 GB/s and a hard drive under 0.3 GB/s.
  • AI accelerators add a tier beside the processor: high-bandwidth memory (HBM) stacks deliver several terabytes per second to a GPU, at far higher cost per gigabyte than ordinary DRAM.
  • CXL-attached memory adds roughly one NUMA hop of latency over local DRAM, so operating systems treat it as a slower memory tier for colder pages.
  • Hard-drive latency is dominated by mechanics: a 7,200 RPM disk spins once every 8.3 ms, so average rotational delay alone is about 4.2 ms before seek time is added.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating latency and bandwidth as the same: a device can stream gigabytes per second yet still take 100 µs to return the first byte.
  • Quoting old numbers: 'disk is 10 ms' still applies to hard drives, but NVMe SSDs answer in tens of microseconds.
  • Assuming more cache always wins: a bigger cache is usually slower to search, which is why CPUs use several levels.

# macOS

docs.title: Key memory types, devices, interfaces, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example RegistersInside every CPU core · Component · Current · Beginner The handful of tiny storage slots inside a core that instructions operate on directly, accessed within a single clock cycle. An x86-64 core exposes 16 general-purpose 64-bit registers; with AVX-512, 32 vector registers each holding 64 bytes. L1 cachePer-core SRAM · Component · Current · Beginner The smallest, fastest cache, split into instruction and data halves, typically 32-64 KiB each per core, about 4-5 cycles away. AMD's Zen 5 core has a 48 KiB L1 data cache and a 32 KiB L1 instruction cache. L2 cachePer-core or per-cluster SRAM · Component · Current · Beginner A larger second-level cache, roughly 1-3 MiB per core in 2026 desktop CPUs, about 12-16 cycles away. Intel's Lion Cove performance cores in Core Ultra 200S chips carry 3 MiB of L2 each. L3 / last-level cacheShared SRAM on the CPU die or stacked on it · Component · Current · Intermediate A big cache shared by many cores, tens to hundreds of MiB, catching data before it goes off-chip to DRAM. A Ryzen 7 9800X3D pairs 32 MB of on-die L3 with 64 MB of stacked 3D V-Cache, 96 MB in total. Main memory (DRAM tier)DDR5, LPDDR5X modules or packages · Component · Current · Beginner Gigabytes of DRAM about 80-120 ns away; the last tier the CPU reaches with ordinary loads and stores. A cloud VM with 64 GiB of DRAM serves a whole product catalogue from memory instead of disk. High-bandwidth memory tierHBM stacks beside GPUs and accelerators · Component · Current · Intermediate Stacked DRAM on the processor package, trading capacity and cost for terabytes per second of bandwidth. An NVIDIA B200 GPU feeds its cores from about 180-192 GB of HBM3E at up to 8 TB/s. CXL memory tierCXL Consortium; memory expanders from Samsung, SK hynix, Micron and others · Technology · Emerging · Advanced Extra DRAM attached over a CXL link, slower than local DRAM but far faster than SSDs. A database server adds 512 GB of CXL memory so cold buffer-pool pages stay in memory rather than on flash. NVMe SSD tierNVM Express SSDs over PCIe · Device · Current · Beginner Flash storage answering random reads in tens of microseconds and streaming several GB/s. A game on a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD loads a level in a few seconds instead of half a minute from a hard drive. Hard-disk tierSeagate, Western Digital, Toshiba · Device · Current · Beginner Spinning magnetic disks with millisecond access but the lowest cost per terabyte for online data. A video-streaming company keeps its full film catalogue on 24-30 TB hard drives and only popular titles on flash. Archive tier (tape and cold cloud)LTO tape libraries; cloud archive classes · Service · Current · Beginner The slowest, cheapest tier: data may take minutes (tape) to hours (cloud deep archive) to return. Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive promises standard retrievals within 12 hours, at a tiny fraction of hot-storage price. Locality of referenceComputer architecture principle · Concept · Beginner Programs reuse recent data (temporal locality) and touch nearby addresses together (spatial locality), which makes caching work. Looping over an array in order is cache-friendly; jumping randomly through a huge linked list causes constant misses. Average memory access time (AMAT)Hennessy & Patterson, Computer Architecture · Metric · Intermediate Hit time plus miss rate times miss penalty — the effective latency a hierarchy delivers. 1 ns hit time, 2% miss rate and a 100 ns DRAM penalty give an AMAT of 3 ns. Latency numbers every programmer should knowPopularised by Jeff Dean and Peter Norvig · Resource · Beginner A famous table of rough costs — cache hit, DRAM access, SSD read, disk seek, network round trip — for back-of-envelope design. In a system-design interview, Sara estimates that 1,000 sequential disk seeks would take about 8 seconds and redesigns around SSDs.

docs.title: 1.4 Volatile vs Non-Volatile Memory
docs.text:
Volatile memory forgets everything when power is removed; non-volatile memory remembers. SRAM and DRAM are volatile, while flash, hard disks, tape and optical discs are non-volatile. Systems combine both: fast volatile memory for work, non-volatile storage for keeping.

Which memories forget when power is lost. The middle tier exists because businesses cannot afford to lose data in flight.

Think of it like…

Volatile memory is a whiteboard in a room where the cleaner wipes everything the moment the lights go out; non-volatile memory is a notebook that keeps your writing until you deliberately erase it.

Real-world example

Carlos closes his laptop lid and it sleeps: the DRAM stays powered in low-power self-refresh, so his work reappears instantly. On a long flight he chooses Hibernate instead: Windows copies RAM to hiberfil.sys on the SSD and powers off completely. Back home, the laptop reads that file back and his apps return in seconds without using battery overnight.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Volatile cells (SRAM latches, DRAM capacitors) need power continuously; DRAM also needs refreshing every few tens of milliseconds.
  2. Non-volatile cells hold state physically — trapped electrons, magnetic direction, a pit or a crystal phase.
  3. Systems protect in-flight data with flushes, batteries or capacitors before power fails.
  4. Sleep keeps RAM powered; hibernate copies RAM to non-volatile storage and switches off.
  5. Even non-volatile media fade eventually, so long-term data needs refreshing or migrating.

Who uses it

Hardware designers, firmware engineers, laptop and server administrators, forensic investigators, and storage engineers designing power-loss protection.

Key takeaway

Remember the exam pair: SRAM/DRAM = volatile; ROM, flash, magnetic and optical media = non-volatile — and 'non-volatile' still does not mean 'forever'.

Going deeper

  • DRAM is not instantly blank at power-off: charge decays over seconds, and much longer when chilled — the basis of the 2008 Princeton 'cold boot' attack that recovered disk-encryption keys from RAM.
  • Self-refresh lets DRAM keep its contents on milliwatts during sleep (ACPI S3 or Modern Standby), while hibernation (S4) writes a compressed RAM image to storage and removes power entirely.
  • Flash retention depends on temperature and wear: JEDEC's JESD218 endurance rules assume client SSDs keep data unpowered for 1 year at 30 °C at end of rated life, enterprise SSDs 3 months at 40 °C.
  • Drives and RAID controllers hold writes briefly in volatile DRAM; enterprise models add capacitors or batteries so that buffer can be flushed to flash if power suddenly fails.
  • Firmware settings that must survive power-off — UEFI variables, boot order — live in a small SPI flash chip, while the real-time clock runs from a coin-cell battery on the motherboard.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming switching off instantly erases RAM: remanence lasts seconds to minutes, so protect encryption keys and physically secure machines.
  • Thinking flash or discs keep data forever unpowered: retention is finite and shrinks with heat and wear; refresh and verify archives.
  • Relying on a consumer drive's write cache during power cuts: without power-loss protection, recently 'written' data can be lost.
