docs.title: Key memory types, devices, interfaces, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example Volatile memorySRAM, DRAM, HBM, GDDR · Concept · Beginner Memory that loses its contents when power is removed, chosen because it is fast and endlessly rewritable. When a server's power supply fails, every open connection's state held in DRAM is lost instantly. Non-volatile memory (NVM)Flash, magnetic, optical, ROM, MRAM · Concept · Beginner Memory that keeps data without power, by storing state physically rather than in a powered circuit. A USB stick left in a drawer for a year still holds Priya's thesis because flash cells trap their charge. Data remanenceSecurity and forensics term · Concept · Intermediate Data that physically lingers after deletion or power-off — in DRAM for seconds, on disks until overwritten. Forensic analysts recover deleted photos from a hard drive because the magnetic patterns were never overwritten. Cold boot attackHalderman et al., Princeton, 2008 · Concept · Advanced Reading secrets from DRAM shortly after power-off; cooling the chips slows charge decay from seconds to minutes. Researchers chilled memory modules, moved them to another PC and recovered BitLocker and FileVault keys. Self-refreshJEDEC DRAM standards · Concept · Current · Intermediate A low-power DRAM mode in which the chip refreshes its own cells while the memory controller sleeps. A laptop in sleep mode keeps 16 GB of LPDDR5X alive for days on a few hundred milliwatts. Sleep vs hibernateACPI S3 / Modern Standby vs S4 · Concept · Current · Beginner Sleep keeps RAM powered for instant resume; hibernate saves RAM to storage and turns the machine fully off. Windows writes hiberfil.sys, often several gigabytes, to the SSD when Carlos chooses Hibernate. Battery-backed write cacheRAID controllers and storage arrays · Component · Current · Intermediate Volatile cache protected by a battery or capacitor plus flash, so acknowledged writes survive a power cut. A hospital's storage array acknowledges database writes from protected cache in under a millisecond. NVDIMM-NJEDEC JESD245; Micron, SMART Modular and others · Device · Legacy · Advanced A DRAM module with on-board flash and a supercapacitor that copies DRAM to flash when power fails. Storage controllers used NVDIMM-N to keep write journals safe before Optane and CXL alternatives arrived. ROM, EPROM and EEPROMMask ROM; Intel EPROM (1971); EEPROM · Component · Current · Beginner Read-only or rarely rewritten non-volatile memory for firmware and settings; EEPROM can be rewritten byte by byte. Every DDR5 module stores its speed and timing data in a small serial EEPROM in the SPD hub. UEFI NVRAM and CMOS batteryMotherboard firmware storage · Component · Current · Beginner Firmware settings live in SPI flash; a coin-cell battery keeps the real-time clock running when the PC is unplugged. When a 10-year-old PC forgets the date at every boot, a new CR2032 coin cell fixes it. Data retention timeJEDEC JESD218 and media vendors · Metric · Intermediate How long a medium keeps readable data without power or refresh; varies with temperature, wear and technology. Archivists rewrite old flash-based camera cards onto fresh media every few years rather than trusting decades. Volatile write cacheDrives, operating systems · Concept · Intermediate A fast buffer that holds data before it reaches durable media; data is safe only after a flush command completes. Databases issue fsync, which makes the OS flush its cache and tell the drive to empty its own buffer.

docs.title: 1.5 Key Metrics: Latency, Bandwidth, IOPS, Endurance and $/GB
docs.text:
Memory and storage are compared with a few numbers: latency (how long one request takes), bandwidth or throughput (how much data per second), IOPS (how many small requests per second), capacity, endurance (how much writing it survives), reliability, power and cost per gigabyte. Which number matters most depends on the job.

The numbers that describe a memory or drive. No single metric decides; match the metric to the workload.

Think of it like…

A road can be judged by travel time (latency), how many cars pass per hour (throughput), how many separate deliveries it handles (IOPS), how long the tarmac lasts (endurance) and what it cost to build (cost per lane-mile).

Real-world example

Fatima compares two SSDs for her company's database. Drive A claims 7,000 MB/s sequential reads; drive B only 5,000 MB/s but 1,000,000 random 4 KiB read IOPS and steady 99th-percentile latency under 200 µs. Because the database makes millions of small random reads, she picks drive B — the sequential headline number barely matters for her workload.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify the workload: big sequential streams, small random requests, or a mix.
  2. Pick matching metrics: throughput for streams, IOPS and latency for random I/O, endurance for write-heavy jobs.
  3. Check the conditions behind each figure: block size, queue depth, read/write mix and test duration.
  4. Look at tail latency (p99, p99.9), not just averages, for user-facing systems.
  5. Divide price by usable capacity and by endurance to compare true cost.

Who uses it

Storage and infrastructure engineers, performance testers, procurement teams, cloud architects choosing volume types, and hardware reviewers.

Key takeaway

Know the identities: throughput = IOPS × block size, and Little's law: requests in flight = IOPS × latency — so 32 outstanding requests at 100 µs each yield 320,000 IOPS.

Going deeper

  • Vendors quote best cases: SSD sequential figures use 128 KiB blocks at high queue depth, random IOPS use 4 KiB blocks at queue depth 32 or more; a single-threaded app at queue depth 1 sees far less.
  • Tail latency matters at scale: if one web page fans out to 100 servers, the slowest 1% of responses decides how fast almost every page loads.
  • Annualised failure rate relates to MTBF as AFR ≈ 8,766 hours ÷ MTBF; a 2.5-million-hour MTBF means about 0.35% of drives failing per year under rated conditions.
  • Endurance is quoted as terabytes written (TBW) or drive writes per day (DWPD) over the warranty; a 3.84 TB drive rated 1 DWPD for 5 years allows about 7,000 TB written.
  • Energy per bit (picojoules per bit moved) increasingly decides AI hardware design, because moving data between memory and processors can cost more energy than computing on it.
  • In 2026 cost per gigabyte is highly volatile: AI demand roughly doubled DRAM contract prices within months, so always date-stamp any $/GB comparison.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing drives on sequential MB/s alone: most operating-system and database work is small random I/O, where IOPS and latency rule.
  • Reading MTBF as lifespan: a 2-million-hour MTBF does not mean a drive lasts 228 years; it is a population failure rate.
  • Ignoring test conditions: an IOPS figure without block size, queue depth and read/write mix is meaningless.

docs.title: Try it: Little's law and throughput maths in Python
docs.text:
qd, lat_s = 32, 100e-6          # 32 requests in flight, 100 µs each
iops = qd / lat_s
print(f"IOPS: {iops:,.0f}")
print(f"Throughput at 4 KiB: {iops*4096/1e9:.2f} GB/s")
print(f"AFR for 2.5M h MTBF: {8766/2.5e6:.2%}")

docs.title: Key memory types, devices, interfaces, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example LatencyMeasured in ns, µs or ms · Metric · Beginner The time from issuing one request until its data arrives or the write is acknowledged. A DDR5 read takes about 100 ns; a 4 KiB NVMe read about 80 µs; a hard-disk read about 8 ms. Tail latency (p99, p99.9)Site-reliability engineering practice · Metric · Intermediate The latency below which 99% or 99.9% of requests finish; it exposes rare slow requests that averages hide. An SSD averages 90 µs but its p99.9 is 4 ms during garbage collection, causing visible app stutters. BandwidthGB/s, often a theoretical peak · Metric · Beginner The maximum data rate an interface or memory can sustain, set by width × transfer rate. One DDR5-6400 channel peaks at 51.2 GB/s; a PCIe 5.0 x4 link at about 15.8 GB/s per direction. ThroughputMB/s or GB/s actually achieved · Metric · Beginner The data rate a real workload achieves, usually below the theoretical bandwidth because of overheads. Copying a 50 GB video folder between two SSDs averages 2.1 GB/s despite a 7 GB/s rating. With 64 requests in flight and 200 µs latency, a drive delivers 320,000 IOPS. A 24-drive array of 30 TB disks holds 720 TB raw but about 600 TB after RAID 6 groups and spares. Hard-drive makers use heat-assisted recording to push platter density past 3 TB per platter. A 2026 storage buyer compares a 30 TB hard drive and a 30 TB QLC SSD by $/TB, power and rack space. A 1.92 TB drive rated 3 DWPD for 5 years may absorb about 10,500 TB of writes. AI-chip architects choose HBM partly because it moves each bit with less energy than off-board memory. MTBF and AFRVendor datasheets; Backblaze fleet statistics · Metric · Intermediate Mean time between failures and annualised failure rate describe how many devices in a large fleet fail per year. Backblaze publishes quarterly hard-drive failure statistics from its fleet of hundreds of thousands of drives, usually around 1-2% AFR.

docs.title: 1.6 How Bits Are Physically Stored: Charge, Magnetism, Light and Resistance
docs.text:
Every memory or storage technology needs some physical thing with two (or more) distinguishable states. Chips store electric charge or switch transistors; hard drives and tape magnetise tiny regions; optical discs change how a spot reflects light; newer memories change a material's electrical resistance. Reading means sensing that state without destroying it — or rewriting it straight after.

Four physical ways to keep a bit

Electric charge Magnetism Light / resistance Where you meet it DRAM, SRAM, flash Hard disks, tape, MRAM Optical discs, PCM, ReRAM How it is written Voltage moves electrons Field flips magnetic grains Laser or current changes material How it is read Sense voltage or current Head senses stray field Reflectivity or resistance Keeps data unpowered DRAM/SRAM no; flash yes Yes Yes Main weakness Leakage, wear (flash) Mechanics, slow access Speed or density limits

Each principle trades speed, density, endurance and cost differently.

Think of it like…

It is like leaving messages using different materials: chalk marks (charge) fade unless retraced, fridge magnets (magnetism) stay where you put them, holes punched in card (optical pits) are permanent, and a dimmer switch's position (resistance) can be read by how bright the lamp is.

Real-world example

Tomás traces one family photo through his devices. On his phone it is electrons trapped in 3D NAND flash cells; in RAM while he edits it, charge in billions of DRAM capacitors; in his NAS it becomes magnetic grains on a hard-drive platter; and on the Blu-ray he gives his grandmother, it is laser-burned marks in a dye layer.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose a physical property with clearly different states: charge, magnetisation, reflectivity, resistance or polarisation.
  2. Write by applying energy: a voltage, a magnetic field, a laser pulse or a current.
  3. Read by sensing: a tiny voltage change, magnetic field, reflected light or current.
  4. Store more than one bit per cell by using several levels (for example 8 or 16 charge levels in flash).
  5. Wrap the noisy physical signal in error-correcting codes so the stored bits come back exact.

Who uses it

Device physicists, semiconductor and media engineers, firmware developers, data-recovery specialists, and students choosing between memory technologies.

Key takeaway

A neat exam table: charge = SRAM/DRAM/flash; magnetism = HDD, tape, MRAM; light = CD/DVD/Blu-ray; resistance = PCM, ReRAM and MRAM read-out.

Going deeper

  • A DRAM cell stores a few femtofarads of charge — only tens of thousands of electrons — in a tall, thin capacitor, so sense amplifiers must detect very small voltage differences on the bitline.
  • Flash stores charge in a floating gate or a silicon-nitride charge trap; with QLC flash the cell must distinguish 16 charge levels, so reading needs careful voltage thresholds and strong ECC.
  • Hard drives store bits as magnetic transitions in grains only nanometres across; read heads use tunnelling magnetoresistance to sense them while flying a few nanometres above the platter.
  • Optical discs encode bits in pits and lands (pressed discs) or in dye and phase-change layers (recordable and rewritable discs), read by a 780 nm (CD), 650 nm (DVD) or 405 nm (Blu-ray) laser.
  • Resistance-based memories change a material's state: phase-change memory switches chalcogenide glass between amorphous and crystalline; ReRAM forms or breaks conductive filaments; MRAM flips a magnetic layer to change tunnelling resistance.
  • Real devices never read perfectly: hard drives use signal processing and LDPC codes, flash SSDs use LDPC, and optical discs use Reed-Solomon codes to turn noisy physics into exact bytes.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming a 'bit' is always one physical cell: QLC flash puts 4 bits in one cell, while some codes spread one bit's information across many cells.
  • Thinking magnets near a laptop wipe its SSD: flash stores charge, not magnetism; strong magnets are a theoretical risk mainly to hard drives and tapes.

docs.title: Key memory types, devices, interfaces, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example Capacitor charge (DRAM)Robert Dennard's 1T1C cell, IBM · Concept · Current · Beginner A tiny capacitor charged or empty represents 1 or 0; it leaks, so it must be refreshed every few tens of milliseconds. Each DRAM chip in a 32 GB DDR5 module contains billions of capacitors refreshed thousands of times per second. Transistor latch (SRAM)Six-transistor cross-coupled inverter cell · Concept · Current · Beginner Two inverters feeding each other hold a 1 or 0 as long as power flows, with no refresh needed. The CPU's L1 cache stores data as SRAM latches switching in well under a nanosecond. Trapped charge (flash)Floating-gate and charge-trap cells · Concept · Current · Beginner Electrons pushed through an insulator stay trapped for years, shifting the transistor's threshold voltage to encode bits. A microSD card in a dashcam stores video as electrons trapped in 3D NAND charge-trap layers. Multi-level cellsFlash (MLC, TLC, QLC, PLC) and some emerging memories · Concept · Current · Intermediate Distinguishing more than two levels per cell stores several bits in one physical spot, cutting cost but reducing margins. A QLC cell uses 16 voltage levels to hold 4 bits, packing more data into the same silicon than TLC. Magnetic domainsHard disks and tape · Concept · Current · Beginner Regions of magnetic grains pointing one way or the other; data is encoded in the transitions between them. An LTO tape cartridge stores tens of terabytes as magnetic transitions on a thin ribbon of tape. Tunnelling magnetoresistanceRead heads and MRAM cells · Concept · Current · Advanced Electrical resistance through a thin insulating barrier changes with the relative magnetic direction of two layers. A hard-drive read head converts the platter's weak field into a measurable resistance change billions of times per second. Pits and landsPressed CD, DVD and Blu-ray discs · Concept · Legacy · Beginner Microscopic bumps and flat areas on a disc change how a laser reflects; transitions between them encode bits. A movie studio stamps millions of Blu-ray discs from one master, each carrying pits only about 150 nm long. Dye and phase-change recordingRecordable (R) and rewritable (RW/RE) optical discs · Concept · Legacy · Intermediate A laser darkens organic dye (write-once) or switches an alloy between crystal and glass (rewritable). A BD-RE disc can be rewritten many times because its phase-change layer switches back to crystalline when gently reheated. Phase-change material (PCM)Chalcogenide alloys such as GST · Concept · Legacy · Advanced A material switched by heat between low-resistance crystal and high-resistance glass; used in rewritable discs and PCM chips. Intel and Micron's 3D XPoint, sold as Optane, used a resistance-change cell with ovonic threshold switches. Resistive switching (ReRAM)Metal-oxide and conductive-bridge memories · Concept · Emerging · Advanced A voltage forms or breaks a tiny conductive filament, toggling a cell between low and high resistance. Some microcontrollers offer embedded ReRAM as an alternative to embedded flash at advanced process nodes. Ferroelectric polarisationFeRAM; hafnium-oxide ferroelectrics · Concept · Current · Advanced A crystal's electric polarisation points up or down and stays put without power, storing a bit with very low write energy. Smart meters use FeRAM chips to log readings every second without wearing out. Laser-written glass voxelsMicrosoft Research Project Silica · Concept · Emerging · Intermediate Femtosecond laser pulses write tiny 3D marks inside quartz glass, read by microscope; designed for very long-term archives. Microsoft demonstrated storing a full-length film in a coaster-sized piece of quartz glass. DNA base sequencesResearch labs and the DNA Data Storage Alliance · Concept · Emerging · Intermediate Bits are encoded as sequences of the bases A, C, G and T in synthetic DNA — extremely dense but slow and costly. Researchers have stored files and short videos in synthetic DNA and read them back by sequencing.

docs.title: 1.7 Addressing, Words and Alignment
docs.text:
Memory is a long numbered row of bytes; each number is an address. The CPU moves data in words (8 bytes on a 64-bit machine) and caches move 64-byte lines, while drives are addressed by block numbers. How addresses are written (hexadecimal), ordered (endianness) and aligned affects correctness and speed.

Units of data, from bit to page. Each layer is how a different part of the system likes to move data.

Think of it like…

Memory is a street of numbered houses. A word is a terrace of eight houses delivered together; a cache line is a whole block of the street; and a disk block number is like a warehouse shelf number rather than a house number.

Real-world example

Nadia's C program reads a 4-byte integer at address 0x7FFE0010. The CPU fetches the whole 64-byte line starting at 0x7FFE0000 into L1. Because her Intel laptop is little-endian, the value 0x12345678 sits in memory as 78 56 34 12. When she saves the data, the file system maps it to logical block address 1,048,576 on her SSD.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Software uses addresses written in hexadecimal, e.g. 0x7FFE0010.
  2. The CPU loads and stores bytes, words or vectors; naturally aligned accesses are fastest.
  3. Caches fetch the whole aligned 64-byte line containing the address.
  4. The memory controller decodes the physical address into channel, rank, bank, row and column.
  5. For storage, the file system translates file offsets into logical block addresses (LBAs) that the drive understands.

Who uses it

Programmers in C, C++, Rust and assembly; embedded and firmware engineers; reverse engineers and exploit developers; anyone debugging crashes or storage layouts.

Key takeaway

Know the cliff: a 32-bit address reaches only 2^32 bytes = 4 GiB, which is why 32-bit Windows could not use more than about 4 GB of RAM.

Going deeper

  • x86-64 CPUs implement 48-bit virtual addresses (256 TiB) with four-level paging, or 57-bit (128 PiB) with five-level paging; physical addresses are limited separately, up to 52 bits by the architecture.
  • Most x86 and Arm systems are little-endian (least significant byte first), while network protocols send multi-byte numbers big-endian, so code converts with functions such as htonl and ntohl.
  • Misaligned accesses that straddle a 64-byte cache line or 4 KiB page cost extra cycles on x86 and can fault on some embedded CPUs, so compilers pad structures to natural alignment.
  • Apple's M-series chips use 128-byte cache lines, while most x86 and many Arm server chips use 64 bytes — one reason performance tuning differs between platforms.
  • Drives moved from 512-byte to 4,096-byte physical sectors (Advanced Format) around 2010; '512e' drives emulate 512-byte addressing, while '4Kn' drives expose 4 KiB natively.
  • Memory controllers scatter consecutive cache lines across channels, ranks and banks using address-hash functions so that streaming accesses use all of them in parallel.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming an address in your program is a physical RAM location: it is virtual, translated by the MMU, and changes between runs because of ASLR.
  • Writing binary files on one machine and reading them on another without fixing endianness, which silently scrambles every multi-byte number.
  • Misaligning partitions on 4K-sector drives, which makes every write touch two physical sectors and halves performance.

docs.title: Try it: Peek at addresses, endianness and word size in Python
docs.text:
import sys, struct, ctypes
print(sys.byteorder)                       # 'little' on x86 and most Arm
print(struct.pack('<I', 0x12345678).hex())  # 78563412
print(ctypes.sizeof(ctypes.c_void_p) * 8, 'bit pointers')
x = ctypes.c_int(42)
print(hex(ctypes.addressof(x)))           # a (virtual) address

docs.title: Key memory types, devices, interfaces, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example Memory addressEvery CPU architecture · Concept · Beginner A number identifying one byte of memory, usually written in hexadecimal such as 0x7FFE0010. A crash log reports an access violation at 0x0000000000000000 — a null-pointer dereference. Hexadecimal notationBase 16, digits 0-9 and A-F · Format · Beginner Each hex digit is 4 bits, so addresses and raw bytes are far shorter and easier to read than in binary. The byte 11111111 is written 0xFF; a 64-bit address needs at most 16 hex digits. Word sizeCPU architecture (16-, 32-, 64-bit) · Concept · Current · Beginner The natural width of a CPU's registers and pointers; today's PCs, phones and servers use 64-bit words. A 64-bit pointer occupies 8 bytes, so a linked list of a million nodes spends 8 MB just on 'next' pointers. Address-space limitPointer and address-bus width · Concept · Beginner N address bits reach 2^N bytes: 32 bits reach 4 GiB; 48-bit virtual addressing reaches 256 TiB. An old 32-bit Windows XP PC with 8 GB installed could use only about 3.25 GB. EndiannessLittle-endian (x86, most Arm) vs big-endian (network order) · Concept · Intermediate The order in which the bytes of a multi-byte number are stored in memory or sent on the wire. 0x12345678 is stored as 78 56 34 12 on a little-endian laptop but sent as 12 34 56 78 in a TCP header. AlignmentCPU and compiler ABIs · Concept · Intermediate Placing data at addresses that are multiples of its size so the CPU can fetch it in one access. A C struct holding a 1-byte char and an 8-byte double usually occupies 16 bytes because of padding. Cache lineCPU caches (64 B on most x86/Arm; 128 B on Apple M-series) · Concept · Current · Intermediate The fixed-size chunk caches move to and from memory; touching one byte brings in the whole line. Two threads updating counters 8 bytes apart in the same line slow each other down — 'false sharing'. PointerC, C++, Rust (references), assembly · Concept · Beginner A variable holding a memory address; dereferencing it reads or writes the data at that address. Rust's borrow checker prevents dangling pointers that cause use-after-free bugs in C programs. Memory-mapped I/O (MMIO)PCIe devices, SoC peripherals · Concept · Current · Advanced Device registers appear at memory addresses, so the CPU controls hardware with ordinary loads and stores. An NVMe driver rings the SSD's 'doorbell' by writing to an MMIO address in the device's PCIe BAR. Logical block address (LBA)ATA, SCSI and NVMe command sets · Concept · Current · Intermediate Drives number their blocks 0, 1, 2 … N; the OS asks for 'LBA 2048, length 8' rather than a physical location. A GPT partition often starts at LBA 2048, which is exactly 1 MiB on a drive with 512-byte logical blocks. Advanced Format sectors (512e / 4Kn)IDEMA Advanced Format, around 2010 · Format · Current · Intermediate Drives with 4,096-byte physical sectors, either emulating 512-byte logical blocks (512e) or exposing 4 KiB natively (4Kn). Running 'fsutil fsinfo sectorinfo C:' on Windows shows logical and physical sector sizes. Physical address decodingIntegrated memory controllers · Concept · Current · Advanced Splitting a physical address into channel, rank, bank group, bank, row and column bits to locate it in DRAM. Consecutive 64-byte lines land in different channels and banks, so a big memory copy uses them all at once.

docs.title: 1.8 Virtual Memory, Pages and Swap
docs.text:
Every program believes it has a huge private memory of its own. The operating system and the CPU's memory-management unit (MMU) secretly map those virtual addresses onto real RAM in fixed-size pages, usually 4 KiB. Pages that do not fit can be compressed or moved out to storage (swap) and brought back when needed.

From a virtual address to data. Most accesses stop at the TLB; page faults are rare but very expensive.

Think of it like…

Virtual memory is like a hotel where every guest is told they are in 'Room 1'. The front desk (the MMU) privately maps each guest's Room 1 to a different real room, and moves rarely-seen guests' luggage into the basement store (swap) until they ask for it.

Real-world example

Daniel runs a browser, Slack and a 12 GB Docker build on a laptop with 16 GB of RAM. Linux maps each program's pages onto physical frames; idle browser tabs get compressed in zram, and some build pages are pushed to the swap file on the SSD. When he switches back to an old tab, a page fault brings its pages back — the short pause he notices is the cost of that trip.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A program uses a virtual address; the CPU's MMU looks up its page in the TLB, a small translation cache.
  2. On a TLB miss, the hardware walks the page tables (four or five levels on x86-64) to find the physical frame.
  3. If the page is not in RAM, a page fault hands control to the OS.
  4. The OS finds a free frame, evicting or compressing another page if memory is full.
  5. It loads the needed page from swap or a file, updates the page table and restarts the instruction.

Who uses it

Operating-system and kernel engineers, Linux and Windows administrators tuning servers, developers chasing memory leaks, and container platform engineers setting memory limits.

Key takeaway

Interview line: virtual memory gives each process isolation, the illusion of a large contiguous space, and lets the OS overcommit RAM — at the cost of page faults when the working set does not fit.

Going deeper

  • A minor page fault (page already in RAM, just unmapped) costs about a microsecond; a major fault that reads from an NVMe SSD costs tens of microseconds, and from a hard drive several milliseconds.
  • With 4 KiB pages, a 1,536-entry second-level TLB covers only 6 MiB; 2 MiB huge pages cover 3 GiB with the same entries, which is why databases and VMs often enable them.
  • Linux overcommits memory by default and, when RAM and swap run out, the OOM killer terminates the process with the highest badness score; containers hit the same mechanism through cgroup memory limits.
  • Memory compression trades CPU time for capacity: macOS has compressed memory since 10.9, Windows 10 and 11 compress pages in the memory manager, and Linux offers zram and zswap.
  • Apple-silicon Macs use 16 KiB pages and Arm64 Linux supports 4, 16 or 64 KiB granules; bigger pages cut TLB misses but waste more memory on small allocations.
  • Address-space layout randomisation (ASLR) places stacks, heaps and libraries at random virtual addresses each run, making memory-corruption exploits much harder to aim.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Disabling swap to 'make things faster': without it, memory spikes trigger the OOM killer or crashes instead of a brief slowdown.
  • Reading 'free' memory as wasted: Linux and Windows deliberately fill spare RAM with file cache; watch 'available', not 'free'.
  • Treating virtual size (VSZ) as real usage: resident set size (RSS) or Windows 'working set' shows what actually occupies RAM.

docs.title: Try it: Watch memory, paging and swap on your own machine
docs.text:
# Linux
getconf PAGESIZE            # usually 4096
free -h
vmstat 1 5                  # si/so columns = swap in/out per second
grep -E 'MemTotal|MemAvailable|SwapTotal|HugePages_Total' /proc/meminfo

# Windows PowerShell
Get-CimInstance Win32_PageFileUsage | Select-Object Name, AllocatedBaseSize, CurrentUsage

docs.title: Key memory types, devices, interfaces, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example Virtual address spaceEvery modern OS (Linux, Windows, macOS, Android, iOS) · Concept · Current · Beginner The private range of addresses each process sees, mapped by the OS onto physical RAM or storage. Two programs can both use address 0x400000 without conflict because each maps it to a different physical frame. Page and page framex86-64, Arm64 MMUs · Concept · Current · Beginner Virtual memory is split into fixed pages (usually 4 KiB) placed into equally sized frames of physical RAM. A 10 MiB image buffer occupies 2,560 pages of 4 KiB, which can sit anywhere in physical memory. Page tableOS-managed, hardware-walked structure · Component · Current · Intermediate A multi-level tree mapping virtual page numbers to physical frames, plus permission bits like read, write and execute. The no-execute bit in a page-table entry stops attackers running code injected into a data page. Memory-management unit (MMU)Part of every application-class CPU · Component · Current · Intermediate Hardware that translates virtual to physical addresses on every access and enforces page permissions. When a buggy app writes to a read-only page, the MMU raises a fault and the OS reports a segmentation fault. Translation lookaside buffer (TLB)CPU cache for address translations · Component · Current · Intermediate A small, fast cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations; misses force slower page-table walks. A graph-analytics job touching memory randomly suffers many TLB misses until huge pages are enabled. Huge pagesx86-64 2 MiB and 1 GiB pages; Linux THP and HugeTLB · Concept · Current · Advanced Larger pages that let each TLB entry cover far more memory, reducing translation overhead for big workloads. A PostgreSQL server with a 64 GB buffer pool uses 2 MiB huge pages to cut TLB misses. Page fault (minor / major)CPU exception handled by the OS · Concept · Intermediate An access to a page not currently mapped; minor faults just fix the mapping, major faults read from storage. Opening a large file with mmap triggers major faults the first time each page is touched. Swap / page fileLinux swap partition or file; Windows pagefile.sys; macOS swapfiles · Concept · Current · Beginner Storage space where the OS parks inactive memory pages so RAM can be reused for active ones. Ana's 8 GB laptop survives a big spreadsheet by paging 3 GB of idle browser tabs to the SSD. Memory compression (zram, zswap)Linux kernel; macOS and Windows memory managers · Software · Current · Intermediate Compressing idle pages in RAM instead of writing them out, trading a little CPU for effective capacity. Fedora and ChromeOS enable zram swap by default, keeping low-memory laptops responsive. Overcommit and the OOM killerLinux memory manager; cgroup limits · Concept · Current · Intermediate Linux lets programs reserve more memory than exists; if real demand exceeds RAM plus swap, it kills a process. A Kubernetes pod exceeding its 2 GiB limit is terminated with reason 'OOMKilled'. Commit chargeMicrosoft Windows memory manager · Metric · Current · Intermediate The total memory Windows has promised to processes, backed by RAM plus page file; it cannot exceed the commit limit. Task Manager shows 'Committed 22/31 GB' on a 16 GB PC with a 15 GB page file. Resident set size (RSS)Linux ps, top; Windows 'working set' · Metric · Intermediate How much of a process's memory is actually in physical RAM right now, as opposed to merely reserved. top shows Java with 30 GB virtual size but only 4 GB resident — the real RAM cost. Memory-mapped files (mmap)POSIX mmap; Windows CreateFileMapping · Concept · Current · Advanced Mapping a file into the address space so reading memory reads the file, with paging handled by the OS. SQLite and many search engines memory-map index files so hot parts stay cached in RAM automatically. Address-space layout randomisation (ASLR)Linux, Windows, macOS, Android, iOS · Concept · Current · Intermediate Randomising where code, stack and heap appear in virtual memory so attackers cannot predict target addresses. Running cat /proc/self/maps twice on Linux shows the stack at a different address each time.

docs.title: 1.9 A Short History, Part 1: Cards, Drums, Core and the First Disk
docs.text:
Before chips, computers remembered data in strange and wonderful ways: holes in cards, sound pulses in tubes of mercury, spots of charge on TV-like screens, magnetised spinning drums, and tiny iron rings. In 1956 IBM shipped the first hard-disk drive, the size of two refrigerators. These ideas shaped words we still use, like 'core dump' and 'drive'.

Storage before the chip. Each step traded mechanical complexity for more capacity and faster access.

Think of it like…

It is like the history of writing: from knots in rope and clay tablets to paper books — each medium remembered more, faster and more cheaply than the one before.

Real-world example

In 1956 a company leasing IBM's RAMAC 305 system got the IBM 350 disk: fifty 24-inch platters spinning at 1,200 RPM, holding about 3.75 MB and weighing around a ton. Today the same 3.75 MB is one smartphone photo — and a 1 TB microSD card the size of a fingernail holds over 250,000 times more.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. 1890s-1950s: punched cards and paper tape store data as holes read by machines.
  2. Late 1940s: the first electronic computers use mercury delay lines and Williams-Kilburn tubes as main memory.
  3. 1950s: magnetic drums and magnetic tape add bigger, slower storage.
  4. 1953 onward: magnetic-core memory becomes the standard main memory for two decades.
  5. 1956: the IBM 350 introduces random-access disk storage; later the floppy disk (1971) makes storage portable.

Who uses it

Computer-science students, museum curators, digital-preservation specialists, and anyone who enjoys knowing why we 'dump core' or call things 'drives'.

Key takeaway

Memorise three anchors: core memory (1950s-1970s main memory), IBM 350 RAMAC (1956, first hard disk, ~3.75 MB) and the Intel 1103 (1970, first commercial DRAM) that ended core's reign.

Going deeper

  • Mercury delay lines stored bits as acoustic pulses travelling through a tube of mercury; data had to be caught and re-sent as it emerged, so access time depended on where in the cycle a bit was.
  • The Williams-Kilburn tube stored bits as charged spots on a cathode-ray-tube screen; it gave the 1948 Manchester Baby, the first stored-program computer, its main memory.
  • Magnetic-core memory threaded tiny ferrite rings on a grid of wires; reading a bit erased it, so every read was followed by a rewrite — a 'destructive read' that DRAM also has.
  • Core memory was non-volatile, so a crashed machine's memory could be printed out afterwards — the origin of the term 'core dump', still used for crash memory images today.
  • The IBM 350 stored about five million characters on fifty 24-inch disks, with one access arm moving between them; average access was around 600 ms — thousands of times slower than a modern SSD read.
  • The Apollo Guidance Computer used core rope memory — wires woven through or around cores to set bits permanently — for about 36K words of fixed programme plus 2K words of erasable core.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking early computers had no RAM: they had random-access main memory, just built from tubes, delay lines or magnetic cores instead of chips.
  • Assuming hard disks came after floppies: the IBM 350 hard disk (1956) predates IBM's first floppy (1971) by fifteen years.

docs.title: Key memory types, devices, interfaces, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example Punched cardsHerman Hollerith; later IBM · Format · Legacy · Beginner Stiff cards with holes in fixed positions encoding data, read by mechanical and later electrical machines. Hollerith's tabulators processed the 1890 US census, and IBM's 80-column card stayed standard for decades. Paper tapeTeleprinters and early computers · Format · Legacy · Beginner A long paper strip with rows of punched holes storing programs and data sequentially. Early minicomputer owners loaded programs from paper tape, and Altair BASIC was famously distributed on it in 1975. Mercury delay-line memoryEDSAC (Cambridge, 1949); UNIVAC I · Technology · Legacy · Intermediate Bits stored as sound pulses circulating through tubes of mercury, re-amplified each time they emerged. EDSAC's first memory used mercury tanks holding about 512 short words in total. Williams-Kilburn tubeFreddie Williams and Tom Kilburn, Manchester, 1947 · Technology · Legacy · Intermediate A cathode-ray tube storing bits as spots of charge on its screen, refreshed continuously like DRAM. The Manchester Baby ran the world's first stored program from a Williams tube in June 1948. Magnetic drum memoryGustav Tauschek (1932); IBM 650 (1954) · Device · Legacy · Intermediate A spinning metal cylinder coated with magnetic material, with fixed read/write heads along its length. The IBM 650 kept 2,000 ten-digit words on a drum spinning at 12,500 RPM. UNISERVO tape driveRemington Rand UNIVAC I, 1951 · Device · Legacy · Intermediate The first tape drive sold with a commercial computer, using metal tape to store data sequentially. UNIVAC I used UNISERVO drives to process US Census Bureau data in the early 1950s. Magnetic-core memoryJay Forrester's team, MIT Whirlwind, 1953 · Technology · Legacy · Beginner Tiny ferrite rings magnetised clockwise or anticlockwise to store bits; the dominant main memory until the mid-1970s. IBM System/360 mainframes in the 1960s used core memory measured in kilobytes to a few megabytes. Core rope memoryMIT Instrumentation Lab; Apollo Guidance Computer · Technology · Legacy · Intermediate Read-only memory made by weaving wires through or around cores, fixing the program physically at manufacture. The Apollo 11 guidance software was literally woven into core rope modules before launch. IBM 350 disk storage unitIBM, shipped with the 305 RAMAC, 1956 · Device · Legacy · Beginner The first commercial hard-disk drive: fifty 24-inch platters at 1,200 RPM storing about 3.75 MB. Businesses could look up any customer record in under a second instead of searching tape reels for minutes. Floppy diskIBM 8-inch diskette, 1971; later 5.25-inch and 3.5-inch · Device · Legacy · Beginner A flexible magnetic disk in a protective sleeve, the main portable storage from the 1970s to the late 1990s. A 3.5-inch high-density floppy held 1.44 MB — the 'Save' icon in many apps still shows one. Core dumpTerm from the core-memory era · Concept · Current · Intermediate A file capturing a program's memory at the moment it crashed, used for debugging; named after core memory. When a Linux service segfaults, systemd-coredump stores a core file that engineers open in gdb. Stored-program conceptJohn von Neumann's 1945 EDVAC report; Manchester and Cambridge machines · Concept · Current · Beginner Keeping instructions in the same memory as data, so programs can be loaded and changed like any data. Every modern computer, from a smartwatch to a supercomputer, loads its programs into memory this way.

docs.title: 1.10 A Short History, Part 2: DRAM, Flash, SSDs and HBM
docs.text:
From the late 1960s, memory moved onto silicon chips. DRAM (1970) replaced core memory, EPROM and then flash (1980s) gave chips that keep data without power, and flash grew into memory cards, USB sticks and SSDs. Since 2013, chips have been stacked vertically — 3D NAND layers and HBM DRAM stacks — to keep capacity and speed rising.

Semiconductor memory milestones. Notice the shift from shrinking cells to stacking them in 3D after 2013.

Think of it like…

It is like cities moving from single houses to apartment blocks and then skyscrapers: once you run out of land (chip area), you build upwards with more layers.

Real-world example

Grace's grandfather bought a 1 KB memory upgrade in the 1970s built from Intel 1103-era chips. Her mother's 2008 laptop got one of the first consumer SSDs at 80 GB. Grace's 2026 gaming PC has 32 GB of DDR5 and a 2 TB NVMe SSD made of 3D NAND with more than 200 stacked layers, while the AI cloud she rents uses GPUs with HBM stacks delivering terabytes per second.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. 1966-1970: Robert Dennard invents the one-transistor DRAM cell; Intel ships the 1103, the first commercial DRAM.
  2. 1970s-1980s: EPROM and EEPROM bring rewritable non-volatile chips; Toshiba's Fujio Masuoka invents flash memory.
  3. 1990s-2000s: synchronous DRAM and DDR raise speeds; flash cards, USB drives and the first SSDs appear.
  4. 2008-2011: consumer SSDs take off and the NVMe specification is released.
  5. 2013-2026: 3D NAND, HBM stacks, DDR5 and HBM4 continue scaling by building upwards.

Who uses it

Students of computer engineering, semiconductor-industry newcomers, analysts and investors, and technicians who meet legacy hardware.

Key takeaway

Know the trio of inventors: Robert Dennard (IBM, DRAM cell), Fujio Masuoka (Toshiba, flash memory) and Simon Sze & Dawon Kahng (Bell Labs, floating-gate transistor, 1967).

Going deeper

  • The Intel 1103 (1970) stored 1,024 bits; by 1972 it was the world's best-selling semiconductor memory chip, and within a few years DRAM had pushed magnetic core out of new computers.
  • Dawon Kahng and Simon Sze's 1967 floating-gate transistor made non-volatile chips possible; Intel's Dov Frohman turned it into the 1971 EPROM, erased by shining ultraviolet light through a quartz window.
  • Fujio Masuoka's team at Toshiba presented NOR flash in 1984 and NAND flash in 1987; the name 'flash' reportedly came from a colleague likening block erase to a camera flash.
  • Samsung began mass-producing 3D 'V-NAND' in 2013 with 24 layers; leading 2025-2026 products stack over 300 layers, the main reason SSD prices per terabyte fell for a decade.
  • SK hynix and AMD drove the first HBM standard (JEDEC JESD235, 2013); AMD's Radeon R9 Fury X in 2015 was the first graphics card to ship with HBM.
  • Intel and Micron's 3D XPoint (sold as Optane, 2017-2022) was the most famous attempt at a new memory class between DRAM and flash; it was discontinued despite strong performance.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing flash was invented by Intel or Samsung: it came from Toshiba's research lab, although Intel shipped the first commercial NOR flash in 1988.
  • Assuming SSDs are a 2000s invention: flash SSDs existed in 1991; what changed later was price per gigabyte.

docs.title: Key memory types, devices, interfaces, standards & tools
docs.text: Name What it does Example One-transistor DRAM cellRobert Dennard, IBM (1966; patented 1968) · Technology · Current · Beginner A single transistor plus one capacitor per bit — the design every DRAM chip still uses, scaled down enormously. Dennard's cell let DRAM pack far more bits than the six-transistor cells used in fast SRAM. Intel 3101Intel, 1969 · Product · Legacy · Intermediate Intel's first product: a 64-bit bipolar static RAM chip, showing that semiconductor memory could replace core. Early Intel engineers bet the young company's future on memory chips like the 3101 before microprocessors existed. Intel 1103Intel, 1970 · Product · Legacy · Beginner The first commercially successful DRAM chip, 1 Kbit; it quickly displaced magnetic-core memory in new designs. Within a few years of launch, computer makers were designing 1103 chips into main memory instead of core. Floating-gate transistorDawon Kahng and Simon Sze, Bell Labs, 1967 · Technology · Legacy · Intermediate A transistor with an isolated gate that traps charge for years — the basis of EPROM, EEPROM and flash. Every planar NAND cell in USB sticks of the 2000s was a descendant of this Bell Labs invention. EPROMDov Frohman, Intel 1702 (1971) · Component · Legacy · Intermediate Erasable programmable ROM, wiped by ultraviolet light through a quartz window and reprogrammed electrically. 1980s arcade machines and PC BIOS chips used EPROMs with stickers covering their windows. Flash memory inventionFujio Masuoka, Toshiba (NOR 1984, NAND 1987) · Technology · Current · Beginner Electrically erasable memory erased in large blocks at once, making it far cheaper per bit than EEPROM. Toshiba's NAND flash later became the storage inside every smartphone, SSD and memory card. SDRAM and DDR SDRAMJEDEC (SDRAM 1990s; DDR JESD79, 2000) · Standard · Legacy · Beginner DRAM synchronised to a clock; DDR transfers data on both clock edges, doubling bandwidth. PCs of the early 2000s moved from PC133 SDRAM to DDR-400 memory, roughly tripling peak bandwidth. First flash SSDSanDisk (then SunDisk), 1991 · Product · Legacy · Intermediate A 20 MB flash-based solid-state drive supplied to IBM for a portable computer, reportedly costing about a thousand dollars. That 20 MB SSD held less than one 2026 smartphone photo burst but proved disks could be solid-state. First USB flash drivesIntroduced around 2000 (M-Systems DiskOnKey, Trek ThumbDrive) · Device · Current · Beginner Pocket flash storage on a USB plug, which quickly replaced floppies and Zip disks. Early 8 MB USB sticks sold in 2000; a 2026 stick holds 1 TB in the same shape. Consumer SSD eraIntel X25-M (2008) and successors · Concept · Current · Beginner Affordable SATA SSDs that made laptops and desktops boot and launch apps several times faster than hard drives. Swapping a 2010 laptop's hard drive for an SSD cut its boot time from about a minute to around 15 seconds. 3D NAND (V-NAND)Samsung, mass production 2013; now all NAND makers · Technology · Current · Intermediate Flash cells stacked vertically in many layers instead of shrinking them flat, restarting capacity growth. Samsung's first 24-layer V-NAND has grown to products with several hundred layers by 2026. First HBM productsSK hynix and AMD; JEDEC JESD235 (2013) · Technology · Current · Intermediate Stacked DRAM dies connected with through-silicon vias, placed beside a GPU for very wide, fast access. AMD's 2015 Radeon R9 Fury X used 4 GB of first-generation HBM at 512 GB/s.

docs.title: 1.11 Follow a File: From 'Save' to the Disk and Back
docs.text:
Pressing Save does not write straight to the drive. Your app hands the data to the operating system, which keeps it in RAM (the page cache), lets the file system decide where it goes, and writes it to the drive a little later. The drive's own controller then stores it in flash or on a platter. Reading it back reverses the journey — often stopping early because the data is still cached in RAM.

What really happens when you press Save. The app regains control long before the drive has the data — fsync is the guarantee.

Think of it like…

Saving is like posting a letter: you drop it in the post box (page cache) and walk away; the postal service (file system and driver) sorts and delivers it on its schedule, and only a recorded-delivery receipt (fsync) proves it has really arrived.

Real-world example

Kofi saves a 2 MB report in a text editor on Linux. write() returns in under a millisecond because the bytes only reached the page cache. About 30 seconds later the kernel's writeback flushes them: ext4 allocates blocks, journals the metadata, and the NVMe driver sends write commands to the SSD. Because the editor also calls fsync, the Save completes only after the SSD confirms the data is durable.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The app calls write() (Linux/macOS) or WriteFile (Windows); data is copied into the OS page cache and marked dirty.
  2. The file system allocates blocks, updates metadata (size, timestamps) and journals or copy-on-writes those changes.
  3. Dirty pages are flushed after a delay, on memory pressure, or immediately when the app calls fsync.
  4. The block layer and driver turn them into commands (e.g. NVMe write at LBA x, length y) for the drive.
  5. The drive's controller places data in flash or on the platter and reports completion; reads later hit the page cache or fetch the blocks again.

Who uses it

Backend and database developers, Linux and Windows administrators, storage engineers investigating data loss, and anyone who has lost work after a crash.

Key takeaway

Remember: write() means 'the OS has it', fsync() means 'the storage has it' — databases call fsync on every commit for exactly this reason.

Going deeper

  • On Linux, dirty pages older than about 30 seconds (vm.dirty_expire_centisecs = 3000) are written back by flusher threads that wake every 5 seconds; heavy writers are throttled once dirty memory passes a threshold.
  • Windows' Cache Manager uses a lazy writer that flushes dirty cached data in the background; apps that need durability call FlushFileBuffers or open files with write-through flags.
  • Saving safely usually means writing a temporary file, calling fsync, then renaming it over the old one, so a crash leaves either the old or the new version, never a half-written mix.
  • Drives also cache writes in their own DRAM; a flush command (NVMe Flush, ATA FLUSH CACHE) or Force Unit Access asks the drive to make data durable before reporting completion.
  • Reads benefit from readahead: when the kernel sees sequential reads it fetches the next blocks early, so streaming a video file rarely waits on the drive.
  • macOS's fsync only reaches the drive's cache; apps needing a full guarantee use fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC), which also forces the drive to flush.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Pulling a USB stick without ejecting: cached writes may not have reached it yet, corrupting files or the file system.
  • Assuming a fast write() means the data is safe: without fsync or a flush, a power cut can lose seconds of 'saved' work.
  • Benchmarking writes that only hit the page cache: you measure RAM speed, not the drive.

docs.title: Try it: Watch dirty data wait in RAM, then flush it (Linux)
docs.text:
dd if=/dev/zero of=~/test.bin bs=1M count=200 status=none
grep -E '^(Dirty|Writeback):' /proc/meminfo   # dirty MiB waiting
sync                                          # flush everything now
grep -E '^(Dirty|Writeback):' /proc/meminfo
rm ~/test.bin

Playing a 4K video, the kernel reads megabytes ahead so playback never waits on the SSD. Safely Remove / ejectWindows, macOS, Linux desktops · Command · Current · Beginner Flushes all cached writes and unmounts a removable drive so it can be unplugged without corruption. docs.title: 1.12 Reliability Basics: Bit Errors, ECC and Bit Rot
docs.text:
Every memory and storage device occasionally gets a bit wrong — from radiation, wear, heat, electrical noise or slow decay. Systems survive by adding extra check bits: parity detects errors, error-correcting codes (ECC) fix them, and checksums catch silent corruption end to end. Regular scrubbing finds problems before they pile up.

How systems keep stored bits honest. Correction is only half the job; logging and scrubbing stop errors accumulating.

Think of it like…

It is like a careful bookkeeper who adds a check digit to every account number and re-adds every column at the end of the day: a single smudged digit is spotted and fixed before it becomes a wrong payment.

Real-world example

A 2003 electronic vote count in Schaerbeek, Belgium, gave one candidate exactly 4,096 extra votes — a single flipped bit (2^12), widely blamed on a cosmic-ray strike. Today Maria's company servers use ECC memory; last month their logs showed 37 corrected single-bit errors on one module, so she replaced it before an uncorrectable error could crash the database.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Add redundancy: store extra check bits computed from the data (parity, Hamming ECC, CRC, Reed-Solomon, LDPC).
  2. On every read, recompute and compare; small errors are corrected on the fly.
  3. Log corrected errors so administrators can spot failing parts early.
  4. Scrub regularly: read everything in the background to fix errors before a second one hits the same word or stripe.
  5. Keep higher-level protection — checksums, RAID or replicas, backups — for errors the hardware cannot fix.

Who uses it

Server and storage administrators, site-reliability engineers, hardware designers, data-centre operators and anyone responsible for data that must not silently change.

Key takeaway

Know the classic: SECDED ECC adds 8 check bits to every 64 data bits (a 72-bit word) to Correct any Single-bit error and Detect any Double-bit error.

Going deeper

  • Soft errors are temporary flips caused by alpha particles from packaging materials or neutrons from cosmic rays; hard errors are permanent faults such as a stuck cell or broken connection.
  • A large 2009 study of Google's servers (Schroeder, Pinheiro and Weber) found about a third of machines and over 8% of DIMMs saw at least one correctable memory error per year — far more than expected.
  • Consumer hard drives often specify one unrecoverable read error per 10^14 bits (about 12.5 TB read), enterprise drives 10^15; JEDEC's SSD classes allow 10^-15 (client) and 10^-16 (enterprise) uncorrectable bit error rates.
  • Flash and modern disks rely on powerful codes — LDPC in SSDs and HDDs, Reed-Solomon in optical discs and tape — that correct dozens of bit errors per sector before anything reaches the host.
  • Silent data corruption — wrong data returned without any error — is why ZFS, Btrfs and object stores keep checksums of every block and verify them on read and during scrubs.
  • Bit rot covers slow decay over time: flash charge leaking, magnetic grains weakening, optical dye fading; archivists counter it with fixity checks (stored hashes) and periodic migration to fresh media.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming RAID or ECC replaces backups: they fix hardware errors, not deletion, ransomware or a corrupted file being faithfully mirrored.
  • Ignoring corrected-error logs: a rising count of corrected errors is an early warning that a module or drive is failing.
  • Believing consumer PCs never see memory errors: they do; without ECC the result is a rare crash or corrupted file nobody can explain.

docs.title: Try it: Detect a flipped bit with a checksum
docs.text:
import hashlib
data = bytearray(b'Quarterly results: profit 4096')
before = hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()
data[5] ^= 0b00000100            # flip one bit
after = hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()
print(data.decode(errors='replace'))
print('match' if before == after else 'CORRUPTION DETECTED')

A single flipped bit in a bank balance stored as binary could change it by thousands of pounds. Aircraft and satellites use ECC and radiation-hardened memory because cosmic-ray flux rises sharply with altitude. docs.title: 1.13 The Memory & Storage Market and Its Big Players
docs.text:
A handful of companies make almost all the world's memory chips, and only three still make hard drives. DRAM comes mostly from Samsung, SK hynix, Micron and China's CXMT; NAND flash from Samsung, SK hynix (with Solidigm), Kioxia, Micron, Sandisk and YMTC. Prices swing wildly in boom-and-bust cycles, and since 2024 AI data centres have driven the strongest boom yet.

DRAM revenue share, Q2 2026. TrendForce revenue shares; the CXMT figure is as reported secondhand from TrendForce data, and 'Others' is the remainder.

Think of it like…

The memory market is like a harvest of a few giant farms: when everyone plants too much, prices crash; when a new crop (AI) suddenly needs far more, shelves empty and prices soar until new fields come in years later.

Real-world example

In early 2026 a fictional PC builder, NovaRig, finds the 32 GB DDR5 kits it bought cheaply in mid-2025 now cost more than double. Its suppliers explain that Samsung, SK hynix and Micron shifted wafers to HBM and server memory for AI. NovaRig ships its budget model with 16 GB instead of 32 GB and raises prices — the same story played out across the PC and phone industry.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Chipmakers invest tens of billions of dollars in fabs years before demand is known.
  2. When supply outruns demand, prices fall below cost and makers cut output (as in 2023).
  3. When new demand arrives faster than fabs can be built (AI from 2024), contract prices jump.
  4. Profits fund new fabs and technology, which add supply two to three years later.
  5. Analysts at TrendForce, Counterpoint, Yole and others track prices and shares quarter by quarter.

Who uses it

Supply-chain and procurement managers, hardware product managers, industry analysts and investors, and job-seekers choosing employers in the semiconductor and storage industries.

Key takeaway

Name the big three DRAM makers (Samsung, SK hynix, Micron) and the three hard-drive makers (Seagate, Western Digital, Toshiba) — a common interview warm-up question.

Going deeper

  • TrendForce put global DRAM revenue at about US$155 billion in Q2 2026 alone, up 59.5% on the previous quarter, as contract prices rose faster than bit shipments.
  • TrendForce reported conventional DRAM contract prices rising 90-95% quarter-on-quarter in Q1 2026, the largest jump it had recorded, driven by AI servers absorbing HBM, high-capacity RDIMMs and LPDDR5X.
  • The same industry lost billions in 2023, when post-pandemic PC and phone demand collapsed; such swings make memory one of the most cyclical sectors in technology.
  • Ownership shifts often: SK hynix bought Intel's NAND business (now Solidigm), Kioxia listed on the Tokyo exchange in December 2024, and Western Digital spun off its flash business as Sandisk in February 2025.
  • Hard drives are a three-company market (Seagate, Western Digital, Toshiba); nearline drives for cloud data centres now make up most of the exabytes shipped.
  • Geopolitics matters: US export rules since late 2024 restrict selling HBM and advanced chip-making tools to China, while Chinese makers CXMT (DRAM) and YMTC (NAND) have grown rapidly.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Quoting old prices as 'normal': memory prices can double or halve within a year; always date your $/GB figures.
  • Confusing chip makers with module and drive brands: many brands buy chips from the same few makers and add controllers, firmware and packaging.

docs.title: 1.14 Who Writes the Rules: Standards Bodies and Industry Groups
docs.text:
Memory modules from one company work in motherboards from another because standards bodies publish shared specifications. JEDEC defines memory chips and modules, NVM Express and PCI-SIG define how SSDs connect, SNIA promotes storage education and specs, and other groups cover SCSI, SATA, CXL, SD cards, tape and units. Knowing who owns which standard tells you where to look up the truth.

Who defines what. Look up the owning body's specification before trusting a datasheet summary.

Think of it like…

Standards bodies are like the people who agree the size of plugs and sockets: thanks to them, any kettle fits any socket in the country, whoever made it.

Real-world example

Omar, a junior hardware engineer, must check whether a new server board supports a vendor's 128 GB DDR5 RDIMM. He reads the JEDEC module standard for the electrical rules, the CPU vendor's memory population guide, and the NVM Express specification for the board's boot SSD. When the vendor quotes 'CXL 2.0 support', he checks the CXL Consortium's specification to see exactly which features that includes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Member companies propose features in a committee (e.g. JEDEC JC-42 for memory devices).
  2. Drafts are debated, simulated and balloted by members over months or years.
  3. The published standard (often free with registration) defines behaviour, timings and compliance tests.
  4. Vendors build products and pass interoperability or compliance testing (plugfests, logos).
  5. Revisions add speeds and fix issues, e.g. DDR5 speed bins added years after the first release.

Who uses it

Hardware and firmware engineers, product managers, test and validation engineers, and anyone who needs authoritative answers instead of marketing claims.

Key takeaway

Quick map: memory chips and modules, eMMC and UFS → JEDEC; SSD command set → NVM Express; slots and links → PCI-SIG; memory over PCIe → CXL Consortium; SCSI/SAS → INCITS T10; ATA → INCITS T13.

Going deeper

  • JEDEC (founded in 1958) works through committees: JC-42 covers memory devices such as DDR5, LPDDR and HBM, JC-45 covers DRAM modules, and JC-64 covers embedded storage like eMMC and UFS.
  • Many JEDEC standards can be downloaded free after registration; document numbers such as JESD79-5 (DDR5), JESD209-6 (LPDDR6) and JESD270-4 (HBM4) are worth recognising on CVs and datasheets.
  • NVM Express, Inc. maintains the NVMe base specification plus separate command-set and transport specifications, a structure introduced with NVMe 2.0 in 2021.
  • SNIA (Storage Networking Industry Association) publishes standards such as SFF form-factor specifications, the Swordfish management API and solid-state performance test specifications, and runs vendor-neutral education.
  • The Open Compute Project, founded by Facebook in 2011, publishes hyperscale hardware specifications, including OCP datacenter NVMe SSD requirements that many enterprise drives now follow.
  • Consortia such as the LTO Program (HPE, IBM, Quantum), SATA-IO and the SD Association license logos and run compliance programmes so interoperable products can be identified.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating vendor marketing as the standard: 'DDR5-8000' kits are overclocked beyond JEDEC speed bins, and 'supports CXL' may mean only a subset of features.
  • Assuming one body owns everything: SSD form factors, protocols, interfaces and security each come from different groups.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Networked, Distributed & Cloud Storage
docs.text: Most data today lives somewhere other than the computer using it. This chapter follows storage out onto the network: DAS, NAS and SAN; the NFS and SMB file protocols; block versus file versus object and the S3 API; distributed and software-defined systems such as Ceph; parallel file systems for HPC and AI; enterprise arrays and hyperconverged clusters; the big clouds' block, file and object services; Kubernetes storage; the special demands of AI training and inference; and how tiering and lifecycle policies keep costs and risks under control.

docs.title: 7.1 DAS, NAS and SAN: Three Ways to Attach Storage
docs.text:
Storage can be plugged straight into one computer (direct-attached storage, DAS), shared as ready-made files over the ordinary network (network-attached storage, NAS), or shared as raw disk blocks over a dedicated storage network (storage area network, SAN). The difference is where the file system lives and how many machines can use the storage.

DAS vs NAS vs SAN

DAS NAS SAN Unit shared Nothing (one host) Files and folders Blocks (LUNs) File system runs on Host NAS appliance Host Typical protocol SATA, SAS, NVMe, USB NFS, SMB FC, iSCSI, NVMe-oF Network None (cable) Ordinary Ethernet Dedicated fabric/VLAN Strength Lowest latency, cheap Easy sharing Shared, fast, highly available Typical user Laptop, DB server Office, home, media VM clusters, big databases

The key question is who runs the file system: the host (DAS, SAN) or the storage box (NAS).

Think of it like…

DAS is a bookshelf in your own room; a NAS is the school library, where you ask the librarian for a book by its title; a SAN is a private warehouse that hands your shop whole empty shelves, and you arrange the books yourself.

Real-world example

Lena runs IT for the fictional Hollis Architecture studio. Each CAD workstation has a fast internal NVMe SSD (DAS) for scratch work. Finished drawings live on a two-controller NAS that 40 staff map as the S: drive over SMB. The studio's virtual-machine cluster boots from LUNs on a small iSCSI SAN, so any host can restart any VM if one server dies.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. DAS: the drive connects over SATA, SAS, NVMe or USB to one host, which formats it and owns it.
  2. NAS: an appliance runs its own file system and exports folders with NFS or SMB over Ethernet.
  3. SAN: an array carves its capacity into LUNs (logical units) and presents them as block devices over Fibre Channel, iSCSI or NVMe-oF.
  4. Zoning and LUN masking decide which hosts may see which LUNs; each host then puts its own file system (or a cluster file system) on top.
  5. Multipathing software keeps two or more paths to every LUN so a failed cable, switch or controller does not stop I/O.

Who uses it

Infrastructure and storage administrators, VMware and Hyper-V teams, small-office IT, video studios and every data centre build on one or more of these three models.

Key takeaway

Memorise the one-liner: DAS = one host owns blocks; NAS = many hosts share files; SAN = many hosts share blocks over a dedicated network.

Going deeper

  • A local NVMe SSD answers in roughly 10-100 microseconds; a well-built SAN or NVMe-oF path adds only tens of microseconds, while NAS adds protocol and metadata round trips, often 0.2-1 ms per operation.
  • Most enterprise arrays have two controllers in active-active or ALUA (asymmetric logical unit access) mode; hosts mark paths 'optimised' or 'non-optimised' and send I/O to the owning controller first.
  • Fibre Channel zoning is configured on switches by WWPN (World Wide Port Name); LUN masking is configured on the array, and both are needed so a host cannot even see another team's disks.
  • Two hosts writing to one SAN LUN with an ordinary file system such as ext4 or NTFS will corrupt it; shared LUNs need a cluster-aware file system such as VMFS, GFS2, OCFS2 or Windows CSV.
  • Scale-up arrays add shelves behind a fixed controller pair; scale-out systems add whole nodes so capacity and performance grow together, which is how most modern NAS and object systems scale.
  • Unified arrays (for example NetApp ONTAP or Dell PowerStore) serve both NAS and SAN protocols from one pool, so small sites can buy a single box for file shares and VM datastores.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking a NAS is just a big USB drive: it is a server with its own OS and file system, and it needs patching, backups and access control.
  • Assuming a SAN means Fibre Channel only: iSCSI and NVMe/TCP build SANs over ordinary Ethernet switches.
  • Calling RAID a backup: DAS, NAS and SAN all still need separate copies elsewhere, because deletion and ransomware hit every mirror instantly.

docs.title: 7.2 NFS and SMB: Sharing Files Over a Network
docs.text:
File-sharing protocols let a computer open, read and save files that physically live on another machine as if they were local. NFS (Network File System) grew up in the Unix and Linux world; SMB (Server Message Block) is the native Windows protocol and is also spoken by macOS and Linux via Samba.

An NFSv4.1 client reading a file. NFSv4.1 bundles requests into COMPOUND calls inside a session, cutting round trips.

Think of it like…

A file protocol is like a library loan desk: you ask for a book by title, the librarian checks your card, lends it, records who has it, and stops two people scribbling in it at once.

Real-world example

Omar's video-production company has Mac editors and Linux render nodes. The NAS exports the project folder over SMB 3.1.1 for the Macs and over NFSv4.1 for the render farm. When a renderer reads a 40 GB clip, its client opens multiple TCP connections (nconnect=8) and reads in 1 MB chunks, keeping its 25 GbE link busy.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The server exports a directory (NFS) or a share (SMB) and sets who may access it.
  2. The client mounts the export or maps the share; authentication happens with Kerberos, NTLM or (for older NFS) trusted host IDs.
  3. Opening a file returns a handle; reads and writes are sent as protocol requests carrying offsets and lengths.
  4. Locks, leases or delegations let a client cache data safely until another client needs the same file.
  5. On close, cached writes are flushed so other clients see the new data (close-to-open consistency).

Who uses it

System and storage administrators, Linux and Windows engineers, media studios, HPC centres and anyone running home directories or shared drives use NFS or SMB daily.

Key takeaway

Remember the ports: NFS uses TCP 2049; SMB uses TCP 445 (and UDP 443 for SMB over QUIC). Never expose either directly to the internet.

Going deeper

  • NFSv3 (RFC 1813, 1995) is stateless and relies on separate helper protocols for mounting and locking; NFSv4 (RFC 7530) folds locking in, uses one port, adds ACLs and strong Kerberos security.
  • NFSv4.1 (RFC 8881) adds sessions with exactly-once semantics and pNFS, where the metadata server hands clients a 'layout' so they read data directly from many storage nodes in parallel.
  • NFSv4.2 (RFC 7862) adds server-side copy, sparse-file support (SEEK_HOLE), space reservation and labeled NFS for SELinux, so copying a 50 GB file can happen entirely on the server.
  • SMB 3.0 arrived with Windows Server 2012 and added Multichannel, transparent failover, SMB Direct over RDMA and encryption; SMB 3.1.1 adds pre-authentication integrity and AES-GCM encryption.
  • Windows Server 2025 makes SMB over QUIC available in all editions and requires SMB signing for outbound connections by default, which can slow very old NAS boxes that sign inefficiently.
  • Kerberos security flavours for NFS are krb5 (authentication only), krb5i (adds integrity checksums) and krb5p (adds encryption); without them NFSv3 trusts whatever user ID the client claims.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Leaving SMB 1 enabled 'for an old scanner': SMB 1 enabled the 2017 WannaCry worm; Windows disables it by default, so replace or isolate the device.
  • Assuming NFS 'root' is safe: by default servers squash remote root to 'nobody'; disabling root_squash lets any client root rewrite every file.
  • Expecting local-disk locking semantics everywhere: mixing NFS and SMB access to the same files needs a NAS that translates locks and permissions carefully.

docs.title: Try it: Mount an NFS export and map an SMB share (replace server names with your own lab NAS)
docs.text:
# Linux: NFSv4.1 with 4 TCP connections
sudo mount -t nfs -o vers=4.1,nconnect=4 nas01:/projects /mnt/projects
nfsstat -m                      # shows negotiated version and options

# Linux: SMB 3.1.1 share via the kernel cifs client
sudo mount -t cifs //nas01/team /mnt/team -o vers=3.1.1,username=lena

# Windows PowerShell
New-SmbMapping -LocalPath S: -RemotePath \\nas01\team
Get-SmbConnection | Select ServerName,ShareName,Dialect

docs.title: 7.3 Block, File and Object: Three Ways to Address Data
docs.text:
Block storage hands out numbered fixed-size chunks and leaves organisation to the user. File storage gives you folders and named files with permissions and locking. Object storage keeps whole objects, each with a unique key and descriptive metadata, in a flat namespace reached over HTTP.

Block vs file vs object

Block File Object Address LBA (sector number) Path /dir/file Bucket + key Access method SCSI, NVMe, iSCSI POSIX, NFS, SMB HTTP REST (S3) Update style In place, any block In place, byte range Replace whole object Metadata None Fixed (owner, times) Rich, user-defined Typical latency Microseconds Sub-millisecond Milliseconds Scale Volumes up to ~64 TiB Petabytes Exabytes, trillions of objects Best for Databases, VM disks Shared folders, HPC Backups, media, data lakes

Moving right trades fine-grained, low-latency access for scale, cost and metadata.

Think of it like…

Block storage is a box of numbered Lego bricks; file storage is a filing cabinet with labelled folders; object storage is a valet coat check: hand over the coat, get a ticket, and later present the ticket to get the whole coat back.

Real-world example

Northwind Clinic's EHR database sits on block volumes because it needs tiny, fast random writes. Doctors' scanned letters go to an SMB file share so staff can browse folders. Ten years of MRI images, 800 TB in all, live in object storage: each image is written once, tagged with patient and study IDs, and read occasionally through an HTTPS API.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Block: the host addresses logical block addresses (LBAs), usually 512-byte or 4 KiB sectors, and a file system or database decides what each block means.
  2. File: a server or local file system maps paths like /reports/q3.pdf to blocks and enforces permissions, locks and directories.
  3. Object: an application sends PUT with a key and metadata; the system stores the object, protects it with replicas or erasure coding and returns an ETag.
  4. Reads use the address style of each model: LBA ranges, file path plus offset, or bucket plus key over HTTP.
  5. Many modern platforms expose more than one model over the same pool, for example Ceph (block, file and object) or Azure Data Lake (blob plus hierarchical file namespace).

Who uses it

Cloud architects, data engineers, DBAs, backup designers and application developers choose between block, file and object every time they place data.

Key takeaway

Interview shortcut: block = lowest latency and in-place updates; file = shared hierarchical access with POSIX semantics; object = cheapest at massive scale, rich metadata, whole-object writes over HTTP.

Going deeper

  • Object stores usually protect data with erasure coding across failure domains; Amazon S3 is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability by storing data across at least three Availability Zones for most classes.
  • Since December 2020 Amazon S3 gives strong read-after-write consistency for all PUTs and DELETEs, removing the old eventual-consistency surprises that early data lakes had to work around.
  • POSIX semantics (rename, append, byte-range locks, mmap) are expensive at scale; that is why object stores drop them and why mounting a bucket with tools like s3fs or Mountpoint for Amazon S3 has limitations.
  • Data lakes store columnar files such as Apache Parquet on object storage and add table formats like Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake or Apache Hudi to provide transactions, schema evolution and time travel.
  • Content-addressable storage names objects by a cryptographic hash of their contents, as Git and many backup tools do, giving automatic deduplication and tamper evidence.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running a busy database on object storage directly: objects cannot be updated in place, so every small change means rewriting whole objects.
  • Treating 'flat namespace' as having folders: the slashes in an object key are just characters; listing a 'folder' is a prefix query.
  • Assuming object storage is always slow: modern all-flash object systems serve hundreds of GB/s, which is why AI pipelines use them.

docs.title: Try it: Feel the difference on your own laptop
docs.text:
# Block: read raw sectors from a disk image (no file system involved)
dd if=/dev/zero of=disk.img bs=1M count=64
xxd -s 0 -l 64 disk.img

# File: path, permissions and metadata
stat disk.img

# Object: a whole value addressed by key over HTTP (public example object)
curl -sI https://www.example.com/ | grep -i -E 'etag|content-length|last-modified'

Analysts query yesterday's version of a sales table with Iceberg time travel after a bad load.
