A backup tool splits files into chunks named by SHA-256; unchanged chunks are never uploaded twice.

docs.title: 7.4 The S3 API and Object Storage Concepts
docs.text:
The S3 API began as Amazon Simple Storage Service's web interface in 2006 and became the common language of object storage. You store objects in buckets using HTTP verbs such as PUT, GET, LIST and DELETE, and add features like versioning, lifecycle rules and write-once locks.

A multipart upload. Parts upload in parallel and can be retried individually; the object appears only after Complete.

Think of it like…

S3 is like a giant self-storage company with standard rules everywhere: you rent a unit (bucket), label every box (key), keep a logbook of old versions, set rules to move boxes to cheaper sheds later, and can padlock some boxes so nobody — not even the manager — can throw them out early.

Real-world example

Kai builds a photo app for the fictional Lakeside Camera Club. Uploads go straight from phones to a bucket using presigned URLs, so photos never pass through the app server. Versioning protects against accidental overwrite, a lifecycle rule moves originals older than 90 days to an infrequent-access class, and Object Lock keeps the club's audit exports immutable for seven years.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Create a bucket with a globally unique name in a chosen region and block public access by default.
  2. Upload with PUT for small objects or multipart upload for big ones (parts of 5 MiB to 5 GiB, up to 10,000 parts).
  3. Every request is signed with Signature Version 4 (an HMAC over the request) using the caller's access key, or authorised by a temporary presigned URL.
  4. Bucket policies, IAM policies and ACL settings decide who may do what; encryption at rest is on by default (SSE-S3).
  5. Turn on versioning, lifecycle rules, replication, event notifications and Object Lock as the data's value grows.

Who uses it

Cloud and backend developers, DevOps engineers, backup vendors, data engineers and security teams all work with the S3 API, whether on AWS or on S3-compatible stores such as Ceph RGW, NetApp StorageGRID or Cloudflare R2.

Key takeaway

Know the numbers: single PUT up to 5 GiB, multipart parts 5 MiB-5 GiB, at most 10,000 parts, and maximum object size 50 TB since December 2025 (previously 5 TB).

Going deeper

  • A PUT replaces the whole object; there is no partial update. The ETag is often the MD5 of a single-part object, but for multipart uploads it is a hash of part hashes plus a '-N' suffix.
  • Versioning keeps every version under a version ID; a DELETE just adds a 'delete marker', so lifecycle rules must also expire noncurrent versions or costs keep growing.
  • Object Lock needs versioning and offers governance mode (privileged users can override) and compliance mode (nobody, including the root account, can shorten retention), plus open-ended legal holds.
  • Conditional writes with If-None-Match: * (2024) let applications create an object only if the key does not exist yet, enabling simple locking and safe concurrent writers without an external database.
  • S3 request rates scale per prefix: at least 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second per partitioned prefix, so very hot workloads spread keys across many prefixes.
  • Since January 2023 new S3 objects are encrypted with SSE-S3 by default; SSE-KMS adds customer-managed keys and audit trails, and SSE-C lets the customer supply the key on each request.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Making a bucket public to share one file: use a presigned URL with a short expiry instead; public buckets cause many real-world data leaks.
  • Forgetting abandoned multipart uploads: unfinished parts are billed until removed, so add a lifecycle rule to abort incomplete uploads after a few days.
  • Assuming S3-compatible means identical: third-party stores often lack features such as Object Lock modes, Select or event notifications, so test the calls you rely on.

docs.title: 7.5 Software-Defined and Distributed Storage: Ceph, HDFS and Friends
docs.text:
Software-defined storage (SDS) is storage whose intelligence lives in software running on ordinary servers rather than in a proprietary box. Distributed storage spreads data across many such servers, copying or encoding it so that whole machines can fail without losing anything.

Ceph's architecture. Every interface sits on top of one object layer, RADOS, which CRUSH spreads across OSDs.

Think of it like…

Instead of one giant bank vault, imagine a town where every household keeps a few sealed envelopes and a shared rulebook says exactly which three houses hold each envelope — lose a house and the town quietly re-copies its envelopes elsewhere.

Real-world example

The fictional Riverside University replaces an ageing array with 12 commodity servers running Ceph, each holding 12 HDDs and two NVMe SSDs. Researchers get S3 buckets through the RADOS Gateway, OpenStack VMs get RBD block devices, and labs mount CephFS. When a server's motherboard dies, Ceph rebuilds its 140 TB of placement groups across the other 11 servers in a few hours.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Install storage software on commodity servers full of disks (each disk usually runs one storage daemon).
  2. A small odd-numbered set of monitor nodes keeps the authoritative cluster map and uses a consensus algorithm (Paxos in Ceph) to agree on it.
  3. A placement algorithm such as Ceph's CRUSH or a consistent-hashing ring computes where each object belongs, so no central lookup table is needed.
  4. Each object is stored as several replicas or as erasure-coded fragments spread across failure domains (disks, hosts, racks).
  5. When a disk or node fails, the survivors detect it via heartbeats and re-create the missing copies automatically.
  6. Clients talk directly to the storage daemons holding their data, so performance grows as nodes are added.

Who uses it

Cloud and OpenStack operators, research computing teams, telecom providers, big-data platforms and Kubernetes platform engineers run SDS and distributed storage.

Key takeaway

Remember Ceph's daemons: MON (cluster map, quorum), MGR (metrics and dashboard), OSD (one per disk, stores data), MDS (metadata for CephFS) and RGW (S3/Swift gateway).

Going deeper

  • Ceph stores objects in placement groups (PGs); CRUSH maps each PG to a set of OSDs using the cluster topology, so clients compute data locations themselves instead of asking a metadata server.
  • Three-way replication costs 200% extra raw capacity; an erasure-coded 8+3 pool costs about 37.5% extra yet survives three simultaneous failures, at the price of more CPU and slower small writes.
  • BlueStore, Ceph's default back end since Luminous (2017), writes directly to raw devices, keeps metadata in RocksDB and checksums every block, avoiding a double-journal through a local file system.
  • Ceph names releases after sea creatures: Reef (v18, 2023), Squid (v19, 2024) and Tentacle (v20, first released November 2025); each stable release is supported for roughly two years.
  • HDFS splits files into large blocks (128 MiB by default) stored three times across DataNodes, with a NameNode holding the namespace in memory; Hadoop 3 added erasure coding and NameNode high availability.
  • MinIO's open-source community edition was stripped of its admin console in 2025, stopped shipping binaries in October 2025 and is no longer maintained; MinIO now sells AIStor, so new labs often use Ceph RGW, Garage or SeaweedFS instead.
  • GlusterFS lost its main sponsor when Red Hat Gluster Storage reached end of life on 31 December 2024; upstream activity has slowed sharply, so treat it as legacy for new designs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Building Ceph on three nodes with one network and expecting enterprise speed: production clusters need separate fast networks, enough RAM per OSD (about 4 GB+) and careful failure-domain design.
  • Running a monitor quorum with an even number of nodes: two monitors cannot survive one failure; use 3 or 5.
  • Assuming replication protects against deletion: every replica deletes instantly; snapshots and off-cluster backups are still required.

docs.title: Try it: Try Ceph on a single Ubuntu VM (lab only — not for production)
docs.text:
sudo snap install microceph
sudo microceph cluster bootstrap
sudo microceph disk add loop,4G,3     # three 4 GB loop-file OSDs
sudo ceph status
sudo ceph osd tree
sudo ceph df

docs.title: 7.6 Parallel File Systems for HPC and AI
docs.text:
A parallel file system stripes each file across many storage servers so thousands of compute nodes can read and write the same namespace at once. It separates metadata (names, permissions, layouts) from the data itself, letting bandwidth grow with every server added.

Lustre components. Clients ask the MDS once, then stream data directly from many OSSs in parallel.

Think of it like…

Instead of one checkout lane with a long queue, a parallel file system opens 200 lanes and splits your shopping across them, with one manager at the door telling you which lanes hold which items.

Real-world example

Asha manages storage for the fictional Northshore Climate Institute. A weather model running on 2,000 nodes writes a 40 TB snapshot every hour. Their Lustre file system stripes each output file over 64 object storage targets, so the snapshot lands at about 400 GB/s in under two minutes and researchers keep computing.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. A client asks the metadata server to open /scratch/run7/out.nc and receives its layout: which data servers hold which stripes.
  2. The client then reads and writes stripes directly and in parallel to those data servers over InfiniBand or fast Ethernet.
  3. Metadata servers handle names, permissions and locks; data servers handle the bulk bytes.
  4. A distributed lock manager keeps clients from overwriting each other's byte ranges.
  5. Adding data servers adds bandwidth; adding metadata servers adds file-create and lookup rates.

Who uses it

HPC system administrators, AI infrastructure engineers, national laboratories, weather centres, oil-and-gas, genomics and media-rendering teams run parallel file systems.

Key takeaway

Interview point: parallel file systems split metadata from data — the metadata service is usually the bottleneck for millions of small files, not raw bandwidth.

Going deeper

  • Lustre has object storage servers (OSS) exporting object storage targets (OSTs), metadata servers exporting MDTs, a management server (MGS) and the LNet networking layer; 2.17.0 shipped at the end of 2025, while 2.15 is the long-term-support branch.
  • IBM Storage Scale (formerly GPFS, first released in 1998) spreads both data and metadata across all nodes and adds policy-driven tiering, AFM caching between sites and native S3 access.
  • VAST Data's DASE design gives every stateless front-end server access to all shared NVMe flash, while WEKA's NeuralMesh (launched June 2025 as the evolution of WekaFS) runs storage as containerised microservices.
  • DAOS, born at Intel for Optane, is now governed by the DAOS Foundation under the Linux Foundation; at Argonne's Aurora it reached roughly 1 TB/s write throughput in MLPerf Storage v2.0 using 128 servers.
  • The IO500 list, published at ISC and SC each year, ranks HPC storage using a mix of IOR bandwidth tests and mdtest metadata tests, rewarding balanced systems rather than raw throughput alone.
  • Wide striping helps big files but hurts tiny ones: many sites set a stripe count of 1 for directories of small files and use Progressive File Layouts that widen striping as a file grows.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using a parallel file system as a home directory full of tiny files: millions of small files overload metadata servers; use NFS homes and parallel scratch.
  • Treating scratch space as safe storage: HPC scratch is usually unprotected and purged after 30-90 days; copy results to project or archive storage.
  • Assuming more stripes is always faster: striping a 1 MB file over 64 servers adds 64 lock and network operations for no gain.

docs.title: Try it: Inspect and set striping on a Lustre client (on an HPC cluster that uses Lustre)
docs.text:
lfs df -h                         # capacity per MDT and OST
lfs getstripe /scratch/me/big.dat
lfs setstripe -c 8 -S 4M /scratch/me/newdir   # 8 OSTs, 4 MiB stripes
lfs find /scratch/me -size +10G -type f

docs.title: 7.7 Enterprise Storage Arrays and Vendors
docs.text:
An enterprise storage array is a purpose-built system — controllers, drives and specialised software — that serves block, file or object storage to many servers with high availability, snapshots, replication and data reduction. A handful of vendors dominate the market, and each has its own product families and terminology.

What an enterprise array adds. Controllers and drives are only the start; the software features are what customers pay for.

Think of it like…

Buying an enterprise array is like hiring a professional warehouse with forklifts, alarms, insurance and a 24-hour manager, instead of stacking boxes in your own garage.

Real-world example

Maria, a storage engineer at the fictional Harbourview Insurance, compares two all-flash arrays for 600 TB of VM and database data. Vendor A guarantees 4:1 data reduction and non-disruptive controller upgrades on a subscription; vendor B offers synchronous replication between two data centres 40 km apart. She runs a proof of concept with fio and production database traces before choosing.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Hosts connect to dual (or more) redundant controllers over FC, iSCSI, NVMe-oF, NFS, SMB or S3.
  2. Controllers cache writes in mirrored, battery- or flash-protected memory and acknowledge quickly.
  3. Data is deduplicated, compressed and written to flash or HDD protected by RAID or erasure coding.
  4. Software adds snapshots, clones, replication, encryption, quality of service and ransomware detection.
  5. Telemetry phones home to the vendor's cloud for support, analytics and capacity planning.

Who uses it

Storage administrators, infrastructure architects, presales and solutions engineers, and support engineers at vendors and resellers work with enterprise arrays daily.

Key takeaway

Learn one platform deeply (ONTAP, Purity, PowerStore) — the concepts transfer — and be ready to explain usable vs raw capacity and effective capacity after data reduction.

Going deeper

  • Raw capacity is the sum of drive sizes; usable capacity subtracts RAID/erasure overhead, spares and system space; effective capacity multiplies usable by expected data reduction, often quoted as 3:1-5:1 for mixed VMs and databases.
  • Active-active synchronous replication (for example NetApp SnapMirror active sync, Everpure ActiveCluster, Dell PowerMax SRDF/Metro) lets a volume be read and written at two sites, usually within about 100 km and a few milliseconds round trip.
  • Pure Storage renamed itself Everpure in early 2026 (ticker PSTG unchanged); its FlashArray, FlashBlade, Purity OS, Evergreen subscriptions and Portworx keep their product names.
  • NetApp's AFX, announced in October 2025, disaggregates ONTAP so controllers and NVMe capacity shelves scale separately up to 128 nodes, aimed at AI clusters; classic AFF, ASA and FAS systems continue alongside.
  • Industry analysts such as Gartner and IDC rank enterprise storage vendors; Dell, NetApp, Huawei, Everpure, HPE, IBM and Hitachi Vantara are usually among the leaders, with order shifting by segment and year.
  • Consumption models (Everpure Evergreen//One, HPE GreenLake, Dell APEX, NetApp Keystone) charge per used terabyte with performance SLAs, and include controller refreshes so arrays need no forklift migration.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing quotes on 'effective' capacity without checking the data-reduction assumption: encrypted or already-compressed data may reduce 1:1.
  • Benchmarking an array with a dataset of zeros: deduplication makes it look impossibly fast; use realistic, incompressible test data.
  • Ignoring firmware upgrade and support lifecycles: an array past end-of-support cannot receive security fixes.

docs.title: 7.8 Hyperconverged Infrastructure (HCI)
docs.text:
Hyperconverged infrastructure puts compute, storage and virtualisation into the same identical servers. Software pools every server's local SSDs into one shared, replicated datastore, so there is no separate SAN to buy or manage.

Three-tier vs HCI

Three-tier (servers + SAN) Hyperconverged Building blocks Servers, SAN switches, array Identical nodes Storage location Central array Local drives in every node Scaling Compute and storage separately Add whole nodes Management Several consoles and teams One console Failure handling Array controllers + MPIO Replicas on other nodes Sweet spot Large, mixed workloads VMs, VDI, branches

HCI removes the separate storage tier but ties compute and storage growth together.

Think of it like…

Traditional infrastructure is a restaurant with separate kitchen, pantry and dining room staff; HCI is a food truck where each truck carries its own cook, stove and fridge — need more capacity, add another truck.

Real-world example

The fictional Pinecrest Medical Group replaces three ageing servers and a SAN with a four-node HCI cluster. Each node has 2 CPUs, 1 TB RAM and eight NVMe SSDs. The software keeps two copies of every VM disk on different nodes, so when a node is patched or fails, its VMs restart elsewhere with no data loss.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Install the hypervisor and HCI software on 3+ identical nodes with local SSDs.
  2. The software pools all nodes' drives into one cluster-wide datastore.
  3. Each VM write is mirrored or erasure-coded to other nodes over a fast network before it is acknowledged.
  4. Policies per VM set protection (RAID-1 / RAID-5 / RAID-6 style), checksums, encryption and deduplication.
  5. Grow by adding nodes; the software rebalances data automatically.

Who uses it

Virtualisation administrators, small and mid-size IT departments, branch offices, retail chains and VDI teams are the main HCI users.

Key takeaway

A two-node HCI cluster needs a separate witness (tie-breaker) to avoid split-brain; know this for any exam or interview.

Going deeper

  • VMware vSAN Express Storage Architecture (ESA, since vSAN 8) uses a single tier of NVMe devices with log-structured writes, making RAID-5/6 erasure coding perform close to mirroring.
  • After Broadcom acquired VMware in November 2023 it moved to subscription bundles — VMware Cloud Foundation and vSphere Foundation — and many customers re-evaluated HCI alternatives such as Nutanix, Azure Local and Proxmox.
  • Nutanix runs a Controller VM (CVM) on every node to serve storage via its Distributed Storage Fabric and keeps a VM's data local to its node for read speed; it has added support for external arrays such as Dell PowerFlex.
  • Microsoft renamed Azure Stack HCI to Azure Local in late 2024; it uses Storage Spaces Direct with SMB Direct over RDMA for node-to-node replication and is managed through Azure Arc.
  • Disaggregated HCI (vSAN Max, HPE dHCI) puts storage on dedicated nodes again to escape the 'buy CPU licences to add capacity' problem, a sign that pure HCI does not fit every workload.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Building HCI on 1 GbE: replica traffic needs at least 10/25 GbE, and RDMA where supported, or latency soars.
  • Mixing node models and drive sizes freely: unbalanced nodes cause uneven capacity and rebuild failures; keep nodes uniform.
  • Filling the datastore to 95%: HCI needs free space (often 20-30%) to rebuild a failed node's data.

docs.title: 7.9 Cloud Block and File Storage Services
docs.text:
Public clouds rent you virtual disks (block storage) that attach to virtual machines, and managed file shares that many machines mount at once. You pick a type, size and performance level, pay per gigabyte-month (and sometimes per IOPS and throughput), and the provider handles the hardware, replication and repairs.

Maximum IOPS per single cloud volume (2026). Premium tiers reach hundreds of thousands of IOPS; HDD-backed volumes are built for throughput, not IOPS.

Think of it like…

Cloud block storage is like renting a storage locker that is delivered to whichever flat you move into; cloud file storage is like a shared office filing room that every team member can walk into.

Real-world example

Jun, a cloud engineer at the fictional Brightpath Logistics, moves a 4 TB PostgreSQL database to AWS. He picks a gp3 EBS volume with 12,000 IOPS and 500 MiB/s provisioned, takes nightly incremental snapshots, and gives the reporting servers a shared Amazon EFS file system for exported CSVs. Monthly cost turns out lower than the old SAN's support contract.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Create a volume, choosing type (SSD or HDD), size, and provisioned IOPS and throughput where the type allows it.
  2. Attach it to a VM in the same zone; it appears as an NVMe or SCSI disk that you partition and format.
  3. The provider replicates the volume inside its zone; snapshots copy changed blocks to regional object storage.
  4. For shared access, create a managed file system (NFS, SMB or Lustre) and mount it from many VMs or containers.
  5. Monitor latency, IOPS and throughput limits — the VM type also caps total disk bandwidth.

Who uses it

Cloud engineers, DevOps and platform teams, database administrators and solutions architects size and tune cloud block and file storage every day.

Key takeaway

A volume's performance is capped by both the volume and the VM: a 256,000-IOPS volume on a small instance will only deliver what that instance's EBS bandwidth allows.

Going deeper

  • EBS gp3 gives a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s at any size; since September 2025 a single gp3 volume can grow to 64 TiB, 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s, provisioned independently of capacity.
  • io2 Block Express offers up to 64 TiB, 256,000 IOPS and 4,000 MiB/s with 99.999% designed durability and sub-millisecond latency, and supports Multi-Attach to up to 16 Nitro instances in a zone.
  • Instance store (AWS) and Local SSD (Google Cloud) are physically attached NVMe drives: millions of IOPS on big instances, but data vanishes when the instance stops, so use them only for caches and scratch.
  • Managed file services include Amazon EFS (NFSv4.1), Amazon FSx for Lustre, Windows File Server, NetApp ONTAP and OpenZFS; Azure Files, Azure NetApp Files and Azure Managed Lustre; and Google Filestore, NetApp Volumes and Managed Lustre (DDN-based, GA in 2025).
  • Snapshots are incremental and stored in regional object storage; the first restore of a block from a snapshot is lazy-loaded, so warm volumes (or use Fast Snapshot Restore) before benchmarking a restored database.
  • On AWS Nitro instances EBS volumes appear to the guest as NVMe devices even though they travel over the network; Azure Elastic SAN instead presents volumes over iSCSI and pools capacity and IOPS for many VMs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Benchmarking a freshly restored snapshot and blaming the disk: blocks are fetched from object storage on first touch, so the first pass is slow.
  • Storing important data only on instance store or Local SSD: it disappears when the VM stops or the host fails.
  • Over-provisioning IOPS 'just in case': provisioned IOPS are billed every hour whether used or not; measure first.

docs.title: 7.10 Cloud Object Storage Services and Storage Classes
docs.text:
Cloud object storage (Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage) keeps unlimited objects at very high durability, billed per gigabyte-month, per request and per gigabyte read out. Storage classes trade a lower monthly price for higher retrieval fees, minimum storage periods and sometimes slower access.

S3 storage price per GB-month (US East list price). Approximate list prices; colder classes cost far less to keep but more to read. Always check current pricing.

Think of it like…

Storage classes are like a self-storage company with a front-room locker (pricey, instant), a back-room locker (cheaper, small fee to open) and an off-site warehouse (very cheap, but you must book collection hours or days ahead).

Real-world example

Priya, a FinOps analyst at the fictional Quillon Media, finds 2 PB of raw footage in S3 Standard costing about $45,000 a month. Access logs show 95% is never read after 60 days. Moving that data to Glacier Instant Retrieval and Deep Archive with a lifecycle rule cuts the bill by more than 80%, while recent footage stays in Standard.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick a provider, region and redundancy option (single zone, multi-zone or geo-redundant).
  2. Write objects into the default class (S3 Standard, Azure Hot, GCS Standard).
  3. Measure access patterns with storage analytics or access logs.
  4. Add lifecycle rules or automatic tiering to move cold objects to cheaper classes.
  5. Remember the hidden costs: requests, retrieval per GB, early-deletion charges and data egress to the internet.

Who uses it

Cloud architects, FinOps practitioners, data engineers, backup administrators and media companies manage cloud object storage classes.

Key takeaway

Memorise the minimum storage durations: S3 Standard-IA 30 days, Glacier Instant/Flexible 90 days, Deep Archive 180 days; Azure Cool 30, Cold 90, Archive 180; GCS Nearline 30, Coldline 90, Archive 365.

Going deeper

  • S3 Standard, Standard-IA, Intelligent-Tiering and the Glacier classes store data across at least three Availability Zones and are designed for 99.999999999% durability; One Zone-IA and Express One Zone keep data in a single zone.
  • Glacier Flexible Retrieval restores take about 1-5 minutes (expedited), 3-5 hours (standard) or 5-12 hours (bulk); Deep Archive restores take up to 12 hours (standard) or 48 hours (bulk).
  • S3 Express One Zone (2023) uses directory buckets in one Availability Zone for single-digit-millisecond access; S3 Tables (2024) stores Apache Iceberg tables, and S3 Vectors stores embeddings for AI search.
  • Azure Blob has Hot, Cool, Cold and Archive tiers; archived blobs must be rehydrated (up to about 15 hours at standard priority) before reading, and the automatic 'smart tier' became generally available in April 2026.
  • Google Cloud Storage classes (Standard, Nearline, Coldline, Archive) all return the first byte in milliseconds — the difference is price, retrieval fees and minimum duration — and Autoclass moves objects automatically.
  • Small objects are costly in cold classes: S3 Standard-IA and Glacier Instant bill at least 128 KB per object, and Glacier Flexible/Deep Archive add about 40 KB of metadata overhead per object.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Archiving millions of tiny files individually: per-object request and overhead fees can exceed the storage saving; bundle them into larger archives first.
  • Forgetting egress: reading 100 TB out to the internet can cost thousands of dollars even when storage is cheap.
  • Using Deep Archive for data you might need urgently: restores take hours, so keep recent backups in an instantly readable class.

docs.title: Try it: See which storage classes your objects use and add a lifecycle rule (AWS CLI)
docs.text:
aws s3api list-objects-v2 --bucket lena-lab-2026 \
  --query 'Contents[].[Key,StorageClass,Size]' --output table

cat > lc.json <<'EOF'
{"Rules":[{"ID":"cold-after-60d","Status":"Enabled","Filter":{"Prefix":"raw/"},
  "Transitions":[{"Days":60,"StorageClass":"GLACIER_IR"},{"Days":365,"StorageClass":"DEEP_ARCHIVE"}],
  "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload":{"DaysAfterInitiation":7}}]}
EOF
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket lena-lab-2026 --lifecycle-configuration file://lc.json

docs.title: 7.11 Kubernetes Storage: Volumes, PV/PVC and CSI
docs.text:
Containers are throw-away by design, so anything they write disappears when they restart. Kubernetes solves this with persistent volumes: an application asks for storage with a PersistentVolumeClaim, and a storage driver following the Container Storage Interface (CSI) creates and attaches a real disk or share for it.

Dynamic provisioning with CSI. The developer only writes the claim; the StorageClass and CSI driver turn it into a real disk.

Think of it like…

A PVC is like a hotel booking request ('a quiet double room for three nights'); the StorageClass is the hotel's room categories; the CSI driver is the front desk that actually hands you a key to a real room.

Real-world example

Diego deploys PostgreSQL on a Kubernetes cluster for the fictional Fernwood Libraries. His StatefulSet asks for a 100 GiB ReadWriteOnce volume from the 'fast-ssd' StorageClass. The cloud's CSI driver creates a disk, attaches it to whichever node runs the pod, and if that node fails the disk follows the pod to a new node. Nightly VolumeSnapshots give quick restore points.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. An admin installs a CSI driver and defines StorageClasses (for example fast-ssd, standard, shared-nfs).
  2. A developer creates a PersistentVolumeClaim asking for size, access mode and class.
  3. The external provisioner calls the driver's CreateVolume; a PersistentVolume (PV) object is created and bound to the claim.
  4. When a pod using the claim is scheduled, the driver attaches the volume to that node and mounts it into the container.
  5. On deletion, the reclaim policy decides whether the real disk is deleted or retained.

Who uses it

Platform engineers, DevOps and SRE teams, Kubernetes administrators and anyone running databases or stateful apps on Kubernetes use PV, PVC and CSI.

Key takeaway

Know the access modes: ReadWriteOnce (one node), ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany (many nodes, needs shared file storage) and ReadWriteOncePod (exactly one pod).

Going deeper

  • CSI became generally available in Kubernetes 1.13 (2018) and replaced most 'in-tree' volume plugins; each driver has a controller part (create, attach, snapshot) and a node part (stage and publish mounts).
  • VolumeSnapshot reached GA in Kubernetes 1.20 and ReadWriteOncePod in 1.29; VolumeAttributesClass, which lets you change a live volume's IOPS or throughput tier, reached GA in 1.34 (2025).
  • volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer delays creating a disk until the pod is scheduled, so a zonal cloud disk is created in the same zone as the node instead of a random one.
  • StatefulSets give each replica a stable name and its own PVC from volumeClaimTemplates; deleting the StatefulSet deliberately leaves PVCs behind so data is not lost by accident.
  • Rook (CNCF graduated) runs Ceph inside Kubernetes, Longhorn (CNCF) replicates volumes across nodes' local disks, and Portworx (acquired by Pure Storage in 2020, now Everpure) adds enterprise data services.
  • Velero backs up Kubernetes objects and persistent volumes (via CSI snapshots or file-level copy) to object storage, enabling cluster migration and disaster recovery.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using emptyDir or hostPath for real data: emptyDir dies with the pod and hostPath ties the pod to one node; use PVCs.
  • Asking for ReadWriteMany on a block-storage class: most block CSI drivers support only RWO; RWX needs NFS, CephFS or a managed file service.
  • Leaving reclaimPolicy: Delete on production classes without backups: deleting a PVC instantly deletes the cloud disk.

docs.title: Try it: A minimal PVC and pod (works on any cluster with a default StorageClass, e.g. kind or minikube)
docs.text:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: data-pvc}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources: {requests: {storage: 1Gi}}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: writer}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox
    command: [sh, -c, 'date >> /data/log.txt; sleep 3600']
    volumeMounts: [{name: d, mountPath: /data}]
  volumes: [{name: d, persistentVolumeClaim: {claimName: data-pvc}}]
EOF
kubectl get pvc,pv
kubectl get storageclass

docs.title: 7.12 Storage for AI Training and Inference
docs.text:
AI systems are hungry for data in three ways: training must stream huge datasets to GPUs without letting them idle, training must save giant checkpoints quickly in case something fails, and inference must store and reload model weights and conversation memory (the KV cache). Storage design decides how much of an expensive GPU cluster is actually working.

Where storage touches the AI lifecycle. Each stage stresses storage differently: capacity, read bandwidth, write bursts, then low latency.

Think of it like…

A GPU cluster is a team of world-class chefs: storage is the kitchen porter. If ingredients arrive late, or the chefs must stop cooking every hour to write the whole recipe book by hand, the restaurant wastes its most expensive staff.

Real-world example

The fictional Aurelia Labs trains a 70-billion-parameter model on 1,024 GPUs. Each full checkpoint (weights plus optimiser state) is about 1 TB. Writing it to a 100 GB/s parallel file system takes about 10 seconds; with asynchronous checkpointing the GPUs copy state to host memory in a second and keep training while it drains. In production, their chatbot offloads KV cache for idle conversations to NVMe instead of recomputing it.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Ingest raw data into object storage (the data lake) and clean, deduplicate and tokenise it.
  2. Pack samples into large shards (for example tar or Parquet files of 100 MB-1 GB) so reads are big and sequential.
  3. During training, data loaders prefetch and shuffle shards from shared storage or local NVMe caches.
  4. Every N steps, write a checkpoint; restart from the newest one after any failure.
  5. For inference, load weights quickly onto many GPUs and keep KV cache in GPU memory, then CPU memory, then NVMe or networked storage.

Who uses it

AI infrastructure engineers, MLOps teams, HPC and storage architects, GPU cloud providers and storage vendors' AI teams design these pipelines.

Key takeaway

Rule of thumb: full training checkpoints with the Adam optimiser in mixed precision need roughly 12-16 bytes per parameter, so a 70B model checkpoint is about 1 TB.

Going deeper

  • MLPerf Storage v2.0 (August 2025) added checkpointing tests using Llama 3 model sizes; Argonne's DAOS submission checkpointed a 405-billion-parameter model in under ten seconds using 128 servers.
  • KV cache per token equals 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes; grouped-query attention cuts it sharply, yet a 128k-token context for a 70B model still needs about 40 GiB.
  • NVIDIA Dynamo (2025) and its NIXL transfer library move KV cache between GPU memory, CPU memory, local SSDs and networked storage; open-source LMCache does similar tiering for vLLM.
  • NVIDIA announced the Inference Context Memory Storage platform, built on BlueField-4 DPUs, at CES in January 2026 as a dedicated shared tier for KV cache, with partners including Dell, HPE, Everpure, IBM, DDN, VAST and WEKA.
  • GPUDirect Storage and RDMA let NVMe or networked storage DMA straight into GPU memory, bypassing a CPU bounce buffer — crucial when hundreds of GB/s must flow into a GPU pod.
  • Model weights are increasingly stored as safetensors files that can be memory-mapped; loading a 140 GB model at 10 GB/s takes 14 seconds, so fast storage directly cuts autoscaling cold-start time.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Feeding GPUs millions of small JPEG files directly: per-file metadata operations dominate; pack them into large shards.
  • Checkpointing only model weights: without optimiser state and data-loader position, a restart is not an exact resume.
  • Assuming bigger GPUs fix slow training: if storage cannot deliver data, GPU utilisation drops and money burns; measure I/O wait first.

docs.title: Try it: Estimate KV-cache size per token for a transformer (Python, no libraries needed)
docs.text:
layers, kv_heads, head_dim, bytes_per_val = 80, 8, 128, 2   # Llama-3-70B-like, FP16/BF16
per_token = 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * bytes_per_val  # 2 = keys + values
print(per_token / 1024, 'KiB per token')                 # 320 KiB
print(per_token * 128_000 / 2**30, 'GiB for a 128k-token context')  # ~39 GiB

docs.title: 7.13 Tiering and Data Lifecycle Management
docs.text:
Most data is busy for a short time and then rarely touched. Tiering moves data automatically between fast, expensive storage and slow, cheap storage according to how often it is used, and lifecycle management decides how long data is kept and when it is safely deleted.

The data lifecycle. Data should flow downhill to cheaper tiers and leave the system on purpose, not by accident.

Think of it like…

It is like a wardrobe: this season's clothes hang in the bedroom, last year's go into boxes under the bed, old keepsakes go to the attic, and once a year you give away what nobody will wear again.

Real-world example

Tom, data manager at the fictional Larkspur Hospital, finds that 70% of 900 TB on all-flash storage has not been opened in a year. He enables cloud tiering so cold blocks move to object storage automatically, sets a seven-year retention policy for medical records with legal-hold exceptions, and schedules defensible deletion of expired data — cutting flash purchases by half.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Classify data by business value, sensitivity and legal retention rules.
  2. Measure 'temperature' — how recently and how often it is read.
  3. Define policies: keep hot data on flash, move cold data to HDD, object or tape tiers after N days.
  4. Let software move data automatically while keeping it reachable (transparent tiering or stub files).
  5. Apply retention, legal holds and immutability where required.
  6. Delete or archive data when its retention period ends, and record that you did.

Who uses it

Storage administrators, records managers, compliance officers, FinOps teams and data governance specialists run tiering and lifecycle programmes.

Key takeaway

Know the difference: caching keeps an extra copy on the fast tier; tiering moves the only copy, so the slow tier must be protected just as well.

Going deeper

  • Analysts commonly find that well over half of stored enterprise data is cold or never reused, which is why automated tiering to HDD, object or tape can halve primary-storage spend.
  • NetApp FabricPool tiers cold 4 KiB blocks from ONTAP flash aggregates to S3-compatible object storage while the file system still shows the data as present; reads pull blocks back transparently.
  • Hierarchical storage management (HSM) systems such as HPSS or IBM Storage Archive move whole files to tape and leave stubs; reading a stub triggers a recall that may take minutes while a tape mounts.
  • GDPR Article 5(1)(e) 'storage limitation' requires that personal data be kept no longer than necessary, so lifecycle policies are a legal duty, not only a cost saving.
  • Data gravity, a term coined by Dave McCrory in 2010, means large datasets attract applications and services; moving petabytes is slow and costly, so place data where it will be processed.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Tiering data that is needed in an emergency to a slow archive: classify by business recovery needs, not just last-access date.
  • Relying on access times on a volume mounted with noatime or relatime: they may be stale; use storage analytics instead.
  • Keeping everything forever 'just in case': it raises cost, breach impact and legal discovery burden.

docs.title: Try it: Find cold files on a Linux file server (not accessed in 365 days) and total their size
docs.text:
# needs a file system mounted without 'noatime' to trust access times
find /srv/share -type f -atime +365 -printf '%s\n' | \
  awk '{s+=$1} END {printf "%.1f GiB cold\n", s/2^30}'

# Top-level folders by size
du -h --max-depth=1 /srv/share | sort -h

docs.title: Chapter 8: Performance, Emerging Tech, Careers & Learning
docs.text: The final chapter turns knowledge into practice and looks ahead. It shows how to benchmark and monitor storage and memory honestly, how to troubleshoot slowdowns on Linux, Windows and macOS, and which technologies may shape the next decade: emerging memories, processing-in-memory, computational storage and CXL memory tiering, along with sustainability and the AI-driven memory market. It closes with careers, certifications, learning resources, home labs, interview questions and a 16-week study plan.

docs.title: 8.1 Benchmarking Storage: fio, CrystalDiskMark and Doing It Right
docs.text:
A storage benchmark runs a controlled pattern of reads and writes and measures how fast and how consistently a device or system responds. Good benchmarking means choosing a pattern that resembles the real workload, removing tricks like caches, and reporting latency as well as speed.

A trustworthy benchmark run. Skipping preconditioning or cache control is the most common reason benchmark numbers mislead.

Think of it like…

Benchmarking a drive is like testing a car: a downhill sprint with a tailwind gives a thrilling number, but you learn more from a full loaded trip in traffic, measured many times.

Real-world example

Sam, a junior admin at the fictional Oakridge Dental, is told a new SSD 'does 7,000 MB/s'. His fio test of 4 KiB random writes at queue depth 1, after filling the drive twice, shows 60 MB/s with a 99.9th-percentile latency of 2 ms. That, not the box number, predicts how the practice-management database will feel.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Write down the question: which workload, which device, which metric (IOPS, MB/s, latency percentiles)?
  2. Prepare the device: secure-erase or precondition SSDs by writing their full capacity (often twice) to reach steady state.
  3. Choose block size, read/write mix, random vs sequential, queue depth and number of jobs to match the real application.
  4. Bypass the OS page cache (direct I/O) unless you deliberately want to test caching, and use incompressible data.
  5. Run long enough (minutes, not seconds), repeat at least three times and record the median and spread.
  6. Report full settings, firmware, OS and kernel versions so others can reproduce the result.

Who uses it

Storage and performance engineers, system administrators, hardware reviewers, SSD vendors' validation teams and solution architects benchmark storage.

Key takeaway

Always quote latency percentiles (p99, p99.9) with IOPS: an SSD averaging 0.1 ms but spiking to 50 ms at p99.9 will hurt a database far more than its average suggests.

Going deeper

  • The SNIA Solid State Storage Performance Test Specification (PTS) defines preconditioning and steady-state rules, because fresh-out-of-box SSDs are much faster until their free blocks run out and garbage collection starts.
  • Consumer SSDs write into a fast SLC cache that may be only tens of gigabytes; sustained writes beyond it can drop from several GB/s to a few hundred MB/s, so short tests overstate speed.
  • IOPS = queue depth ÷ latency (Little's law): 32 outstanding I/Os at 0.2 ms each gives about 160,000 IOPS; one outstanding I/O at the same latency gives only 5,000.
  • fio's ioengine choice matters: psync tests one blocking I/O at a time, libaio and io_uring test asynchronous queues, and on Windows windowsaio is used; results differ by engine.
  • Compressing or deduplicating systems need realistic data: fio's refill_buffers and buffer_compress_percentage options stop arrays from 'cheating' with zero-filled buffers.
  • CrystalDiskMark's default profile runs SEQ1M Q8T1, SEQ1M Q1T1, RND4K Q32T1 and RND4K Q1T1; the RND4K Q1T1 line best predicts everyday desktop responsiveness.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using dd if=/dev/zero for throughput: it is single-threaded, often cached and compressible, so it measures the page cache, not the disk.
  • Testing a 1 GB file on a server with 256 GB of RAM without direct I/O: every read comes from memory.
  • Running fio against a raw device that holds data: write tests overwrite it; use a scratch file or an empty test disk.

docs.title: Try it: Three classic fio tests (Linux; run against a test file, never a disk holding data)
docs.text:
# 4 KiB random read, QD32, 4 jobs, 60 s, bypass page cache
fio --name=randread --filename=/tmp/fio.test --size=4G --direct=1 \
    --ioengine=libaio --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=32 --numjobs=4 \
    --runtime=60 --time_based --group_reporting

# 1 MiB sequential write (throughput)
fio --name=seqwrite --filename=/tmp/fio.test --size=4G --direct=1 --rw=write --bs=1M --iodepth=8

# 4 KiB random write at QD1 (latency, like a database log)
fio --name=qd1 --filename=/tmp/fio.test --size=4G --direct=1 --rw=randwrite --bs=4k --iodepth=1 \
    --runtime=30 --time_based --percentile_list=50:99:99.9

docs.title: 8.2 Memory Benchmarks and Industry Benchmark Suites
docs.text:
Memory benchmarks measure how many gigabytes per second a system can move between memory and CPU, and how long a single access takes. Industry suites such as MLPerf Storage and SPECstorage Solution define standard workloads and publication rules so that vendors' results can be compared fairly.

Theoretical peak memory bandwidth. Each step up — more channels, faster DRAM, then stacked HBM — multiplies bandwidth.

Think of it like…

Memory bandwidth is how many lanes a motorway has; memory latency is how long one car takes to drive the route; an industry benchmark is an official race with published rules and referees.

Real-world example

Ines tunes a weather code at the fictional Fjord Research Centre. STREAM Triad shows her new two-socket server reaching about 700 GB/s, but only when all memory channels are populated and threads are pinned to the right NUMA node. Intel MLC shows remote-socket latency of about 200 ns versus about 110 ns locally, so she binds each MPI rank to its local memory.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Measure peak bandwidth with STREAM (Copy, Scale, Add, Triad) using arrays much larger than the CPU caches.
  2. Measure idle and loaded latency with Intel MLC or lmbench's pointer-chasing tests.
  3. Repeat with different thread counts and NUMA placements to see scaling and cross-socket penalties.
  4. For storage systems, run standard suites (MLPerf Storage, SPECstorage Solution 2020) under their published rules.
  5. Compare against theoretical peak: channels × transfer rate × 8 bytes per 64-bit channel.

Who uses it

Performance engineers, HPC centres, CPU and server vendors, hardware reviewers and storage vendors' benchmarking teams use these tools.

Key takeaway

Theoretical DDR bandwidth = channels × MT/s × 8 bytes; one DDR5-6400 channel is 51.2 GB/s, and STREAM usually reaches about 70-90% of the total.

Going deeper

  • STREAM, written by John McCalpin in the early 1990s, reports four kernels; Triad (a = b + q×c) is the headline figure and each array should be at least four times the total last-level cache.
  • Intel Memory Latency Checker (MLC) measures idle latency, peak bandwidth by read/write ratio, and loaded-latency curves showing how latency climbs as bandwidth demand approaches saturation.
  • MLPerf Storage, from MLCommons, uses the DLIO tool to emulate accelerators reading training data (3D U-Net, ResNet-50, CosmoFlow) and, from v2.0 in 2025, checkpoint workloads.
  • SPECstorage Solution 2020 measures file-storage systems with workloads such as AI_IMAGE, EDA_BLENDED, GENOMICS, SWBUILD and VDA, reporting business metrics alongside latency.
  • The Storage Performance Council's SPC-1 and SPC-2 were once the main block-array benchmarks, but few results have been published in recent years; the IO500 list now drives HPC storage comparisons.
  • Published results are only comparable within the same benchmark version and rules; always read the full disclosure (hardware, cost, settings) rather than just the headline number.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running STREAM with arrays that fit in cache: results show cache bandwidth and can be several times higher than real memory bandwidth.
  • Populating only some memory channels: a server with 4 of 8 channels filled loses half its bandwidth even with the same total GB.
  • Comparing vendors' MLPerf Storage numbers without checking how many simulated accelerators and clients each used.

docs.title: Try it: Build and run STREAM on Linux (GCC with OpenMP)
docs.text:
curl -O https://www.cs.virginia.edu/stream/FTP/Code/stream.c
gcc -O3 -fopenmp -DSTREAM_ARRAY_SIZE=100000000 stream.c -o stream
OMP_NUM_THREADS=$(nproc) OMP_PROC_BIND=spread ./stream | grep -E 'Copy|Scale|Add|Triad'

numactl --hardware        # see NUMA nodes and their memory

docs.title: 8.3 Monitoring Storage and Memory on Linux
docs.text:
Linux ships with tools that show, layer by layer, how memory is used and how busy each disk is. Knowing a handful of commands lets you answer the key questions quickly: is the system short of memory, which disk is slow, and which process is causing it.

Which tool sees which layer. Work top-down to find where time is being spent, then confirm at the device.

Think of it like…

Monitoring is like a car dashboard plus a mechanic's diagnostic plug: iostat and vmstat are the speedometer and fuel gauge; tracing tools are the plug that tells you exactly which part is struggling.

Real-world example

Raj, an SRE at the fictional Coastline Bank, gets an alert that the payments API slowed down. vmstat shows high 'wa' (I/O wait); iostat -x shows /dev/nvme2n1 with r_await jumping from 0.2 to 9 ms; iotop points to a backup job reading at full speed. Throttling the backup with ionice restores normal latency in minutes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start broad: uptime, vmstat 1 and free -h show load, memory, swapping and I/O wait.
  2. Find the busy device: iostat -xz 1 shows per-device IOPS, MB/s, average wait and queue size.
  3. Find the process: iotop or pidstat -d 1 show who is reading and writing.
  4. Check pressure: /proc/pressure/io and /proc/pressure/memory show how long tasks were stalled.
  5. Dig deeper with tracing (biolatency, blktrace, perf) and check device health (nvme-cli, smartctl, dmesg).

Who uses it

Linux administrators, SREs, DevOps engineers, database administrators and support engineers use these tools during every performance incident.

Key takeaway

In iostat -x, look first at r_await/w_await (latency) and aqu-sz (queue); %util near 100% is meaningless for NVMe SSDs that serve many requests in parallel.

Going deeper

  • iostat's columns come from /proc/diskstats: r/s and w/s are IOPS, rkB/s and wkB/s are throughput, r_await and w_await are average milliseconds including queueing, and aqu-sz is average queue length.
  • Pressure Stall Information (PSI, Linux 4.20+) reports the share of time some or all tasks were stalled on CPU, memory or I/O over 10, 60 and 300 seconds, and can trigger alerts before users notice.
  • biolatency and biosnoop from the BCC/bpftrace collections use eBPF to print a latency histogram per disk or every I/O with its process, with very low overhead in production.
  • free's 'available' column, not 'free', shows how much memory can be used without swapping, because Linux deliberately fills spare RAM with page cache that it can drop instantly.
  • numastat and numactl --hardware show per-NUMA-node memory use; heavy 'other_node' counts mean threads are reading remote memory and losing bandwidth.
  • Prometheus node_exporter exposes the same kernel counters (node_disk_*, node_memory_*, node_pressure_*) for dashboards in Grafana, turning one-off checks into continuous monitoring.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Panicking when 'free' memory is near zero: Linux uses spare RAM as cache; check 'available' and swap activity instead.
  • Trusting %util for SSDs: it only shows the device had at least one I/O in flight; an NVMe drive at 100% util may have plenty of headroom.
  • Reading only averages: a 1-second iostat average can hide 50 ms spikes; use latency histograms for tail behaviour.

docs.title: Try it: A first-five-minutes storage check on Linux
docs.text:
uptime; free -h
vmstat 1 5                          # si/so = swapping, wa = I/O wait
iostat -xz 1 5                      # per-device latency and queue
sudo iotop -oPa                     # processes doing I/O
cat /proc/pressure/io /proc/pressure/memory
sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0      # NVMe health
sudo smartctl -H -A /dev/sda        # SATA/SAS health
sudo dmesg -T | grep -iE 'error|timeout|reset' | tail

docs.title: 8.4 Troubleshooting Playbook and Windows/macOS Tools
docs.text:
Troubleshooting is a method, not a tool: describe the symptom precisely, check each resource for utilisation, saturation and errors, narrow down the layer at fault, fix it and confirm. Windows and macOS have their own built-in tools for the same checks.

From complaint to confirmed fix. Measure before and after with the same metric, or you cannot prove the fix worked.

Think of it like…

A good troubleshooter works like a doctor: ask what hurts and since when, check vital signs in a fixed order, order targeted tests, treat the cause rather than the symptom, then schedule a follow-up.

Real-world example

Amira supports the fictional Westfield Accountants. Staff say 'the file server is slow'. Performance Monitor shows Avg. Disk sec/Read at 45 ms on the data volume; Get-PhysicalDisk reports one disk 'Warning'; the System log lists repeated Event ID 153 retries. Replacing the failing disk brings latency back to 3 ms.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Define the symptom: what is slow, since when, for whom, and how is it measured?
  2. Apply the USE method to each resource (CPU, memory, disk, network): utilisation, saturation, errors.
  3. Check recent changes: updates, new workloads, backups, firmware, capacity near full.
  4. Isolate the layer: application, OS cache, file system, driver, path, device or remote array.
  5. Fix the cause, then measure again with the same metric to prove the improvement.
  6. Write a short post-incident note so the next person solves it faster.

Who uses it

Help-desk and support engineers, system administrators, SREs and storage specialists all follow this playbook.

Key takeaway

On Windows, Avg. Disk sec/Read and sec/Write in Performance Monitor are the latency counters; sustained values above about 20 ms for SSD-backed volumes usually mean trouble.

Going deeper

  • Brendan Gregg's USE method checks every resource for utilisation (busy time), saturation (queued work) and errors, giving a complete checklist that avoids guessing.
  • Windows Event ID 129 (storport reset to device) and 153 (I/O retried) often point to failing disks, bad cables, HBA firmware or overloaded SAN paths rather than to the application.
  • A volume above roughly 80-90% full often slows down: copy-on-write file systems fragment, SSDs have fewer free blocks for garbage collection, and some arrays throttle near full.
  • On macOS, Activity Monitor's Disk and Memory tabs show per-process I/O and memory pressure, fs_usage traces file-system calls live, and diskutil plus Disk Utility's First Aid check volumes.
  • In shared environments a 'noisy neighbour' — another VM, container or tenant hammering the same disk or array — is a common cause; QoS limits or moving the workload fix it.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Rebooting first: it may clear the symptom and destroy the evidence; capture counters and logs before restarting.
  • Upgrading hardware before measuring: many 'slow storage' complaints are actually memory shortage causing swapping or network latency.
  • Running chkdsk /f or fsck on a failing disk before copying data off: repair attempts can stress a dying drive; image or back it up first.

docs.title: 8.5 Emerging Memories: MRAM, ReRAM, PCM, FeRAM — and Optane's Story
docs.text:
Researchers have long sought a 'universal memory' as fast as DRAM, as dense and cheap as flash, and non-volatile. Candidates store bits as magnetic orientation (MRAM), resistance (ReRAM, PCM) or electric polarisation (FeRAM). Several are now in real chips — mainly as embedded memory — while Intel's Optane showed both the promise and the business risk.

The rise and end of 3D XPoint / Optane. Excellent technology, but too expensive per bit and dependent on one CPU vendor's platforms.

Think of it like…

DRAM is a whiteboard that must be rewritten constantly and is wiped when the lights go off; flash is a notebook written in pen that wears out; emerging memories try to be a magic slate that is fast, permanent and never wears out — so far each gets two of three.

Real-world example

The fictional Velta Motors designs a car controller. Its old microcontroller held firmware in embedded NOR flash, which is hard to shrink below about 28-40 nm. The new chip uses embedded MRAM, which writes faster with far less energy and survives 150 °C under the bonnet, so over-the-air updates finish in seconds.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. MRAM: a magnetic tunnel junction's free layer is set parallel or anti-parallel to a fixed layer, giving low or high resistance.
  2. ReRAM: a voltage forms or breaks a tiny conductive filament in an oxide, switching between low and high resistance.
  3. PCM: a heater melts and quenches a chalcogenide glass (amorphous, high resistance) or anneals it (crystalline, low resistance).
  4. FeRAM / FeFET: an electric field flips a ferroelectric material's polarisation, which stays put without power.
  5. Each technology is read by sensing resistance or charge and judged on speed, endurance, retention, density and cost per bit.

Who uses it

Semiconductor device and process engineers, embedded-systems designers, automotive and IoT chip teams and memory researchers work with emerging memories.

Key takeaway

Know Optane's timeline: 3D XPoint announced 2015, Optane SSDs 2017, Optane Persistent Memory 2019, Micron exits 2021, Intel winds Optane down in 2022.

Going deeper

  • STT-MRAM writes in roughly 10-100 ns with endurance far beyond flash and ten-year retention; foundries including TSMC, Samsung and GlobalFoundries offer embedded MRAM as a replacement for embedded flash at 28 nm and below.
  • Phase-change memory switches a Ge-Sb-Te alloy between amorphous and crystalline states; besides Optane, STMicroelectronics uses embedded PCM in its Stellar automotive microcontrollers.
  • ReRAM is simple to build in the back-end metal layers, which makes it cheap to embed; Weebit Nano and TSMC offer embedded ReRAM IP, and researchers use ReRAM crossbars for analogue in-memory AI computing.
  • FeRAM (F-RAM) has offered fast, low-power, very-high-endurance non-volatile memory for decades in meters and medical devices; ferroelectric hafnium oxide makes FeRAM and FeFETs compatible with modern CMOS.
  • Optane Persistent Memory offered Memory Mode (large, cheap-ish volatile RAM) and App Direct mode (byte-addressable persistence via DAX and PMDK); Intel recorded an inventory write-down of about $559 million when it exited in 2022.
  • Optane's lessons — tiered memory, byte-addressable persistence, latency between DRAM and NAND — now inform CXL memory expansion and storage-class-memory designs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling MRAM or ReRAM a DRAM replacement today: they mainly replace embedded flash and SRAM in small chips; standalone densities are far below DRAM and NAND.
  • Assuming Optane failed technically: it worked well; it failed commercially due to cost per bit, limited platforms and slow software adoption.
  • Confusing FeRAM with ferrite-core memory: core memory used magnetised rings; FeRAM uses ferroelectric polarisation, not magnetism.

docs.title: 8.6 Processing-in-Memory and Computational Storage
docs.text:
Moving data between memory, storage and the processor now costs more time and energy than the arithmetic itself. Processing-in-memory (PIM) puts simple compute units inside or beside memory chips, and computational storage puts processors inside SSDs or storage nodes, so that work happens where the data already sits.

Where the computing happens

Conventional Processing-in-memory Computational storage Compute location CPU / GPU only Inside or beside DRAM/HBM Inside SSD or storage node Data moved Everything Results only Filtered results Typical tasks Anything Vector math, AI inference Compression, filter, search Examples Servers today HBM-PIM, GDDR6-AiM, UPMEM ScaleFlux CSDs, SmartSSD Maturity Mainstream Early products Niche, growing

Both approaches shrink data before it travels; they differ in which device does the work.

Think of it like…

Instead of trucking every crate from the warehouse to head office to count the apples, you give the warehouse staff a calculator and ask them to phone in the total.

Real-world example

The fictional Corvid Analytics scans 200 TB of compressed logs each night looking for rare error codes. With computational storage drives that decompress and filter data inside the SSD, only 0.5% of the data — the matching lines — crosses PCIe to the CPUs, cutting the job from five hours to under one and freeing the servers for other work.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify operations that are simple but data-heavy: filtering, compression, search, reductions, vector multiply-accumulate.
  2. Offload them to compute engines inside the memory device (PIM) or storage device (computational storage drive).
  3. The host sends a command or small program plus the data location instead of reading the whole dataset.
  4. The device processes data locally at its internal bandwidth and returns only results.
  5. Software libraries and standards (SNIA, NVMe command sets) hide device details from applications.

Who uses it

Computer architects, memory and SSD vendors' R&D teams, database and analytics engineers, AI-accelerator designers and researchers work on PIM and computational storage.

Key takeaway

Remember the motivation in one phrase — the memory wall: processors got faster much more quickly than memory, so moving data, not computing, is now the bottleneck.

Going deeper

  • Moving 64 bits from off-chip DRAM costs on the order of a hundred times more energy than a 64-bit arithmetic operation, which is why architects call data movement the dominant cost.
  • Samsung's HBM-PIM (2021) placed programmable compute units in HBM stacks, and SK hynix's GDDR6-AiM (2022) adds multiply-accumulate engines to each bank, aimed at AI inference matrix-vector work.
  • UPMEM ships DDR4 DIMMs whose DRAM chips contain small general-purpose 'DPUs', giving thousands of simple cores right next to memory for genomics, search and analytics.
  • SNIA's Computational Storage Architecture and Programming Model (v1.0, 2022) defines computational storage drives, processors and arrays; NVMe added Computational Programs and Subsystem Local Memory command sets in 2024.
  • The most widespread form today is transparent: drives that compress data internally (for example ScaleFlux CSDs or IBM FlashCore Modules) without any application changes.
  • DPUs such as NVIDIA BlueField handle storage protocols, encryption and erasure coding on the network card, a related form of offload close to the data path.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Expecting PIM to run whole programs: PIM units are simple and best at narrow, highly parallel, data-heavy operations.
  • Ignoring the software cost: without standard APIs and drivers, special-purpose devices end up unused.
  • Assuming compression in the SSD frees host-visible capacity automatically: some drives only report extra space if configured with a larger logical size.

docs.title: 8.7 CXL Memory Tiering and the Composable Future
docs.text:
Compute Express Link (CXL) lets servers add memory over PCIe-style slots and, in later versions, share or pool memory between machines. The big practical question is software: deciding which data lives in fast local DRAM and which can sit in slightly slower CXL memory, and moving pages between them automatically.

The emerging memory tiers. Approximate latencies; CXL fills the gap between DRAM and SSDs.

Think of it like…

Think of a kitchen: local DRAM is the worktop within arm's reach, CXL memory is the pantry a few steps away, and pooled CXL memory is a shared storeroom down the hall — a smart cook keeps today's ingredients on the worktop and fetches the rest when needed.

Real-world example

The fictional Meridian Cloud runs in-memory databases needing 4 TB of RAM per server, but their CPUs only have enough DIMM slots for 2 TB at sensible prices. They add 2 TB of CXL memory expanders; the Linux kernel's tiering keeps hot pages in local DDR5 and demotes cold ones to CXL, and throughput drops only a few percent compared with all-local RAM at a much lower cost.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. CXL Type 3 memory devices appear to Linux as extra NUMA nodes with memory but no CPUs.
  2. The kernel or a user-space daemon tracks which pages are hot and which are cold.
  3. Cold pages are demoted from local DRAM to CXL memory; hot pages found in CXL memory are promoted back.
  4. Applications can also choose placement directly with numactl or interleaving policies.
  5. With CXL switches and pooling, memory can be assigned to whichever host needs it, reducing stranded RAM.

Who uses it

Hyperscale and cloud infrastructure teams, database engineers, Linux kernel developers, server architects and memory vendors are building CXL tiering.

Key takeaway

Rough latency ladder to remember: local DDR5 about 100 ns, direct-attached CXL memory roughly 170-250 ns, switched or pooled CXL more again — still about 100 times faster than an NVMe SSD.

Going deeper

  • CXL 2.0 (2020) added switching and memory pooling, CXL 3.0 (2022) added multi-level fabrics and true memory sharing, and CXL 4.0 (November 2025) doubles link speed using PCIe 7.0 signalling.
  • Meta's Transparent Page Placement (TPP), presented at ASPLOS 2023, demotes cold pages to CXL memory and promotes hot ones; its ideas went into the Linux kernel's memory-tiering support.
  • Linux 6.9 added weighted interleaving, letting administrators spread allocations across DRAM and CXL nodes in proportion to their bandwidth, for example 3:1, to raise total bandwidth.
  • DAMON (Data Access MONitor, Linux 5.15+) samples memory access patterns cheaply, and DAMOS policies can act on them — for example proactively reclaiming or demoting cold regions.
  • Microsoft's Pond research (ASPLOS 2023) found much of cloud server memory is 'stranded' — installed but unrentable — and argued that pooling could reduce total DRAM purchases.
  • Products include Samsung CMM-D, Micron CZ120 and SK hynix CMM-DDR5 memory expanders, Astera Labs Leo and Montage controllers, and CXL switches from vendors such as XConn.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming CXL memory is as fast as local DRAM: it adds tens to hundreds of nanoseconds; latency-critical data must stay local.
  • Expecting memory sharing everywhere in 2026: most deployments are single-host expansion; pooled and shared fabrics are still early.
  • Forgetting software support: without a tiering-aware kernel or application, pages land on CXL randomly and performance becomes unpredictable.

docs.title: Try it: See NUMA nodes (CXL memory shows up as a CPU-less node) and the kernel's tiering switches
docs.text:
numactl --hardware
lscpu | grep -i numa
cat /sys/kernel/mm/numa/demotion_enabled 2>/dev/null
cat /proc/sys/kernel/numa_balancing     # 2 = memory-tiering mode on recent kernels
# Run a program with memory interleaved across nodes 0 and 1
numactl --interleave=0,1 ./my_app

docs.title: 8.8 Sustainability, $/GB Trends and the AI-Driven Market
docs.text:
Every stored byte costs money and energy twice: once to manufacture the chips and drives (embodied carbon) and again to power and cool them (operational energy). Prices per gigabyte usually fall over time, but memory markets swing in booms and busts — and since 2024-2025 AI demand for HBM and high-capacity SSDs has pushed prices sharply upwards.

Rough cost per GB by medium (order of magnitude). Indicative street prices only; 2025-2026 DRAM and SSD prices have been unusually volatile.

Think of it like…

Storage is like a city's housing: building new homes has a big up-front carbon cost, heating them costs every month, and prices rise fast when a wave of newcomers (AI data centres) arrives faster than builders can build.

Real-world example

Elena, infrastructure lead at the fictional Hearth Insurance, must add 5 PB. Tape for the 4 PB of rarely read archives uses almost no power on the shelf; high-capacity QLC SSDs for the hot 1 PB replace racks of HDDs with far fewer watts per TB. But a 2026 quote for server DRAM has risen steeply, so she buys memory early under a long-term agreement and right-sizes VM RAM.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Measure: capacity, utilisation, watts per TB and data growth for each tier.
  2. Reduce: delete expired data, deduplicate and compress, stop keeping unnecessary copies.
  3. Place: hot data on dense flash, warm on HDD, cold on tape or archive classes that use little power at rest.
  4. Extend and reuse: run hardware longer where safe, sanitise and refurbish rather than shred when possible.
  5. Buy smart: track price cycles, use long-term agreements and model total cost of ownership, not just $/GB.

Who uses it

Infrastructure planners, procurement and FinOps teams, sustainability officers, data-centre operators and market analysts work on these questions.

Key takeaway

Remember the rough $/GB ladder: DRAM costs hundreds of times more per GB than SSD, and SSD several times more than HDD, which in turn costs a few times more than tape.

Going deeper

  • Life-cycle studies generally find that flash has higher embodied carbon per terabyte than hard drives because chip fabrication is energy-intensive, while SSDs use less power per I/O; the greener choice depends on how hard the data works.
  • The EU Ecodesign Regulation (EU) 2019/424 sets efficiency and information requirements for servers and data storage products, and the recast Energy Efficiency Directive (EU) 2023/1791 requires larger data centres to report energy data.
  • SNIA's Emerald program defines how to measure storage power efficiency, and its methods underpin the US ENERGY STAR Data Center Storage specification.
  • HBM uses roughly three times as much wafer area per bit as standard DRAM, so the AI boom diverts DRAM production capacity and tightens supply of conventional DRAM and modules.
  • Memory prices are cyclical: suppliers add capacity in booms, prices crash in gluts (as in 2019 and 2023), then rise again; the 2025-2026 upswing driven by AI was one of the sharpest on record.
  • Kryder's law, the rapid fall in HDD cost per GB, has slowed sharply since about 2010; new recording methods such as HAMR are needed to keep capacity per drive and $/TB improving.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Judging only by price per GB: power, space, cooling, performance, failure rates and staff time often matter more over five years.
  • Assuming SSDs are always greener: for rarely read archives, HDD or tape can have far lower lifetime carbon per TB.
  • Assuming memory prices only fall: plan budgets for cycles where DRAM or NAND prices double within a year.

Deleting 400 TB of duplicate test copies saves more energy than any hardware upgrade. Tape for cold dataIndustry practice · Concept · Current · Beginner Using tape for rarely accessed archives because cartridges use no power while stored on a shelf. A broadcaster keeps 20 PB on LTO in a library, powering only the drives when reading. An analyst models five-year cost per usable PB, including racks and power, not just purchase $/GB. A procurement team checks quarterly contract-price forecasts before timing a large server order. A cloud provider signs a two-year LTA for HBM and DDR5 to guarantee supply during the AI build-out. HDD $/GB fell roughly a thousandfold from 1990s levels, but improvements since 2010 are far slower. Micron announced in December 2025 it would exit its Crucial consumer business to prioritise data-centre customers.

docs.title: 8.9 Careers in Memory and Storage
docs.text:
Memory and storage jobs range from designing transistors in a fab to keeping a bank's data safe and fast, to writing the firmware inside SSDs. Because every organisation stores data, there are roles for beginners in operations and support as well as deep specialists in hardware and software.

Roles built on memory and storage skills. Operations, software and hardware roles all share the same fundamentals.

Think of it like…

The storage world is like the water industry: some people design the reservoirs and pipes, some run the pumping stations day and night, some test the water quality, and others sell and install systems to new towns — all essential, all different.

Real-world example

Zara studies computing at a fictional polytechnic. She starts as a data-centre technician replacing failed drives, earns a Linux and a cloud certification, moves into a storage administrator role managing NetApp and S3, and after three years becomes a cloud storage engineer automating backup and tiering with Terraform and Python.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick an entry route: operations (technician, help desk), software (developer, SRE) or hardware (electronics, physics, materials).
  2. Build fundamentals: Linux, networking, file systems, RAID, backup, scripting (Python, Bash, PowerShell).
  3. Add one platform (an enterprise array, Ceph or a cloud) and one certification.
  4. Show evidence: home-lab write-ups, GitHub projects, benchmark reports, contributions to open-source storage projects.
  5. Specialise over time: performance, data protection, AI storage, firmware, memory design or architecture.

Who uses it

Employers include storage and memory vendors, cloud providers, banks, hospitals, universities, HPC centres, managed service providers and semiconductor fabs.

Key takeaway

In interviews, tie every answer to data safety and performance: employers want people who protect data first and measure before they change things.

Going deeper

  • Operations roles (technician, storage administrator, backup engineer) value hands-on troubleshooting, change discipline and certifications, and are the most common entry points for graduates and career changers.
  • Engineering roles in storage software (kernel block layer, file systems, Ceph, databases) expect strong C, C++, Rust or Go, data structures, concurrency and crash-consistency knowledge.
  • SSD firmware engineers write embedded C for controllers: flash translation layers, wear levelling, error correction management and NVMe command handling, often on multi-core ARM or RISC-V chips.
  • Memory design and process roles at companies such as Samsung, SK hynix, Micron, Kioxia, SanDisk and YMTC usually require degrees in electrical engineering, physics or materials science.
  • The 2025-2026 AI build-out raised demand for engineers who understand GPU data pipelines, parallel file systems, HBM and CXL, making AI infrastructure storage a fast-growing specialism.
  • Salary levels vary widely by country and employer; check sources such as national labour statistics, Levels.fyi and local job boards rather than relying on a single quoted figure.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking storage is a dying niche because 'everything is in the cloud': cloud providers and their customers employ many storage specialists.
  • Collecting certificates without hands-on practice: interviewers quickly ask what you have built and broken.
  • Ignoring soft skills: storage work involves change windows, incident calls and explaining risk to managers.

docs.title: 8.10 Certifications: Proving Your Skills to Employers
docs.text:
Certifications prove to employers that you know a body of material and, for performance-based exams, that you can do real tasks. In storage there are general IT foundations, vendor-neutral storage courses, vendor platform certifications and cloud and Kubernetes certifications.

A sensible certification path. Build from general IT to storage concepts, then a platform, then cloud and specialisms.

Think of it like…

Certifications are like driving licences for different vehicles: a general car licence first, then extra endorsements for lorries, motorbikes or buses depending on the job you want.

Real-world example

Leo wants a storage admin job. He earns CompTIA A+ while working on a help desk, then RHCSA to prove Linux skills. His employer uses NetApp and AWS, so he takes the NetApp NCDA and AWS Solutions Architect – Associate within a year, documenting his home-lab practice on a blog that interviewers later ask about.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start with one foundation (CompTIA A+ or a Linux certification) if you are new to IT.
  2. Learn storage concepts in a vendor-neutral course (Dell ISM or SNIA material).
  3. Pick a platform your target employers use: NetApp, Everpure, Dell, VMware, Nutanix or a cloud.
  4. Practise in labs or simulators until tasks feel routine, then book the exam.
  5. Keep certifications current — most expire or need renewal every two to three years.

Who uses it

Job seekers, career changers, administrators seeking promotion and consultants who must show partner credentials pursue these certifications.

Key takeaway

Choose certifications by job adverts in your area: count which platforms appear most often and certify in those first.

Going deeper

  • Performance-based exams such as RHCSA and CKA are hands-on: you configure real systems under time pressure, so lab practice matters more than memorising facts.
  • Vendor programmes are renamed often — Pure Storage became Everpure in 2026 and Broadcom restructured VMware certifications around VMware Cloud Foundation — so always check the vendor's current certification page.
  • Cloud associate exams cover storage heavily: block volumes and snapshots, object storage classes and lifecycle, file services, encryption and backup appear in most domains.
  • The CKA exam includes storage tasks such as creating PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims and StorageClasses and mounting them into pods.
  • Many vendors offer free foundation-level training and discounted exams to students and partners; university academic programmes (for example Dell's and AWS's) can cut costs further.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Collecting many entry-level certificates instead of one deeper one: employers prefer evidence of depth plus hands-on projects.
  • Using exam 'dumps': it breaks vendor rules, can get certifications revoked, and leaves you unable to answer interview questions.
  • Letting certifications lapse: many expire after two to three years unless renewed.
